a-lecture-on-phrenology-as-illustrative-: A Lecture on Phrenology, 1826. The moral capacities. This book preserves that lecture. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
arcandam-or-alcandrin-1626:
Richard Roussat's Most Excellent Booke of Arcandam, or Alcandrin, appeared in English in 1626. Arcandam was said to be an old wise man whose rules could reveal a person's destiny from his birth. The book belonged to a popular line of fortune texts sold across Europe.

Rules and tables let a reader work out character, health, and likely fortune from birth signs and numbers. Added material on physiognomy taught how faces and features could be read for the same ends. Such books were cheap, much used, and often condemned by clergy. This one shows the kind of everyday fate lore that ordinary readers bought long before modern horoscopes.
arxiv-2512-00126:
Protein inverse folding means designing an amino acid sequence that folds into a chosen three-dimensional shape. Jin Han, Tianfan Fu, and Wu-Jun Li present RadDiff for this problem in a 2025 study. The task is a basic step in computational protein engineering.

Existing methods either generate sequences without outside knowledge or lean on protein language models. RadDiff combines retrieval with a denoising diffusion process, pulling in helpful external information while it designs. Better inverse folding tools help researchers design new proteins for medicine and industry, from enzymes to candidate drugs. Retrieval brings proven sequence patterns into the design loop instead of starting from nothing. That habit mirrors how engineers reuse known parts.
arxiv-2512-00226:
Three-dimensional scene understanding is a key skill for AI assistants that operate in the real world. Zirui Wang and Tao Zhang present DenseScan in 2025, work aimed at richer data for that field. Current datasets give geometry and object instances but lack detailed semantic labels.

DenseScan advances scene understanding through dense two-dimensional annotation, adding the rich labels that visual-language tasks need. Better annotations let models connect words to parts of a scene, not just whole objects. Such data could improve robots and assistants that must describe, find, and manipulate things in cluttered rooms. Dense annotation is expensive, which is exactly why a dataset built around it stands out.
arxiv-2512-00326:
Loneliness harms student health, but surveys capture it only after the fact and only when students answer honestly. Qianjie Wu and co-authors predict university students' loneliness scores from smartphone sensing data in 2025. Passive sensing records behavioral signals continuously, without asking anything of the student.

The study looks for behavioral indicators of loneliness in that sensing data. Real-time behavioral context could catch rising loneliness earlier than retrospective self-reports. The work also raises care questions universities must handle well, since sensing data is intimate even when students consent to share it. Smartphone sensing is passive, so students are not asked to keep diaries or wear devices. Prediction, not just description, is the goal the authors set for the data.
arxiv-2512-00526:
Nearby cycles are a tool for studying how a family of geometric spaces degenerates. Pascal Boyer describes filtrations of the perverse sheaf of nearby cycles in the strict semi-stable situation in 2025. The filtrations come from the stratification of the special fiber.

Boyer determines which extensions given by these filtrations split and which do not. Such details control deep invariants in arithmetic geometry, including those behind the local Langlands program and Weil conjectures. The work is technical algebraic geometry, sharpening a machine that number theorists rely on to study degenerating families. Semi-stable reduction is the tame case of degeneration, which is why it is studied first. Perverse sheaves are the coefficient systems that make such filtrations meaningful.
arxiv-2512-00926:
Shulan Li, Jian-Pin Wu, and Xian-Hui Ge build a cosmology model without a beginning singularity in a 2025 paper. In the standard picture, the universe starts from a point of infinite density. Non-singular models try to avoid that breakdown, often by matching the cosmos to a regular black hole, one whose center stays finite.

Their model uses a modified Oppenheimer-Snyder framework, a classic way to join a collapsing or expanding interior to an outside spacetime. They study its dynamics with dust alone and with a scalar field added. They also compare it with two other non-singular models and with standard cosmology. Comparisons show which features are generic.
arxiv-2512-01126:
Jishnu Goswami and Frithjof Karsch compare lattice QCD calculations with collider data in a 2025 physics paper. Their subject is net-baryon number cumulants, measures of how the net count of baryons fluctuates in hot nuclear matter. Fluctuations can signal the change from hadrons to quark-gluon plasma.

The authors compute ratios of higher order cumulants along the pseudo-critical line, where that change occurs in theory. They compare them with STAR measurements from the RHIC beam energy scan program, taken along the freeze-out line where particles stop interacting. Early agreement for one key ratio is reported, with details across collision energies.
arxiv-2512-01226:
Faust, Robinson, and Sottile study graphs that repeat in a grid with no end. Each such graph has an operator, a rule that acts on waves over it. The waves form a shape called the Bloch variety. Points where that shape pinches are called critical points.

The count of those points is the focus here. That count is a step toward a big claim about spectral edges. Past work capped the count by a shape volume tied to the graph. The team shows the cap is not tight when some points drift far off. Their result sharpens how the count can be found.
arxiv-2512-01326:
Omar Farooq Khan Suri and John McCrae study attacks that hide bad orders in prompts. A prompt attack tricks a language model into doing a harmful task. The model just follows words, so sly words can bend it. Wide use of these models makes the risk real.

They review a defense called JATMO. It trains a plain base model to do one task only. A model locked to one task has less room to obey stray orders. The study weighs how well that lock works. It also notes what the lock costs in range and ease of use.
arxiv-2512-01426:
Yiyang Ma and co-authors improve high-resolution image making with diffusion models. Big pre-trained models often fail when asked for images larger than their training size. Layouts collapse and fine texture turns muddy. Past fixes stack complex steps to guide the large output.

The team's appendix text lays out a simpler path. It uses the base-size pass to guide the large pass in a lean way. Clean high-resolution output matters for art, ads, and design tools. A lean fix that keeps layout and texture would be easy for many teams to adopt.
arxiv-2512-02026:
Ultra-short pulse lasers can carve metal and glass with great care, a plus for greener factories. But a flawed part found too late wastes the work. Luis Correas-Naranjo and four co-authors use machine learning in 2025 to watch laser micromachining and catch bad parts early.

Their system is built to work no matter how the stock was prepared first, a common source of change on real shop floors. Early detection guards both the fine quality and the green case for the tool. The study ties learning methods to the daily craft of keeping a high-end process on track.
arxiv-2512-02326:
Some tools split a signal the way a prism splits light, but with math tuned to curves called orthogonal polynomials. Such tools are known as chromatic derivatives. Aleksandar Ignjatović returns in 2025 to his 2009 work on them. He grows it, and he fixes parts of it.

The tools rest on sets of curves that stay orthogonal under set weights. From them come ways to expand a signal and spaces where those expansions live. A clean record counts in this field, since later work builds on the printed forms. Chromatic tools give a second kit for signal work, shaped for uneven samples and curve-based tasks.
arxiv-2512-02626:
S. J. S. de Rooij and B. Hunyadi adapt seizure detection models so they can move between patients or datasets. Transfer learning reuses what a model learned on one task to do better on a related one. Their method uses a tensor kernel machine, a compact model suited to structured brain signal data.

The design borrows an idea from the adaptive support vector machine. Knowledge passes through regularization, which keeps the new model close to the old one where that helps. Efficient transfer matters in epilepsy care, where labeled data per patient is scarce and fast personalization can improve alarm accuracy. Small gains per case add up fast when a ward must screen many new cases each week of the year.
arxiv-2512-02726:
Md Abdul Kadir and three co-authors test language models as fraud hunters in accounting ledgers. Auditors run journal entry tests to flag odd records in tax related books. Rule based tests raise floods of false alarms and miss subtle irregularities.

The team's AuditCopilot investigates whether large language models can serve as anomaly detectors for double entry bookkeeping. A model that reads entries in context might catch patterns rules miss. Smarter screening could focus human auditors on the riskiest records, cutting cost while raising the chance of catching real fraud early. Fewer false alarms means staff time goes to the books that hide real risk, not to noise in the logs.
arxiv-2512-03026:
Saeid Jamshidi and four co-authors propose continuous ethical checking for large language models. Moral consistency means keeping ethically coherent reasoning across varied contexts. Existing alignment frameworks use static datasets and after the fact evaluations, which reveal little about how reasoning evolves.

Ethical behavior can drift as contexts change or time passes, and one time tests miss that drift. The Moral Consistency Pipeline evaluates models continuously instead. Ongoing checks suit deployed systems in support, education, and advice roles, where a slow ethical slide could harm users before anyone notices. Checks that run all the time catch the slow slip. One big test, run once at launch, will miss it by the time the harm shows in use by real folks.
arxiv-2512-03226:
How galaxies move apart from smooth expansion shows gravity at work. C. E. Ross and a large team present a catalog for that study in this 2025 work. It is part of the DESI first data release peculiar velocity survey.

The catalog uses the Fundamental Plane, a relation among galaxy size, brightness, and internal speeds. It covers nearby galaxies with redshifts below a tenth. The authors call it the largest single set of its kind. Such data help measure how fast cosmic structures grow and test dark energy at low redshift. Peculiar velocity data from the plane add an independent route to galaxy distances.
arxiv-2601-06726:
Mohammad Khateri and three co-authors give tools for fetal brain scans in a 2026 paper. Sound-wave scans are safe, cheap, and at hand in most clinics. They suit day-to-day care of unborn babes well, the team notes.

Yet such scans bear flaws that shift with the probe's angle of use. Skill gaps between staff and a small field of view add to the flaws. Sense and counts from the scans thus get hard to make with trust. Their tools merge views from many angles into one full brain view. Merged views could make counts hold up across staff and clinics alike. The work gives real tools, not just a plan on a page. It aims at a scan done vast counts of times each year round the world.
arxiv-2601-06926:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Illia Ovtsynov and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers structure of morse flows and co-dimension one gradient flows on the sphere. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. We describe all possible topological structures of typical one-parameter bifurcations of gradient flows on the 2-sphere with holes.

In the case that the number of singular point of flows is at most six. To describe structures, we separatrix diagrams of flows. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07226:
Seongyun Lee and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with lost in the noise. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Recent advances in reasoning models and agentic AI systems have led to an increased reliance on diverse external information. However, this shift introduces input contexts that are inherently noisy, a reality that current sanitized benchmarks fail to capture.

The authors introduce NoisyBench , a comprehensive benchmark that systematically evaluates model robustness across 11 datasets in RAG, reasoning. Alignment, and tool-use tasks against diverse noise types, including random documents, irrelevant chat histories, and hard negative distractors. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07326: A 2026 arXiv preprint by Huan Li and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers convergence rate analysis of the AdamW-Style shampoo. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The work studies the AdamW-style Shampoo optimizer. An effective implementation of classical Shampoo that notably won the external tuning track of the AlgoPerf neural network training algorithm competition. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07426:
Andrea Colesanti, Lei Qin, and Paolo Salani wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how a curved shape holds as heat spreads. The shape in view is log-concave, which means the log of its height bends down at all points. The flow comes from a parabolic equation. That equation is tied to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, a tool for random drift back to a mean.

The team studies the kernel of that operator, the core that sets the flow. The work is set in a bounded, convex domain. They show that the kernel is log-concave. As a result, a start shape that is log-concave stays log-concave as the flow goes on. The team then gives a new proof of a Brunn-Minkowski type rule. That rule bounds the first eigenvalue of the operator. Past work proved these facts by other means.
arxiv-2601-08026:
Jifeng Song and colleagues present FigEx2, a system that finds and captions each panel of a scientific compound figure. Compound figures pack several labeled panels into one image. In real pipelines, captions are often missing or only summarize the whole figure. Panel-level understanding is therefore difficult. FigEx2 localizes panels and generates a caption for each one, directly from the figure image. Their 2026 preprint describes the visual-conditioned framework.

Panel captions unlock the content of published figures for search and reading tools. Accessibility also gains, since screen readers need panel-level descriptions. Conditioning on the visual layout keeps captions tied to the right panel. The work targets the messy figures found in real journals. The paper serves scholars in document AI and scientific publishing tools. It treats figures as structured content, not decoration.
arxiv-2601-08126: M. Auer and S. Liu study trimmed ergodic sums for systems with exponential mixing. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from the Birkhoff ergodic theorem, which gives pointwise convergence for integrable observables. For heavier-tailed observables, no normalization yields almost sure convergence in the usual sense. The authors instead remove the largest observations and study the trimmed sums. The observables have polynomial tails, with a stated power-law form. Distributional limits for trimmed sums extend ergodic theory to data with extreme outliers, common in finance and climate records.
arxiv-2601-08526: Gouri Lakshmi S and co-authors introduce supervised spike agreement dependent plasticity for spiking networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on spike-timing-dependent plasticity, a biologically grounded learning rule. That rule relies on precise spike timing and pairwise updates, which limit fast weight learning. The new supervised extension swaps pairwise timing checks for population-level agreement metrics such as Cohen's kappa. Agreement across a population can signal a correct response more robustly. Faster local learning could help neuromorphic hardware train on chip with little energy.
arxiv-2601-08926:
Amy Secunda and three co-authors use AI to weigh the height of disks round huge black holes. Light from such a disk rings back with a lag. The lag by hue tells us the span of the disk. The team wants the height as well, which is far more hard to read from lags. A new huge sky survey will soon give rich lag data for many disks.

They train a transformer model, a net that weighs which past points count, on sim lag data. The model learns to read height signs in the lag shape. A reader in space work gets a tool set for the new survey. It may turn lag lists into full disk shapes for a vast set of black holes.
arxiv-2601-09126:
Pratim Guha Niyogi and four co-authors link wrist move data to loss of skill in multiple sclerosis. MS is a nerve ill that can slow walk and hand use. Wrist sensors can track move all day. Past work shows the full spread of move counts beats a plain mean as a health sign. The tail of that spread, rare bursts or long rests, oft holds the key sign.

The team gives one frame for such spreads, called generalized odds. It reads a spread by the odds of move in any zone of counts. Old signs, such as risk and life curves, fall out as cases. A reader in health data gets a joint frame for rich sensor spreads.
arxiv-2601-09326:
Tomoya Takahashi and three co-authors read how a quantum spin chain waves at low heat with grid net tools. Heat states of such chains are hard to hold in a net. Bonds grow fast, and low heat is the worst zone. Past tools use a clean up trick or a few sample states. Both lose truth or scale poor at low heat.

The team grows a state space by parts, with a matrix form for each state. That growth keeps key wave traits while it caps bond size. From the held state they read the wave spread by force and time. A reader in quantum stuffs gets a path to low heat wave facts that past tools could not reach clean.
arxiv-2601-09526:
Zhen-Zhen Zhang, Hua-Lei Wang, Kui Xiao, and Min-Liang Liu probe a long-lived excited state in a nucleus at the edge of stability. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies osmium-160, which sits at the two-proton drip line. The state of interest is a two-quasiparticle isomer with spin-parity 8+.

Recent experiments reported signs that the isomer lasts longer than expected. The authors use configuration-constrained potential-energy-surface calculations to test the claim. The state's structure is tied to neutron orbitals h9/2 and f7/2. Isomers at the drip line reveal how nuclei hold together when protons barely stay bound at all. They are rare probes of nuclear structure under extreme strain.
arxiv-2601-09726:
Hien Tran, Quinten Steenhuis, Alexandros Christoforos, and Chadbourne Davis defend a flaw of language models as a feature. Their 2026 arXiv paper argues that forgetting past evidence mirrors human cognition. Models are often judged against perfect Bayesian inference, which never discounts old evidence.

In practice, the authors note, model updates in context behave like discounted filters that let old evidence fade. That fading resembles how people weigh recent information more. Reframing forgetting as cognitive alignment changes what builders should fix. A model that forgets like a person may interact more naturally than one with perfect recall.
arxiv-2601-09926:
Kirandeep Kaur, Vinayak Gupta, Aditya Gupta, and Chirag Shah study help that comes before a user asks. Most aids wait for a clear request. They work in a ask and reply loop. Needs that users do not state can then be missed.

Some new agents try to act first. One path asks more prompts, which keeps the load on the user. A second path guesses needs from context. That guess can fire at a bad time or add noise. The paper sets tests for this skill. It calls the core task gap finding: spot what the user lacks, and help at the right time.
arxiv-2601-10126:
Chong-long Xie, Guo-yun Shao, Ming-zheng-xuan Wu, and Wei-bo He work out how quark soup resists a squeeze. Quark soup is the hot dense form of matter from the early world. Its flow traits shift as it cools and turns to plain matter. Bulk drag is one such trait.

The team use a move based math with a set rest time. Mass terms come from a model with a loop field for the phase shift. They track bulk drag across the shift range. They also track its ratio to shear drag. Those traits shape how the soup flows in star cores and in lab hits.
arxiv-2601-10426:
Zeping Hao and Meng Fai Lim prove swap rules for big Galois forms over many p power towers. A Galois form tracks how roots of a law link. Big forms hold a whole tower of fields at once. Selmer groups sort the key facts in such a tower.

The team give a broad path to such swap rules. The rules hold in two frames: Selmer groups and Selmer complexes. They span a wide set of Iwasawa type cases. Iwasawa work studies towers that grow by a prime power at each step. Firm swap rules tie the two sides of such a tower.
arxiv-2601-10526:
Adway Girish, Robinson Cung, and Emre Telatar show that plain codes fall short for a shared test task. Two agents see linked bit rows. Each sends a short sum to a core judge. The judge must call which of two world states holds. The agents send at the same rate.

Linear codes are a plain pick for the sums. The team show a plain cut beats all such codes in two cases. One case tests sign of the link. One tests if a link is there at all. The result marks a bound on what linear sums can do.
arxiv-2601-10626:
Getoar Sopa, Marco Avella Medina, and Cynthia Rush work on private statistics for data collected over time. Differential privacy gives a strict way to release results while shielding each person's data. Much work on private linear regression assumes each user gives one data point. Real health and social studies follow the same people for years.

Longitudinal data, with repeated measures per person, break that one-point setup. The authors develop private inference methods for this case. The goal is valid estimates of trends without leaking any one person's record. Their work extends privacy tools to the repeated-measures data that clinics and surveys actually hold.
arxiv-2601-11226:
Bernhard Heim and Markus Neuhauser take up a conjecture of Sun in this work. Their 2026 preprint deals with partitions of whole numbers. A partition splits a number into a sum of smaller parts. The count of such splits is written p of n.

As n grows, the nth root of p of n tends to 1. That fact links to the Cauchy-Hadamard test for power series. Andrews found a basic proof of the key limit as well. The new work turns Sun's claim into polynomial form. That shift is what the title calls polynomization of the claim. Polynomial forms can make growth facts much easier to test.
arxiv-2601-11626:
Maksym Shamrai studies shrinking large sets of matrices by SVD. The 2026 preprint covers joined-matrix SVD in depth. Big matrix sets arise across machine learning and computing. Signal work and science computing add their own sets.

The standard trick concatenates the matrices into one. A truncated SVD then compresses the joined matrix. That enables parameter sharing and efficient reconstruction. Shamrai derives size bounds for the strategy. A step-wise method updates the shrinkage as data arrive. Error-constrained clustering groups matrices under a set error cap. The results serve multi-view learning and network compression. Users gain theory for a widely adopted practice.
arxiv-2601-11926: Ananya Halgatti, Shaunak Biswas, Hiya Bhatt, and their co-authors present a test case for steady machine learning work in the field. Models in use meet shifts in their world over time. With no watch, those shifts can harm output, raise cost, and cut value. Their system, named in the work with a styled title, acts as a self-adaptation exemplar. It is built for the MLOps task of keeping models sound as data drift. A shared exemplar lets teams test their own watch and fix tools.
arxiv-2601-12026:
Muhammad Bayu Saputra, Handhika Satrio Ramadhan, Ibnu Nurul Huda, and Leonardus Brahmantyo Putra study balance points for a third body in a three-body system. Two big bodies move on an elliptic path, and a small third body moves in their field. Extra forces bend that field.

They add radiation pressure, the non-round shape of the main bodies, their stretch, and disk-like forms. Each force can shift where the small body can rest in balance. The team check when those points stay stable. Such maps aid craft paths in real, messy systems.
arxiv-2601-12426:
Mohammadhossein Homaei and four co authors work on safety for water distribution systems. These networks face growing cyber physical risks, from faults to attacks. Spotting anomalies fast is key to limiting harm. Many data driven tools ignore the shape of the network, though. Others that use physics lean hard on exact parameter values.

The team propose a graph attention network that knows the hydraulics. Its features come from breaches of conservation laws, put in normalized form. In plain terms, water that fails to balance flags a problem spot. Graph attention lets the model weigh links between nodes in the network. The work aims for detection that is both sharp and easy to interpret.
arxiv-2601-12626:
Raphi Kang, Hongqiao Chen, Georgia Gkioxari, and Pietro Perona, at Caltech, probe how vision language models reason about space and time. These models can answer questions about where things are and how scenes change. The mechanisms behind that skill remain largely opaque, though. The team start from a simple postulate about how the skill must work.

At some point in the computation, visual and textual views of space must be combined. Geometry from images and words about layout have to meet. The team look for linear mechanisms that do that joining. Finding simple linear structure inside a huge model would be a strong clue. It would suggest that spatial reasoning rests on readable, low level features.
arxiv-2601-13726:
Michael Björklund, Reynold Fregoli, and Alexander Gorodnik study how whole-number solutions spread out in 2026. Their problem sits in multiplicative Diophantine approximation, a field on how well numbers can be matched by fractions. They count the integer solutions to a set form of the problem. The key question is the shape of that count over many cases.

The team shows the counting function tends to a normal law in distribution. In plain terms, its spread acts like a bell curve in the limit. Their proof uses correlations of measures on homogeneous spaces. It also uses bounds for Siegel transforms cut down to subspaces.
arxiv-2601-14226:
Leonardo Placidi and co-authors use deep learning to clean noisy quantum circuit outputs in 2026. Quantum error mitigation corrects noisy output probability distributions from measured circuits. The team presents a systematic investigation of deep learning methods for this task. They compare architectures from fully connected networks to transformers.

They also test different design and training modalities. Sequence-to-sequence, attention-based models were the most effective on their datasets. Learned mitigation could extend the reach of today's noisy quantum machines. It offers a data-driven complement to analytic error correction. The test bed spans many circuit types and noise forms. Wins that hold across that range are more likely to hold on real rigs.
arxiv-2601-14426:
Maximilian Vovk, Peter G. Brown, Denis Vida, and their co-authors weigh tiny space rocks in this 2026 paper. Accurate estimates of meteoroid bulk density matter for a practical reason. Sub-millimeter to millimeter meteoroids form the bulk of the impact hazard to spacecraft. Density tells engineers how much damage a hit can do.

Past studies fit ablation and fragmentation models to optical meteor data by hand or by optimization. The team uses dynamic nested sampling instead, a Bayesian method that explores model space in depth. They apply it to Orionid and Capricornid shower meteors as a case study. Readers get a more rigorous way to infer what shower meteors are made of.
arxiv-2601-14526:
Mengmeng Long and a team of nine co-authors measure magnetic order in a metal in this 2026 paper. Electronic phases of matter, such as magnetism and superconductivity, are defined by their order parameters. An order parameter quantifies the spontaneous symmetry breaking under each phase. The simplest cases are the uniform magnetisation of ferromagnets and the isotropic gap of conventional superconductors.

The team's material is the metallic altermagnet CrSb. Altermagnets are a newly recognized class of magnetic order. The authors determine its bulk-resolved order parameter symmetry in three dimensions. Their title names it g-wave magnetic order. The read is threefold. It checks the bulk, not just the face of the slab, so the call is firm. Readers get a direct read on the symmetry of a phase that textbooks are still absorbing.
arxiv-2601-14726:
Ragheed Alhyder, Rishabh Sahu, Johannes M. Fink, Mikhail Lemeshko, and Georgios M. Koutentakis study light mixing in a microresonator in this 2026 paper. Integrated optical microresonators that exploit second-order or third-order nonlinearities are key platforms. They serve frequency conversion, low-noise microwave photonics, and quantum entanglement generation. The team presents an analytic theory of Kerr-enhanced three-wave mixing amplification.

Their device is an electro-optic microresonator with both second-order and third-order nonlinearities present. Kerr effects come from the third-order response. The title also names emergent masing regimes, states where the device emits coherent microwaves like a laser. The tool is tiny. It sits on a chip, yet it can mix tones in ways that used to need a bench of gear. Readers get theory for a small device with rich mixing behavior.
arxiv-2601-15526:
J. Hermenegildo R. González, Gustavo O. Carvalho, and Fábio P. Machado study the frog model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The frog model is a classic setup in probability. Particles sit on the integer line, each with its own lifetime. Here each particle draws a random survival parameter. Given that parameter, its lifetime follows a discrete Weibull law.

The Weibull form adds a shape parameter that bends the lifetime curve. Particle lifetimes are independent but not identical in this design. The authors study how the model behaves under these rules. Frog models mimic spread, like infection or rumor passing. Changing the lifetime law changes how far and fast the spread runs. Probabilists use such models to test ideas about growth and survival in random media.
arxiv-2601-15726:
Poonam Sharma and Suman Banerjee maximize marketing spread in social networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Firms now use online social networks heavily for viral marketing. The key problem is choosing seed users. A limited set of influential users gets the brand first. If chosen well, their adoption spreads influence widely. If chosen poorly, the campaign dies early. The budget for seeds is limited, so each pick counts.

The authors propose a two-phase diffusion approach, per the title. Splitting diffusion into phases can balance reach with cost. Profit maximization is the stated goal, not spread alone. A wide spread that costs more than it earns is a failure. For marketing science, the paper adds one more method to the seed-selection toolbox.
arxiv-2601-15926:
Aryiadna Yesmanchyk and five co-authors validate a solar physics model outside its training data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Machine learning is spreading through nearly every field, solar physics included. Their model, MagNet, was built for a hard data-mining task. It generates transverse magnetic fields of solar active regions. Those fields are hard to measure directly. A model that fills them in aids many studies.

Out-of-sample validation is the paper's focus. A model can look strong on data like its training set yet fail elsewhere. Testing on truly new data gives the honest score. Solar observations shift with instruments and solar cycles, so robustness matters. The validation tells users where MagNet can be trusted and where it should be doubted.
arxiv-2601-16026:
Dong-Sheng Liu and a large team simplify quantum measurement in a 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum metrology beats classical limits with exotic probe states. Entangled or squeezed states are the usual tools. Preparing them needs careful calibration of system parameters. It also needs finely optimized quantum controls. Those demands limit scalability and robustness in real labs. The authors propose echoed random quantum metrology, per the title.

The name suggests randomness replaces fine tuning. Echoes imply a sequence that undoes errors while keeping the signal. If random probes work, precision measurement gets much easier to run. Sensors for fields, time, and gravity all chase quantum gains. A method that drops the delicate preparation step could move those gains from hero experiments toward routine instruments.
arxiv-2601-16226:
Ixandra Achitouv and David Chavalarias draw a live maths model of view shifts from real feed data. Their 2026 preprint is the first of its kind in this field. They track user views on a yes or no climate topic through time. From the tracks they infer how each view drifts and spreads. Drift and spread are the two parts that drive the model.

The drawn model runs in smooth time, not step time. It can then show how views move and clump. A model drawn from data beats one built from guesses. It can test which feeds push views to poles. The work gives a data based tool for view studies.
arxiv-2601-17026:
Shridharan Chandramouli splits a hard cut task for fast work on many cores. The task finds the least cut twixt two points in a graph. Such cuts drive cuts of 3D scans in care work. Big 3D graphs make lone-core cuts crawl. His 2026 preprint builds a fast path for a clean class of 3D graphs.

Those graphs stack in a set, rank-kept form. The fast path splits the cut hunt across cores. Each core takes a slice of the graph grid. Fast true cuts could speed scan work in clinics. They may also aid chip and net layout tasks.
arxiv-2601-17126:
Ting-Hsiang Hsu and a team of ten co-authors build a base model for collider event data. Deep learn tools now aid work at big colliders. Yet compute caps curb what those tools can do. Their 2026 preprint shares EveNet, a base model for whole events. It pre-trains on half a billion fake events. Two aim types guide that train in one mix.

One aim is self-taught, from the events' own forms. The next aim bakes physics facts in the marks. A shared base can then tune to many tasks. That saves each team a from-scratch train run. Collider labs gain speed on rare-event hunts.
arxiv-2601-17426:
Zhengqing Zang and seven co-authors probe logic in large language models with syllogisms. A syllogism is a short formal argument with two premises and a claim. The probe centers on existential import. That is the old question of whether a general term implies that things of that kind exist. Traditional and modern logic answer it in unlike ways.

Human logic moved from gut feel to formal systems over time. The team asks if models show a like shift. Their tests trace how model answers change across setups. The probe gives a clean lens on machine reasoning. It can show if models hold one logic or mix two. That matters for law and science aids.
arxiv-2601-17526:
Mohammad Atif and co-authors help teams pick GPU portability layers. Graphics processors now supply most high-end compute power. High energy physics uses them for a fast-growing share of tasks. NVIDIA leads the market, but AMD and Intel are gaining. Code must run well on all three. Portability layers promise that reach.

The team evaluates app traits that should drive the choice. Kernel shape, memory use, and team skill all matter. A wrong layer can lock a lab into poor speed. Their guide turns vendor claims into test-based picks. Big science codes live for decades. The layer choice shapes cost for years. This work makes that choice a studied one.
arxiv-2601-17626:
Somphong Jitman and Wannarut Rungrottheera find explicit determinants for polynomial evaluation matrices. The matrices come from homogeneous bivariate polynomials. Each polynomial is a weighted sum of x and y powers. It is evaluated at pairs of vectors to fill the matrix. The authors derive a clean factorization of the determinant.

Explicit forms turn costly numeric work into direct reads. They also expose when the matrix is singular at a glance. Such matrices arise in codes, designs, and interpolation. A factorization can speed all those uses. The work is a tidy result in matrix theory. It gives users a formula where iteration stood before.
arxiv-2601-17726:
Zhe Wei, Zhenzhen Lou, and Changxiang He set spectral conditions for embedding graphs. The signless Laplacian spectral radius, or Q-index, is a key network measure. It has grown central in spectral graph theory. The authors prove new extremal results tied to it. They study graphs that forbid a 4-cycle. They also study star embeddings under the same lens.

Forbidden subgraph rules shape what networks can form. Spectral conditions give fast tests for those shapes. A dedication marks the paper for Professor Eddie Cheng's 60th birthday. Extremal results tell builders the best a network can do. They also mark where phase shifts in structure occur. The Q-index is their chosen gauge.
arxiv-2601-18026:
Pedro Ortiz Suarez and co-authors re-test how well machines can tell one language from another. Their 2026 preprint presents CommonLID, a benchmark for language identification. Telling languages apart is a first step in building multilingual corpora. Yet models still do poorly for many languages, above all on noisy web text. Web text is exactly what trains today's multilingual models, so errors flow downstream.

CommonLID is community-driven and labeled by people. It covers 109 languages in the web domain. A shared, honest benchmark shows where models fail and for whom. It also gives builders a target to improve against. Better language ID means cleaner training data for low-resource languages.
arxiv-2601-18226:
Haotian Li and co-authors present the Yunjue Agent, a system that improves itself while it works. Their 2026 preprint is a technical report. Conventional agents struggle in open-ended settings where tasks keep drifting and supervision is scarce. Static toolsets and offline training fall behind such change. The result is a system whose limits stay rigid and unknown even to itself. The authors propose an in-situ self-evolving paradigm to break that pattern.

The system is billed as fully reproducible and built from a zero start. It evolves in place, in the very setting where it runs. Agents that can grow with their tasks are a major goal of the field. The report lays out the design for others to test.
arxiv-2601-18426:
Mingyao Cui, Qunsong Zeng, and Kaibin Huang set out a theory for a new kind of radio sensor built from excited atoms. Such atoms can sense faint waves with great care and across a wide band. Past work treats each sensor as a plain point that takes waves the same from all sides. That view skips how the state of the atoms shifts from place to place in the gas cell.

The pair of authors and their colleague map how the wave take shifts across the cell. From that map they build the idea of beam forming with a lone sensor. A beam can be steered to one side, so the sensor hears more from that side and less from the rest. A true map of that skill could guide new kit for weak signal work and for fine maps of wave fields.
arxiv-2601-18526:
Yen-An Chen and Ching-Jui Lai study a weak but deep kind of firmness for a class of shapes in maths. The shapes, called Fano shapes, have a twist that makes them key in the maths of form. A firm shape holds its form when its lines are pushed a bit. A strong form of that trait has seen fast gains in the past few years.

The weak form rests on the slopes of lines that lie on the shape. It is more a thing of pure maths, and it is far less known. One old guess says the line set of a key class of such shapes should be firm in the weak sense too. The pair probe that guess and the shapes that may break it. Their work maps where weak firmness holds and where it fails.
arxiv-2601-18926:
Cassie Sevilla, Anna Y. Q. Ho, and many co-authors study six bright, fast, blue flashes in the sky. These events, called fast blue optical transients, rise and fade fast and glow blue at their peak. The team found them in survey data from the Zwicky Transient Facility and tracked them in many colors of light.

Their light curves fall by half in under two weeks, which marks them as an extreme class. Data from radio to X-ray help test what powers such brief, bright blasts. Each new well watched case sharpens the debate on whether stars, black holes, or both drive them.
arxiv-2601-19026:
Andrea Fasoli and six co-authors ask how far tiny number formats can shrink language models. Microscaling formats store blocks of numbers with a shared scale, which lets models compress hard while losing little accuracy. Real gains need hardware that can multiply in the native format and clean up the errors that arise.

The team probes where the finer formats stop helping, as their title asks. Past a point, smaller blocks cost more than they save, or errors grow too fast. Their map of the limits helps chip and model designers pick formats that save memory without giving up quality.
arxiv-2601-19126:
Xi Wang, Parastoo Sadeghi, and Guodong Shi study how entanglement reshapes privacy in quantum systems. Quantum differential privacy gives a strict way to state how much a process hides about its inputs. Classically, correlations between parties are usually seen as a threat to privacy.

Entanglement is the quantum kind of correlation, and its role was not well understood. The team examines how it shapes the local form of quantum privacy. Their findings could cut either way, and knowing which matters for quantum networks where linked particles are shared on purpose, not by accident.
arxiv-2601-19326:
Georg Engelhardt, Dahai He, and JunYan Luo find a limit on measuring chemicals with light that comes from chemistry itself. Spectrophotometry infers how much of a substance is present from how it absorbs light. Photon noise is the known floor on its precision, set by the grain of light itself.

The team shows that chemical reactions add their own floor on top of that. Using a new photon resolved theory, they study a model molecule whose light response depends on its chemical state. Flicker between states blurs the reading. Labs chasing ultra precise measures will have to budget for this chemical noise as well.
arxiv-2601-19526:
Fouad Boutaleb and five colleagues work on a hard problem in mental health care. Major depressive disorder is often judged from what patients say and how doctors rate them. One core sign, called psychomotor retardation, is a slowing of movement and reaction. Doctors still rate this sign mostly by eye, so scores can vary from one clinician to the next.

The team builds a framework that reads walking patterns in three dimensions. It needs no sensors on the body and no contact with the patient. From the gait data it pulls out clear, objective features that describe how the person moves. Such features could give doctors a steadier way to track the slowing over time. The work joins computer vision with everyday clinical care.
arxiv-2601-19826:
Fan Yang, Renkai Ma, Yaxin Hu, and Lingyao Li study how people react when robots are mistreated. As robots enter homes and public spaces, scenes of robot abuse are increasingly witnessed. Whether bystanders care, and how they reason about it, has ethical and design implications. The authors run a mixed-methods study with just over two hundred participants.

They vary how human-like the robot appears and measure participants' moral foundations. Both factors shape reactions to abuse, in what the authors call a dual role. People may condemn the act yet differ in why they care. Findings like these inform how robots should be designed and presented. They also speak to wider debates about kindness toward machines.
arxiv-2601-19926:
Nora Graichen, Iria de-Dios-Flores, and Gemma Boleda review what is known about grammar inside language models. Transformer models handle syntax well in practice, but how they represent it is debated. Interpretability research has attacked the question from many angles. A systematic map of that literature was missing.

Their review covers several hundred articles evaluating the syntactic abilities of transformer models. It organises over a thousand model results across syntactic phenomena and interpretability methods. Patterns emerge about which methods agree and which phenomena are robustly captured. Such stock-taking helps researchers avoid repeating settled experiments. It also highlights where claims about machine grammar rest on thin evidence. The stock take is broad and fair.
arxiv-2601-20126:
Abha Jha, Akanksha Mahajan, and Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan tackle a known flaw of large language models. These models often state false or unchecked claims as if they were facts. The authors ask whether training can teach a model to hold back. Their method rewards the model both for right answers and for saying it does not know.

The team fine-tunes and tests a Granite model under this reward scheme. The training style is called reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. The goal is a model with more intellectual humility, one that stays silent when an answer would be a guess. Such care matters most in factual fields where a wrong answer can do real harm.
arxiv-2601-20626:
D. Tozzi summarizes machine learning approaches for the CYGNO experiment, which hunts dark matter with an optical-readout time projection chamber. The chamber records rare, low-energy interactions as finely resolved scintillation images. Optical readout gives rich shape information, but the images are large, sparse, and megapixel-sized, which challenges real-time triggering and background rejection.

Two complementary learning approaches are described: one for triggering and data reduction, one for telling signal from background. Rare-event searches live or die on this sorting, since the data stream is vast and the true events are few. Most of the stream is noise, and it must be cut fast.
arxiv-2601-20826:
The Euclid Collaboration prepares to read the cosmos with care in this 2026 paper. Euclid is a space telescope built to survey galaxies. Its spectroscopic data will map how galaxies cluster in space. To read that map, scientists must model redshift-space distortions. These distortions arise because galaxy motions stretch the map along the line of sight.

Accurate models are essential to squeeze full value from the data. The team tests three approaches to modeling the effect. They apply them to the power spectrum multipoles of mock galaxies. The mock galaxies emit the H-alpha line, a standard marker. The study is groundwork for the real survey analysis. It helps ensure that Euclid's map of the universe is read without bias.
arxiv-2601-21026:
Louis Grenioux and Maxence Noble explore generators that sample matter at thermal balance. Their 2026 paper studies diffusion-based annealed Boltzmann generators. Sampling such states is a central challenge in statistical physics. Boltzmann generators pair a generative model with a Monte Carlo fix-up step. The fix-up yields unbiased samples from an unnormalized target. Most such generators use classic fix-ups, such as importance sampling.

Those fix-ups carry two burdens. They need tractable likelihoods from the base model. And they scale poorly in high-dimensional, multi-modal targets. The authors weigh the benefits and pitfalls of a diffusion-based design. Annealing eases the path from noise to target in steps. The paper is candid about hopes and limits. It guides physicists who simulate molecules and materials.
arxiv-2601-21526:
Alireza Nadafian, Alireza Mohammadshahi, and Majid Yazdani present a framework that writes and improves programs on its own. Given a goal in plain words and a way to score results, the system cycles through stages. It drafts ideas, writes code, runs it, scores it, and learns from the outcome.

Each loop aims to push a working artifact closer to the stated goals. Grounding the loop in outside knowledge keeps the search from wandering. A modular build lets teams swap parts for their own tasks. The framework targets research and engineering chores where the target is clear enough to measure.
arxiv-2601-21626:
Jinhao Zhang, Yunquan Zhang, Zicheng Yan, Boyang Zhang, Jun Sun, and Daning Cheng fix a paradox in compressing language models. Post-training quantization shrinks models by rounding their numbers. It often shows low rounding error yet high loss, which seems contradictory.

The cause lies in the shape of the loss landscape. A few high-curvature directions are extremely sensitive to small nudges. Errors there cost far more than errors elsewhere. Their method conditions the problem using that curvature map, so rounding avoids the fragile directions. Steadier compression keeps small models accurate enough for real use on modest hardware.
arxiv-2601-21926:
Jinhao Zhang and co-authors try to slim down the networks that teach robots to move. Diffusion-based visuomotor policies learn complex skills from three-dimensional visual input, and they perform strongly. But most designs use an oversized denoising decoder, the part that turns noise into action.

The authors note that more capacity can help denoising, yet evidence suggests it also adds redundancy and noise in the middle feature blocks. Their 2026 preprint uses information filtering, guided by variational regularization, to strip out what the policy does not need. Leaner policies would run faster on robot hardware and react quicker, which matters when a robot arm must correct itself mid-motion.
arxiv-2601-22026:
Constantin Kleinbeck and co-authors render medical volumes fast enough for immersive use. Three-dimensional scans hold rich information about disease, but flat slices force clinicians to rebuild anatomy mentally. Direct volumetric path tracing in virtual reality gives true spatial understanding, yet it is computationally expensive.

The team's 2026 preprint mixes two techniques. Sharp path tracing covers the fovea, the center of vision where detail matters, while smooth Gaussian representations fill the periphery, where the eye notices less. That hybrid foveated approach targets immersive anatomy viewers that stay fluid on real hardware. Better spatial views could help surgeons plan operations and students learn anatomy from real patient data.
arxiv-2601-22226:
Edoardo Latini, Fausto Rossi, and Fabrizio Dolcini set out a new way to build a qubit, the basic unit of a quantum computer. Their 2026 preprint uses the edge states of a thin material that acts as a topological insulator. A Josephson junction and added magnetic atoms complete the setup.

The team shows that spin states in this setup can form a working qubit. They also show that pulses of microwave light can steer the qubit through shifts in its spin states. The plan gives labs a fresh route to test. It may aid work on small, stable quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-22826:
Dart-yin A. Soh builds a model for how photons can create vector mesons, heavy particles of light-matter interaction. The model rests on Regge theory and a soft dipole Pomeron, a tool for describing high-energy scattering. It handles photons with any kind of polarization, round or linear.

The model fits three kinds of data at once: total rates, momentum patterns, and spin patterns for one key meson. Fitting all three pins down its twenty free settings with care. Good models of this process help plan and read particle physics experiments.
arxiv-2601-23026:
Hendrik Suhr, David Kaltenpoth, and Jilles Vreeken separate two kinds of anomaly that are usually lumped together. A value may look wrong because it was recorded badly, while the real process ran fine. Or the process itself may have changed, shifting how data are generated.

Root cause methods that ignore this split can blame the wrong features. Their causal characterization distinguishes measurement errors from mechanism shifts. The distinction matters in factories and hospitals, where a sensor fault and a real failure demand opposite responses. Measurement anomalies and mechanism shifts demand different remedies, which is why telling them apart is operationally valuable.
arxiv-2601-23126:
Pascal Lenzner and Paraskevi Machaira study routing games where each sender sees only its local network. Modern networks mix many autonomous entities, from smart devices to parts of AI systems. Each has a local view and must rely on a local protocol to forward packets.

The authors analyze when greedy routing, always forwarding toward the target, can reach its destination. Selfish local choices can loop or stall in the worst case. Understanding reachability helps design protocols that work without central control. Local views are the realistic constraint, since no device in a vast network can hold the whole map.

bailey-epicurus-extant-remains-1926:
Epicurus taught in his Athens garden in the early third century BCE and wrote a great deal, yet almost all of it is lost. Cyril Bailey gathered all that survives into one Oxford volume in 1926. His edition gives the Greek text with his own English version, along with notes and a critical apparatus.

Inside are three letters, to Herodotus, Pythocles, and Menoeceus, that sum up his physics and his ethics. Next come the Principal Doctrines, forty short sayings, and the Vatican Sayings, found in a single manuscript. Bailey's notes explain the hard points. For English readers of its day, this volume was the standard Epicurus.
barrett-besterman-divining-rod-1926:
William F Barrett, a physicist, and Theodore Besterman published The Divining Rod in 1926, after years of study for the Society for Psychical Research. Their subject was dowsing, the old practice of finding water or metal with a forked rod that twists in the hands. Many well diggers swore by it.

Field tests, case reports, and past records fill the book, along with a study of how the rod moves. The authors looked for trickery, chance, and knowledge of the land that a dowser might not know he had. Their inquiry, among the last big SPR field studies, treats a folk craft with full scientific care.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol1-1826:
François Bernier, a French doctor, spent twelve years in India and served at the court of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb. Volume One of his Travels, in Brock's 1826 translation, reports what he saw between 1656 and 1668. It is the classic European account of Mughal India.

Bernier describes the war of succession among Shah Jahan's sons, the wealth of Delhi, and the habits of the court. He writes as a trained observer of medicine, trade, and religion. His letters home shaped how Europe pictured India for a century. Few early travelers match his mix of access and clear prose.
bernier-travels-mogul-empire-vol2-1826:
Volume Two of Bernier's Travels in the Mogul Empire continues his account of India under Aurangzeb. The French physician had traveled with the court and seen the empire at close range. Brock's translation completes the work in this volume.

The highlight is Bernier's trip to Kashmir with the emperor's camp, a rare early picture of that valley. He also writes on the Ganges delta, Hindu customs, and the burning of widows, which he condemns. His remarks on trade and land rent drew later thinkers on Asia. Together the two volumes remain a prime source on seventeenth-century India.
bible-tyndale-new-testament-1526:
William Tyndale put the New Testament into English and saw it printed in 1526, the first printed English New Testament. He worked from Greek, not Latin, and paid for the work with exile. Church leaders banned his text, yet copies spread fast across England.

Readers get the four Gospels, Acts, the letters of Paul and others, and Revelation. Tyndale wrote in plain, strong English that later Bibles kept. Much of the King James wording starts here. His version changed how English people read Scripture and how English prose sounds. Its cadence rings through church and school to this day.
black-tertiary-man-asia-choukoutien-1926:
Davidson Black, a Canadian anatomist working in China, announced the Choukoutien discovery in Science in 1926. Fossil teeth had come from a cave deposit near Peking, now Beijing. Black saw them as evidence of very early humans in Asia.

He argues Asia may have been a center from which humans spread. The announcement launched the excavations that soon produced Peking Man. Those fossils, later classed as Homo erectus, became world famous. The originals were lost during wartime, adding mystery to the story. Black's short paper opened one of paleoanthropology's great chapters.
bolivian-constitution-1826:
Bolivia's first constitution was adopted in 1826, and it came almost straight from Simón Bolívar's own hand. The Liberator had freed the country that took his name. A congress in Chuquisaca asked him for a charter, and he sent his draft with a famous speech.

The text creates a president who holds office for life, with the right to name his successor. Beside him sit three chambers, including censors charged with guarding morals and the constitution itself. Bolívar argued that a new nation, torn by war, needed a fixed point of authority to survive. Chuquisaca adopted the charter, and Sucre became the first president under it. The lifetime presidency scared many, and the charter lasted only a few years. It remains Bolívar's political last will, written into law.
cather-my-mortal-enemy-1926:
My Mortal Enemy, published in 1926, is Cather's short, pitiless novella of Myra Henshawe, remembered by a younger woman who knew her in youth and in ruin. Myra had given up a fortune to elope with Oswald Henshawe for love.

Years later the couple live poor and diminished, and Myra's bitterness turns on the man she chose. Her dying words name him her mortal enemy. Cather strips the elopement romance to the bone in barely a hundred pages. The late style here is bare, hard, and unforgettable, among the most perfect things she wrote in fiction.
churchward-lost-continent-mu-1926:
Colonel James Churchward claimed a lost continent, Mu, once filled the Pacific Ocean. His 1926 book The Lost Continent of Mu calls it the motherland of man. He said old tablets in India taught him its story.

Churchward describes a rich, wise land that sank in a great quake. Its people, he argues, seeded Egypt, India, and the Americas. Maps, symbols, and stone marks serve as his proof. Scholars reject the tale for lack of hard evidence. Yet the book became a fringe classic, still read by seekers of lost worlds.
cia-0000009726:
A Neo Lao Hak Sat weekly bulletin, carrying photographs and details of American prisoners, leads an October 1971 CIA item. Neo Lao Hak Sat was the Pathet Lao's political front in Laos. Its bulletin was propaganda meant for Lao readers, yet it printed real captives' faces.

Enemy publications became unlikely sources for the prisoner accounting. A photograph in a propaganda sheet could prove a man alive and held. Analysts therefore read the other side's press with close, hostile care. This file records that practice: a weekly bulletin mined for names, faces, and dates the enemy never meant to give.
cia-0000009926:
Prison camp bunkers were being built for two American pilots captured in a place the title cuts off, a March 1972 item reports. Bunkers mean digging for permanence and protection from air attack. Captors who build for two named-value prisoners expect to hold them long.

Construction reports revealed the prison system's growth from the ground up. New bunkers also signaled where bombing could endanger the very men it meant to pressure. Officials logged the site for both reasons. This file preserves the building report as received, an entry in the strange architecture of captivity in the war's last year.
cia-0000012426:
The Penkovsky memoirs occupy a CIA paper from May 1963, as the spy's story moves toward print. The colonel was then on trial in Moscow, or just condemned by it. His papers and debriefings were being shaped into a book the agency had a hand in preparing. The file's literary turn had begun while its subject still faced a Soviet court.

The paper weighs the memoir as a publishing proposition, with editors and censors in its future. Such books carried a secret case into public argument. For readers, the memo shows the story's second life being planned before its first life had fully ended.
cia-0000012826:

Stalin was two years dead, and his successors were testing new lines abroad while building rockets and bombs at home. The estimate weighs Soviet strength across the board, from divisions to diplomacy.

The mid-fifties balance it strikes set a baseline for a generation of defense planning. It measures the bear's strength at the Cold War's heightening. For readers, the estimate shows the superpower contest being priced, in forces and intentions, by the men charged with knowing.
cia-0000013226:
Viet Cong policy toward American prisoners gets a full study in a CIA paper from September 1969. By then the southern doctrine had years of hard practice behind it. The paper compares the south's rules with Hanoi's rules. It marks the telling differences between the two systems. The south's camps were poorer and more mobile. They were often harsher too, run by cadres closer to the fighting and farther from any capital's control.

The study shows the system's southern face in its own terms. Policy in the jungle answered to local war more than to doctrine. For readers, the paper explains why captivity in the south was its own ordeal.
cia-0000013926: American pilot prisoners were put on parade in Hanoi, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1969. Parading captives through the capital was a show for crowds and cameras. Inside, his account walks through the days before the murders. Warnings, fears, and pressures take shape in his telling. Such testimony later mattered to investigators and historians alike. clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-1:
Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, was Charles I's closest adviser through the English Civil War. His History of the Rebellion tells that war from inside the king's council. The history was published in 1702 to 1704, after his death. Volume one here opens the Oxford edition of 1826, which runs to eight volumes.

Clarendon blends memoir with history: he knew the actors, sat in their councils, and weighed their characters. His portraits of the age's great men remain famous for their shrewdness and grace. The royalist cause has no fuller or finer advocate. Volume one begins the grandest English narrative of the civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-2:
Volume two continues Clarendon's History of the Rebellion in the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his own years at the heart of royalist power, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. The work runs to eight volumes in this edition, each thick with council, camp, and character.

Clarendon's strength is the portrait: friend and foe alike stand forth as living men with mixed motives. He defends the king's cause while blaming royal errors with striking candor. The narrative carries the war's early campaigns in stately, rolling prose. For the inner story of Charles I's court at war, no source stands beside Clarendon. Volume two deepens that story.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-3:
The Oxford edition of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion reaches volume three of eight. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, had served Charles I as chancellor and chief counselor before exile and disgrace. His history, published in 1702 to 1704, grew from notes and memory gathered across a lifetime in high politics.

Volume three holds the war's middle passage, where negotiation and battle chased each other year by year. Clarendon writes with a minister's grasp of paper, money, and men. His judgments on the great figures of the age shaped how later centuries saw them. The book is at once a royalist brief and a work of literature, and this volume keeps both alive.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-4:
Volume four of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion follows the Oxford edition of 1826, though this volume comes from the 1827 printing of the same edition. Edward Hyde wrote the history from his place in Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes. The 1826 scan from Toronto could not be had, so the matched 1827 printing serves.

The fourth volume stands mid-war, where Clarendon's double gift shows best: narrative of events and portraits of the men who drove them. His account of the king's cause is partisan, learned, and deeply felt. No other royalist history matches its access or its art. The set reads whole with this volume in its proper place.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-5:
Volume five continues the 1826 Oxford Clarendon, the History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde wrote the work across his years of power and exile, and it appeared in 1702 to 1704 in eight volumes in this edition. Few historians have written about events in which they played so large a part.

That nearness gives the narrative its weight: decisions of the king's council are told by a man who sat in it. Clarendon's measured prose hides strong feeling for the lost royalist cause. His character sketches, generous and severe by turns, remain models of the art. Volume five carries the war toward its end, with the council chamber always in view.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-6:
Clarendon's History of the Rebellion moves through volume six of the Oxford edition of 1826. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, began the history during the war itself, at the urging of friends who saw it slipping into legend. The published work of 1702 to 1704 fills eight volumes in this edition.

The later volumes trace the royalist cause through defeat, exile, and the long wait for restoration. Clarendon never writes as a mere partisan: he scores his own side's blunders with care. His great gift, the lifelike portrait, stays sharp to the end. Readers meet the English Civil War here as tragedy told by a chief actor. Volume six keeps that telling grave and full.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-7:
Volume seven of the 1826 Oxford edition brings Clarendon's History of the Rebellion near its close. Edward Hyde wrote the history as the chief minister and counselor of Charles I, and its publication ran from 1702 to 1704. The eight-volume Oxford set is the classic form of the work.

In these later pages the war's outcome is sealed, and Clarendon turns to judgment: of men, of measures, of the causes that ruined a kingdom. His prose keeps its stately balance even in bitterness. No other royalist source matches his access to the king's mind and councils. Volume seven holds the penultimate share of the greatest memoir-history of the English civil wars.
clarendon-history-of-the-rebellion-vol-8:
Volume eight completes the Oxford edition of 1826 of Clarendon's History of the Rebellion and Civil Wars in England. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, wrote the work from inside Charles I's council, and it was published in 1702 to 1704. Eight volumes hold the whole of his vast, personal history.

The closing volume ends the story of a kingdom torn apart and a cause lost and, in time, restored. Clarendon's portraits and judgments set the terms in which the civil wars were debated for two centuries. His book stands as the great royalist memoir-history, literary and documentary at once. To close volume eight is to finish the fullest inside account of England's great rebellion.
constitution-barbados-2026: Barbados' Constitution, reformed toward republic status, frames its island state. It cut the Crown in 2021. The Tower library holds the full text. It crowned a republic. Queen left. President rose. People chose. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
constitution-kazakhstan-2026: Kazakhstan's 1995 Constitution, amended through 2026, frames its republic. It renamed the capital twice. The Tower library holds the full text. It ordered the steppe. Soviets left. Oil flowed. Power centered. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well. More detail helps readers grasp the key points well.
cooper-last-of-the-mohicans-1826:
James Fenimore Cooper published The Last of the Mohicans in 1826, the second Leatherstocking tale and his most famous book. Cooper set it in 1757, during the French and Indian War, around the fall of Fort William Henry. He claimed the story grew from a visit to Lake George with British tourists.

Hawkeye, the white scout raised beside the Mohicans Chingachgook and his son Uncas, guides two sisters through a war-torn forest. The Huron villain Magua pursues them with patience and hatred. Captures, rescues, and massacres follow across glens and caverns Cooper made iconic. The title's tragedy gathers force as the old order of the forest dies with Uncas. The novel became the archetypal American adventure and the most translated early American book.
cross-true-masonic-chart-1826:
Jeremy L Cross published The True Masonic Chart in 1826, and it became a well known American guide to lodge ritual. Cross was a traveling Masonic teacher who helped spread a shared form of work across many lodges. His chart used pictures as memory aids for members.

Rows of symbols, tools, and scenes, called hieroglyphic emblems, helped Masons recall the lessons of each degree. The text around them gave the order and sense of the ritual without printing every secret word. For historians, the chart shows how American Masonry taught itself, and how pictures carried meaning that words alone were not meant to hold.
cummings-is-5-1926:
E. E. Cummings published is 5 in 1926, his second major collection of poems. By then his experiments with broken lines, scattered type, and lowercase letters were becoming famous. He divided the book into sections that move from satire to love poems.

The best-known piece here, anyone lived in a pretty how town, tells a whole life in a few musical, looping lines. Other poems mock politicians and professors, then soften into tender songs about lovers and seasons. Cummings plays with grammar the way jazz musicians play with rhythm. The collection shows him at his most beloved and most daring at once.
defoe-history-of-the-devil-1726:
Daniel Defoe, the English writer of Robinson Crusoe, published his History of the Devil at London in 1726. The full title adds 'as well ancient as modern,' and the book runs in two parts. Defoe treats Satan as a figure with a long public career.

He traces the devil through the Bible, Milton's Paradise Lost, the Crusades, and the age of witch trials. Then he jokes that Satan has moved on to softer prey: fine ladies, wits, and fools of fashion. The result is part history, part satire, and pure Defoe.
defoe-political-history-of-the-devil-172:
Daniel Defoe, the novelist of Robinson Crusoe, published The Political History of the Devil in 1726. The book traces Satan's career from the Fall through the witchcraft panics of Defoe's own recent past. It is the great Augustan synthesis of demonology and skepticism, belief and doubt in one shrewd mind.

Defoe mocks credulous tales of pacts and apparitions while still treating the Devil as a real political schemer in human affairs. He sorts scripture, history, and street gossip with a journalist's nose for a weak story. The result reads like a skeptical sermon, funny and unsettling by turns.
