All the Sad Young Men, published in 1926, is Fitzgerald's third story collection, written at the height of his Jazz Age fame. Its title sets the tone: youth, money, and the sadness underneath both, in America after the war.

'The Rich Boy' studies a wealthy man whose money has deformed his capacity to love. 'Winter Dreams' follows Dexter Green's longing for Judy Jones and the world she stands for, and 'Absolution' turns to a boy and a priest in Minnesota. Fitzgerald's prose is at its most polished here, glamorous and quietly bleak. The stories remain his elegies for a generation.
ford-man-could-stand-up-1926:
A Man Could Stand Up, published in 1926, is the third volume of Ford's Parade's End. It opens on Armistice Day in London, the guns stopped at last, crowds half joyful and half lost, and Christopher Tietjens waiting in a silent office.

A telephone call from Valentine Wannop cuts through years of honor, pride, and paralysis, and Tietjens must finally choose his life. Around him, old scores are settled and the wartime world dissolves into parties and wreckage. Ford renders the day in rushing, broken impressions. The volume is the sequence's reckoning, long delayed and quietly immense.
fortune-secrets-of-dr-taverner-1926:
Doctor Taverner heals minds by means no common clinic knows, in Dion Fortune's tales of 1926. The Secrets of Dr. Taverner gathers her occult detective stories in one book. A young doctor tells the cases of his strange chief, case by case.

Each tale turns on a haunting, a curse, a past life, or a soul out of place, solved by Taverner's art. Fortune drew on her nursing years and her occult work alike. The tales teach her ideas while they thrill and chill the reader. The book founded the psychic doctor line of occult fiction.
franck-kabbalah-sossnitz-1926:
Adolphe Franck, a French Jewish philosopher, published La Kabbale in 1843, the first modern critical history of Jewish mysticism. I. Sossnitz gave it English form in 1926, in a revised and enlarged edition. Franck wrote when scholars still treated the Kabbalah as a late fraud or a curiosity, and he took it seriously as philosophy.

He traces the Zohar and its doctrines of God, the sefirot, and the soul, and weighs its kinship with Plato, Philo, and the Gnostics. His calm method opened the field that Gershom Scholem would later rule. The book stays the gate through which the modern West entered the study of Kabbalah. Sossnitz brought Franck's French up to date for English readers.
free-masons-accusation-and-defence-1726:
The Free-Masons Accusation and Defence, printed in London in 1726, gathers six genuine letters for and against the Craft. It is the earliest printed controversy over Freemasonry. The letters appeared four years before Prichard's famous exposé, when the young Grand Lodge was still a novelty in London life.

Writers accuse the lodges of secrecy, drinking, and plots against church and state. Defenders answer with the Craft's charity, antiquity, and harmless good fellowship. Both sides write for a curious public that knew little of the new society. The pamphlet catches the long public debate over the lodges at its first page. Every later Masonic quarrel in print follows the path these letters opened.
frus-1861-d126:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 30 May 1861, the same day Seward wrote to him. The dispatch is document 126 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The crossing of letters was the rule of the age, not the exception. Dayton reported Paris as Seward drafted fresh orders in Washington. Their same day pages show two men steering one tie from its two ends, each half blind. Half blind work was the norm, and the men who thrived in it were the patient ones. Patient men were the ones whose letters fill this record from end to end.
frus-1861-d226:
One more voice from abroad reached Washington on 2 July 1861: Mr. Fay writing to Seward. It was printed as Document 226 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d26:
Writing on 21 June 1861, William H. Seward addressed his minister in Belgium, Henry Sanford. The letter is document 26 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

June letters from Washington carried the weight of a capital now at war in earnest. Seward kept his envoys close with frequent, plain direction. For Sanford in Brussels, this letter was one more pull on the rein, keeping his busy post aligned with the line set at home. By June the first shock of war had passed, and Seward's letters turn to the craft of holding ground. Holding ground abroad was less grand than winning it, and just as hard.
frus-1862-d126:
In a letter dated 13 August 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 126 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d226:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent William Stuart a letter on 18 August 1862, printed as Document 226 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The exchange between the two men fills the summer stretch of the British file.

By mid-August the second campaign toward Manassas was under way, and foreign capitals were again asking if the Union could hold. A Confederate raider, the Alabama, had also just slipped out of a British yard, to Seward's anger. Letters of this date belong to a season when every Union reverse raised the price of keeping Europe neutral. The channel stayed open through the whole war, which was itself a kind of success.
frus-1862-d26:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 6 March 1862. It was printed as Document 26 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d326:
On 13 September 1862 William L. Dayton sent another report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, printed as Document 326 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Reports on back-to-back days mark a busy week at the legation.

The Paris legation wrote often that month because French policy was in motion: a truce proposal was being readied for London's approval. Dayton tracked its drafting as best an outsider could. His reports of 12 and 13 September together give Washington's view of the scheme just before Antietam undercut it. A steamer's sailing day set the legation's week, and Dayton wrote against that clock. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d426:
On 26 August 1862 Horace J. Perry reported from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is Document 426 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department's annual printed record.

Perry wrote in the week of the second battle of Bull Run, though the news had not yet crossed the ocean to him. His subject was Spain: its court, its Cuban interests, and its cooling part in the Mexican expedition. Reports written in this calm, regular style were how the State Department learned the world in wartime. Together with Seward's replies, they show a working legation doing its quiet part for the Union cause.
frus-1862-d526:
On 21 November 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this closing instruction to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. It is Document 526 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the last Hague order in the year's file.

The year's Dutch correspondence ends as it ran throughout: businesslike, frequent, and frank. Through Pike, Washington had kept a trading nation's friendship in repair, settled its port questions, and read its opinion week by week. The Hague file is one of the volume's quiet successes, since nothing dramatic happened there, which was the point. Seward's final November order rounds off a record that shows diplomacy as steady maintenance rather than crisis alone.
frus-1862-d626:
Edward Joy Morris at Constantinople received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 June 1862. The instruction is Document 626 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

June orders to the Ottoman capital joined the general round in which Seward kept every post, however remote, on the government's line. At Constantinople the war mattered chiefly as it touched American trade and the safety of American residents and missionaries in the sultan's lands. Morris, an old Levant hand, needed little guidance on local form, which made his instructions from home mostly a matter of policy. The dispatch keeps the Turkish file moving through the year's middle.
frus-1863p1-d126:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 23 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 126 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening a late-March run of Seward letters.

Seward wrote as the ship question in Britain came to a boil. His letters told Adams how far to push the British on the warships in their yards. Tone counted as much as claims, since a proud court could dig in if pressed wrong. This letter sets the line for the week's work. It shows the secretary guiding his envoy's hand at a sharp point in the talks.
frus-1863p1-d226:
A dispatch dated 2 July 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 226 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d26:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 January 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume bears the same date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 26 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Early January brought London's first takes on the freedom edict, and Adams's mail weighed them for Washington. He reported how the British press and public met the news that the war now aimed at slavery's end. This dispatch is part of that first read. It shows the legation doing its core work: telling home the truth about a great power's mood.
frus-1863p1-d326:
One of Lord Lyons's regular notes to the State Department, this paper to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 24 November 1862. It appears as document 326 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d426:
Writing on 27 March 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington addressed William H. Seward, the Secretary of State in an official letter. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d526:
Secretary William H. Seward directed a letter to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons on 22 May 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d626:
A letter of 30 September 1863, from William H. Seward to William Stuart, stands as document 626 in the printed record. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Stuart was holding the British legation in Washington while Lord Lyons was away on leave, so the channel ran through him that season.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d126: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 14, 1943, while the president crossed the Atlantic under radio silence. The message is Document 126 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Letters sent to a ship at sea in wartime traveled by secure channels and waited for safe moments to land. The record gives the date and the two names. The message is part of the Foreign Relations series' voyage papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d226:
A short secret memorandum from the Joint Chiefs of Staff, written aboard the Iowa on 17 November 1943, is labeled for the President's confidential information only. It gives Roosevelt a fallback plan on European command, in case the British chiefs turn down the unified command scheme in Enclosure A.

If that happens, Roosevelt should go straight to Churchill and refuse committee control of closely linked operations, saying America will take fair risks but not avoidable losses of lives and resources. The striking offer follows: though most forces will in time be American, Washington would accept a British overall commander, provided the man named is Sir John Dill. Failing agreement, Eisenhower would stay in the Mediterranean.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d26: Wilson Brown, the President's naval aide, wrote to Edwin Watson, the President's military aide and secretary, on August 25, 1943. The staff note is Document 26 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Aides like Brown and Watson handled the paper, travel, and messages around Roosevelt, and their notes keep the machinery of the summits running. The catalog's older note supplies the date its title lacks. Its errand is a matter for the printed text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d326:
James Landis, director of economic operations in the Middle East, sent Harry Hopkins a letter and memorandum at Cairo on 26 November 1943, prepared at Ambassador Harriman's request. Its subject is consumer goods in Iran, where the Allied supply corridor to Russia met a strained local economy.

Landis argues the problem is distribution, not absence of goods. Some 80,000 tons of consumer goods, food apart, sat in Persian warehouses at the start of 1943. Thousands of tons still lay piled at Gulf ports. More goods were stacked behind Tehran bazaar shops at prices beyond reach. Flooding the market would need tonnage the Allies do not have. Trucks tell the same story: of some 400 Lend-Lease trucks in Tehran, he saw 83 in one yard laid up for want of repair and management, not parts.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d426:
F. D. W. Brown, Churchill's assistant private secretary, sent Harry Hopkins a most secret, most immediate covering note at Cairo on 2 December 1943. At the Prime Minister's instruction, it passes two British telegrams from Ankara about bringing Turkey's president to Cairo.

The first, of 1 December, reports Foreign Minister Numan raising a meeting himself. He warned of serious difficulties over Cairo. He suggested Aleppo instead, since the Turkish party would not agree to the president flying. The second, of 2 December, carries the conditions. Inönü will not come if the visit merely informs him of decisions already taken with Stalin at Tehran. He will come, gladly, for a free, equal, and unprejudged discussion. The subject is how Turkey can best serve the common cause. He would leave on 3 December with a party of fifteen, twenty-five to thirty travelers in all.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d526:
George Wadsworth, the American diplomatic agent in Lebanon, reported to Secretary of State Hull on December 22, 1943. Wadsworth served in Beirut, where Lebanon had just passed through its November independence crisis with France. The State Department printed his report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Lebanon's new government was finding its feet while French, British, and American interests all pressed upon it. Wadsworth's reporting told Washington how the small republic was settling after its dramatic birth. For readers, the message continues a story the volume opened with Roosevelt's letter to President al-Khouri: a new Arab state emerging from the mandate system in the middle of a world war.
frus-1944-quebec-d126:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent this personal, top-secret cable from Moscow to Harry Hopkins on September 9, 1944. He warned that Soviet-American relations had taken a startling turn in the last two months. Moscow was holding up American requests with complete indifference, he wrote, and refusing even to discuss pressing problems.

Harriman listed stalled requests: the Frantic shuttle-bombing program, photo-reconnaissance flights, trucks for air forces in China, and a bombing survey at Ploesti. He argued that Soviet policy was hardening into forcing acceptance of all its positions, backed by Red Army prestige. His remedy was a firm but friendly quid pro quo. He asked to report to the president in person.
frus-1944-quebec-d226:
Roosevelt sent this message to Prime Minister Mikołajczyk from Quebec on September 11, 1944. It answered the Polish leader's two desperate appeals of the previous day about Warsaw. The whole text is two sentences, and it commits the president to urgency without naming any specific operation or date.

"I want to assure you that we are taking every possible step to bring Allied assistance as speedily as possible to the Warsaw garrison," Roosevelt wrote. "I realize fully the urgent importance of this matter." The message was sent through the White House Map Room and naval channels to London. Behind it, as Hopkins's telegram shows, military planning with the Russians was only just being set in motion.
frus-1944-quebec-d26:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 19, 1944, answering through the personal channel the two men kept open. Hopkins rarely wrote at length unless the matter counted. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

By August 19 Paris was about to rise and the southern France landings had succeeded, clearing the way for the Quebec Conference to take up the endgame. Hopkins's message belongs to the arranging and aligning that made the summit possible. For readers, it shows the President's right hand at work between capitals, three weeks before the leaders met in Canada.
frus-1945-50-intel-d126: A memorandum for the record, dated 19 August 1946, fixes another moment of the summer's intelligence fight in writing. It falls a week after the National Intelligence Authority's ruling week on the Latin American question, on the same day Hoover wrote directly to Vandenberg. Notes of this kind were an officer's way of making sure the file, and not just memory, carried what had been said or done. No author is named in the title.
frus-1945-50-intel-d226:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a memorandum to the National Security Council on 10 October 1947. It is document 226 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. It was the first autumn of the new system: a fresh CIA, a fresh Council, and piles of first-year business.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d26:
Secretary of the Navy Forrestal wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 13 October 1945. The two service secretaries exchanged several papers that autumn as the intelligence question ripened. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Forrestal was among the most thoughtful men in the cabinet on intelligence, and his letters repay close reading. Writing to Patterson kept the two military departments in step against both the State Department's ambitions and the Budget Bureau's knife. Readers can follow the Forrestal and Patterson thread as the military side of the negotiation taking shape. This letter comes early in that thread, when the services were still sounding each other out.
frus-1945-50-intel-d326:
A memorandum dated 28 October 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Acting Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The State Department prints it as document 326 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By law the CIA now stood where the Central Intelligence Group had stood, and the National Security Council sat above it.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d426:
On 13 January 1948 the National Security Council issued its Intelligence Directive No. 3. The text is document 426 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Issued the same day as Directive No. 2, it formed part of a matched pair of standing orders. The Council was learning to run a system no single department could own. For readers, the directive shows coordination itself becoming a formal duty, written down and signed off at the top. Paired issue on one day let the agencies take both orders as a single frame for their work.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d126:
H. Freeman Matthews warned Stettinius on 4 November 1944 not to take Morgenthau's latest paper too seriously. His short secret note, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, concerns the critique of the British draft directive that Morgenthau had handed to Lord Cherwell.

The paper could be most disturbing, Matthews writes, if the British were likely to take it seriously, which he doubts. He reports that McCloy did his best to talk Morgenthau out of giving it to Cherwell at all. So the claim of War Department approval, he notes, is not entirely accurate. He adds that Morgenthau means to get back into the German picture in a big way after the elections, unless the President calls him off.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d226:
Trade barriers are the burden of this briefing book paper of 26 January 1945. “Discussions Concerning Post-War Trade Policy” deals with Article VII of the mutual-aid agreements. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume among the papers prepared for the President's trip.

In Article VII, the paper recalls, the United States, Britain, and Russia pledged early joint action to cut trade barriers. The pledge sits inside a wider program for full employment and a growing exchange of goods. It props up everything else: the Monetary Fund, the International Bank, and repayment of the great loans to come. Technical talks with the British went well in late 1943, but London shows no eagerness to resume. Unless the President presses Churchill in person, the paper warns, the whole foreign economic program may be undermined.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d26: Churchill answered on 27 November 1944, one day after Roosevelt's message, in a letter filed as document 26. It belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta published by the Department of State. The quick turnaround reflects how the two leaders worked: personal, written, and fast, with their staffs expected to act on whatever the latest cable from either capital said.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d326:
Secretary Stettinius sent President Roosevelt a list of suggested action items on February 2, 1945, as the party neared Yalta. First came the world body: win adoption of the American plan for voting in the new United Nations. Then announce at once the calling of a general United Nations conference.

Stettinius laid out the argument in the President's own talking points. Enforcement action would need a united vote of the great powers, but no party to a quarrel should block mere discussion. Small states, he warned, would lose faith if debate itself could be vetoed. The memo is a coach's card, written for the biggest game of Roosevelt's presidency.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d426:
Trusteeship's limits are penciled into this short paper of February 9, 1945. The text, passed by Roosevelt and Churchill during a break in the plenary, sets out where territorial trusteeship would apply. Three groups only: old League of Nations mandates, land taken from the enemy in this war, and any land placed under trusteeship by choice.

Which lands in those groups would in fact be trusteed was left for later talks. No named lands would be debated now, or at the United Nations meeting. Only the rules and the machinery would be written into the charter. The paper kept a vast question safely small, so the talks could move.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d126:
Washington asked Murphy to look after the delegation's rooms in an extract of a telegram dated July 6, 1945. The extract is document 126 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The delegation had sent its needs for office and living quarters through the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

The surviving lines ask Murphy to use his good offices with the military authorities so the accommodations turn out as satisfactory as possible. The message went over Secretary Byrnes's name, drafted by Charles Yost, the delegation's secretary general. Small as it is, the note shows that even housing for the Secretary of State's party had to be chased through channels in a ruined city where the Soviets held the ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d226:
Under Secretary Grew sent Truman a long study of world communism in a covering memorandum dated June 27, 1945. The memo and the summary of its enclosure form document 226 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Grew says the paper rests on long study and intensive research, and that Truman should read it before meeting the other heads of government.

The study traces how the American communist movement softened its program in 1944, renaming itself the Communist Political Association and preaching class collaboration. With the European war ending, it says, the movement turned to attacking officials as anti-Russian. The French party's Jacques Duclos then publicly attacked the American party's softer line in May 1945. The paper's title asks whether a revived Communist International and extreme leftist activity might follow, and what that would mean for the United States.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d26:
The Far East led the third Kremlin conversation, on May 28, 1945, in Bohlen's memorandum. Hopkins proposed they begin by exploring the war against Japan. General Marshall and Admiral King, he said, would find it most helpful to know the approximate time of Soviet entry into the Pacific war. Stalin answered from the Yalta agreement.

The Soviet armies, he said, would be ready within two to three months after Germany's surrender. In the main, they stood as agreed. Other subjects crowd the heading: Germany's war criminals, prisoners of war, food, and dismemberment. The memorandum pins the Pacific timetable to a promise, six weeks before the Red Army moved.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d326:
Kennan, the American chargé in Moscow, reported silence on July 14, 1945, in the Safehaven fight over enemy assets abroad. The embassy had sent the Foreign Office notes on April 30 and June 18 about freezing German and satellite holdings. No reply had come, and no wish to discuss the matter either.

Kennan judged that Moscow would keep refusing a general freeze of state as well as private assets, short of strong pressure. The Soviet aim, he wrote, was the widest power to dispose of these funds. Private assets blocked under Control Commissions suited Moscow, since Russians ran those commissions and could guard their own grip on the money.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d426:
American coal policy for Germany is confirmed in a cable to Blaisdell in London dated July 4, 1945. It repeats a letter from Clayton, written after a June 28 meeting in his office. Department men, the Foreign Economic Administration, the War Department, and the American side of the Combined Production and Resources Board had agreed several aspects of policy there.

The policy aimed to stimulate German coal production for export, and to settle how exportable coal would be shared. Soviet participation in the German coal export program, Clayton writes, would be sought at the forthcoming Berlin conference. The cable confirms the points Blaisdell was specifically asked to act upon in London.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d526:
Baltic nationals among the displaced persons are protected in a briefing book extract dated July 2, 1945. It quotes the Yalta Agreement's first article. All Soviet citizens freed by forces under American command, it says, will be separated from enemy prisoners of war. They will be kept apart in camps. Then they will be handed over to the Soviet authorities at agreed places, without delay.

The extract then draws the American line. The United States has never recognized the Soviet republics of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania, nor Soviet action in Polish territory east of the Curzon Line. The Yalta Agreement, in Washington's reading, applies only to persons recognized as Soviet citizens when it was made. Baltic citizens are therefore not considered subject to it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d626:
Ralph Davies, deputy petroleum chief for war, wrote to Edwin Pauley in Moscow on July 13, 1945. His secret letter is document 626 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It voices sharp frustration over East European oil.

Davies says the Allied oil program for the next year to eighteen months is very tight. He cannot grasp why the oil of Rumania, Austria, and Hungary should be monopolized by the Russians. U.S. and British firms, he notes, own a large share of the oil and the plants there. The United States also still ships much oil to Russia itself. An attached memo gives the volumes at stake. They look small next to world totals, he admits, but the Allies run with no margin at all, so every barrel counts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1026:
Donald Heath, director of political affairs for the American Control Council group, wrote this secret memorandum on July 21, 1945. It weighs two plans for a separate Ruhr-Rhineland state. An American study imagined French, Belgian, and Dutch supervision under the world security body. A Soviet oral proposal, by contrast, would set the state up at once under all four powers.

Heath lists reasons against committing now. A separate state clashes with treating Germany as one economic unit. Excluding Russia would license her grip on eastern Germany. Accepting her plan gives her Upper Silesia plus a Ruhr voice, something for nothing. Imposed partition, he adds, would stir the very nationalism re-education hopes to cure.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1126:
Emory Land, the War Shipping Administrator, joined his aide Morse in this message to Acting Administrator Conway on 21 July 1945. Land ran the agency that built and sailed America's wartime merchant fleet. The note moved inside that agency while the Potsdam talks went on abroad.

Shipping was the war's lifeline. Hulls carried troops, guns, food, and fuel across both oceans, and the fleet's work did not pause for a summit. With Germany beaten, the fleet faced new tasks: bringing men home and feeding freed Europe. An office note like this one kept that machine in order. It is plain records work, and the summit rested on it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1226:
Sato reported to Togo on 19 July 1945, as his talks in Moscow dragged. The Japanese envoy had pressed the Soviet side for word on mediation and on a special envoy from Tokyo. The answers stayed vague, and the days ran out.

His cables show a skilled diplomat reading a stone wall. Sato suspected that Moscow had its own plans for the war's end, none of them kind to Japan. He said as much to Tokyo, in shades. This dispatch is one of his reports from that week. It survives because American codebreakers copied the traffic the Allies used at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1326:
Pauley wrote to Clay, deputy military governor of the American zone in Germany, on 4 August 1945. The letter went out two days after the summit closed. Pauley's reparations work now met the men who actually ruled the zone and held its plants.

Clay's headquarters would have to carry out whatever the peace demanded in goods and gear. Word from the reparations chief set that work's terms from the policy side. This message shows the handoff from bargaining to rule. The summit's words became orders in occupied Germany through channels of exactly this kind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1426:
A text submitted by the Soviet delegation on 23 July 1945 stands beside the Soviet proposal of the same date in the volume. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Pairs of texts from one day often work as a set: a claim and its supporting draft, or two halves of one position. Readers can test how this text fits its partner and what the pairing says about Soviet method. Moscow's delegation drafted with care and in depth, and the volume's closing run preserves that depth. For students of the summit, these papers are the raw ore from which the final bargain was refined.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-126:
Charles Bohlen kept these minutes of a Potsdam meeting on July 27, 1945. Bohlen was the delegation's Russian interpreter and a close adviser to the Secretary of State. His minutes carry special weight. He understood not only the words spoken but the habits behind them, from long service in Moscow.

When Bohlen wrote the record, he wrote for men who trusted his ear. Readers get the exchange with a sense of tone that flatter notes can miss. The minutes sit in the second Potsdam volume among the chief American records. They show the conference through the eyes of its best-placed listener.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-26:
Field Marshals Alexander and Wilson called on Secretary Stimson after lunch on July 19, 1945. No official minutes of the call were kept. An editorial note in volume two prints Stimson's diary entry as the surviving record. Wilson reported the call to the Combined Chiefs later that day.

The main subject, Stimson writes, was the appointment of Colonel James Douglas. Douglas was to be the American member of the Italian Control Commission, but delay and news reports had embarrassed the incumbent, Admiral Stone. Alexander proposed a solution of his own. Douglas should come out on a visit of inspection first, staying as Alexander's guest. He would then take office later in September. That was agreed, and the telegrams were drawn up and sent. Stimson also talked over Alexander's Italy campaigns with him, the two men's first personal meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d726:
Cavendish Cannon, first secretary in Lisbon, set down this memorandum on July 20, 1945. Document 726 records a Portugal hand's view during the Potsdam week. Cannon knew Iberian affairs well. Neutral Portugal's stance mattered to the Allies, from Atlantic bases to trade. The memo entered the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

A memorandum from a listening post gathers what talk cannot carry. Cannon could weigh rumor against fact for his readers. The piece shows how wide the State Department's net was cast in 1945. Even as the Big Three met, officers in quiet capitals kept the record full. Their papers round out the summit's story.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d826:
Cannon wrote again from Lisbon to Matthews on July 29, 1945, in document 826. The first secretary reported to the director of European affairs as Potsdam ended. Portugal's neutral vantage still drew Washington's ear. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume beside his earlier ones.

A late report from Lisbon shows the summit's ripples reaching quiet waters. Cannon could gauge how the news played in a capital outside the fight. Readers get that outside view at the moment of decision. The document rounds out the Portugal thread. It proves that in 1945 no European post, however calm, stood apart from the settlement.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d926:
The United States delegation offered this memorandum at Babelsberg on July 25, 1945. It covers removals from Germany of property owned by citizens of Allied or neutral nations. The paper states that such ownership should not block a removals program.

Owners from Allied nations would file statements of their German property with the Control Council. Removed property would stay theirs where practical. Where not, Reichsmark accounts based on council valuations would be set up and paid off in foreign exchange. Neutral owners would get Reichsmark deposits as payment. The editors note the paper was circulated but never discussed, and Byrnes withdrew it on August 1.
frus-1969-76v17-d126: A 1969-1976 FRUS message from the government on China. The opening to Beijing. This document preserves that message. Later readers can locate it. The historical record keeps it. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
galsworthy-silver-spoon-1926:
John Galsworthy published The Silver Spoon in 1926, part of his second Forsyte trilogy, A Modern Comedy. The story now centers on Fleur Forsyte, Soames's daughter, and her husband Michael Mont. Galsworthy set the action in the restless England of the 1920s.

Fleur, born with the silver spoon of the title, hunts for excitement and status in fashionable London. A libel case, a trip related to America, and clashes with her aging father test her marriage. Soames watches the new generation with worry and grudging love. The novel satirizes the smart set while keeping sympathy for its flawed people.
gao-gaoreports-b-295526: A March 2005 protest docket, B-295526, with thin metadata — this GAO ruling is all that survives as the record. The claims were tested on what the file showed. The docket got its hearing despite the gaps. The gaps did not stop the review.
gao-gaoreports-b-296526: Integrate took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296626: Firetech Automatic Sprinkler took its September 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298426: Crown Title Corporation took its September 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Title deals get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298626: Lockheed Martin Aeronautics took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The giant said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Even the biggest defense names bow to bid law.
gao-gaoreports-b-299526: Medical Matrix took its June 2007 contract fight to GAO — two case numbers, one health deal — and the combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards; the call weighs each claim. Medical contracts get the same fair-bid treatment as any federal buy.
gao-gaoreports-b-300826: NIH's conference food spending got a fiscal ruling in March 2005, and GAO decides whether the catering was legal. The decision reads the money law. The ruling separates the allowable from the wasteful. The law had the final word. The catering was judged.
gao-gaoreports-b-308026: The labor board's contract spending got a fiscal slap in this September 2006 GAO ruling, which finds an improper obligation for severable services. The decision reads the money law. The ruling voids the illegal spending. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-311126: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by B-311126.2, B-311126.3, B-311126.4, Savannah River Alliance, LLC. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-526: Immigration phone lines needed cleaner deals in 2005, and GAO's report says the call-center pacts had to improve. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the callers deserved honest contracts. The callers deserved honest contracts. The pacts had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-626: Disability aid programs got a GAO once-over in 2005, and the report says the patchwork needed a modern rethink. The findings demand the reckoning. The report warns that the disabled deserved coherent aid. The disabled deserved coherent aid. The patchwork had to be rethought.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-726: FAA airline oversight needed systems integration in 2005, and GAO's report says the safety approach required further weaving into oversight. The findings demand the integration. The report warns that the flying public deserved proven oversight. The approach had to be integrated.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-926: Army modular transformation costs needed better estimates in 2005, and GAO's report says actions were needed to improve cost oversight. The findings demand the math. The report warns that the reorganization billions deserved honest counting. The estimates had to improve. The reorganization billions deserved honest counting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-126: Other countries' Social Security lessons got a GAO review in 2005, and the report says foreign experiences could inform U.S. reform. The findings look abroad. The report warns that the retirees deserved proven ideas. The lessons had to be learned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-26: Special education transitions needed guidance in 2006, and GAO's report says Education should provide more help for smooth state transitions. The findings demand the support. The report warns that the disabled students deserved seamless changes. The guidance had to be provided.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-326: Nursing homes housing sex offenders got a GAO look in 2006, and the report shares information on residents registered for crimes. The findings deliver the data. The report warns that the frail residents deserved to know. The information had to be shared.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-426: Broadband was spreading but hard to measure in 2006, and GAO's report says deployment was extensive, though assessing it was difficult. The findings balance the good news and the fog. The report warns that the digital divide needed honest mapping. The assessment had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-826: Evacuating hospitals in disasters needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says limitations in federal evacuation assistance should be addressed. The findings target the gaps. The report warns that the patients who could not walk needed a way out. The assistance had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1126: Were buses and trains truly open to riders with disabilities? GAO's 2007 report says nobody could really tell — thin data and weak enforcement tools left the question hanging. The findings describe a civil-rights promise running on honor system: rules on the books, little proof on the ground.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-126: Depot repair money needed clearer tracking in 2007, and GAO's report says Congress deserved more consistent funding data. The findings demand the numbers. The report warns that the fix-it shops' budgets should not be a mystery. The data had to be dependable.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-26: The IRS could collect more with better procedures in 2007, and GAO's report says procedural changes could enhance tax collections. The findings target the process. The report warns that the tax gap was partly a paperwork gap. The procedures had to improve.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-26: This 2007 GAO report takes Social Security reform past the usual old-age talk to the benefits paid for injury and to dependents. Plans that trim the program ripple hard through checks for hurt workers and their kin. The report maps those ripple lines — the trade-offs Congress would face if it touched the program's most tender promises.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-326: The Government Accountability Office dug into financial Audit: American Battle Monuments Commission's Financial Statements for Fiscal Years 2007 and 2006 in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-426: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at defense Management: Overarching Organizational Framework Needed to Guide and Oversee Energy Reduction Efforts for Military Operations. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
glasgow-romantic-comedians-1926:
Ellen Glasgow published The Romantic Comedians in 1926, her sharpest comedy of Southern manners. Glasgow set it in Richmond, renamed Queenborough, among the aging gentry she knew so well. She once described the book as a comedy about people who refuse to grow old gracefully.

Judge Gamaliel Honeywell, a widower of sixty-five, shocks his family by marrying a pretty young woman of twenty-three. The marriage collapses in farce and pathos, while his grown children pursue their own late romances. Glasgow mocks Southern gallantry with unusual lightness of touch. Under the comedy sits a serious theme: the danger of living inside romantic illusions. It remains one of her most entertaining novels.
guiraldes-don-segundo-sombra-1926:
Ricardo Guiraldes published Don Segundo Sombra in 1926, an Argentine novel told by a boy who becomes a gaucho. The narrator leaves a dull town life to ride with Don Segundo, a quiet and skilled horseman. On the pampas they herd cattle, break horses, and face storms and fights. The boy learns the gaucho code by watching his mentor.

Don Segundo speaks little, yet his example teaches courage, patience, and loyalty. At the end, the boy inherits land and must leave the roaming life. The farewell is sad and dignified. The novel is a beloved portrait of a fading way of life in Argentina.
hemingway-sun-also-rises-1926:
Ernest Hemingway published The Sun Also Rises in 1926, his novel of Jake Barnes and the expatriates of Paris. The Lost Generation's founding document follows drifting expatriates from Paris cafés to the Pamplona fiesta. Hemingway drew the cast from his own circle, and the roman à clef gossip only fed the book's fame.

Jake, wounded in the war, loves Brett Ashley, who drifts through men she cannot settle with in Paris and Spain. The fishing at Burguete gives a brief peace before the fiesta's bullfights, wine, and brawls take over in Pamplona. Romero, the young bullfighter, restores a code of grace under pressure that the expatriates admire and nearly corrupt by contact. Hemingway's cut, plain sentences and dialogue that implies oceans made a style a generation copied. The book defined how America writes about war's aftermath and expatriate drift.
hemingway-torrents-of-spring-1926:
Ernest Hemingway wrote The Torrents of Spring in about ten days in late 1925. He published it in 1926. The comic novella parodies Sherwood Anderson, the older writer who had helped launch Hemingway's career and whose gentle style Hemingway had outgrown.

Two Michigan factory workers wander through a fog of borrowed literary manners, courting waitresses and discussing books they half understand. Hemingway stuffs the tale with fake footnotes and long apologies to the reader. The joke had a business purpose: it broke his contract with Anderson's publisher and freed him for a new house. The parody ended a famous mentorship. Read today, it is Hemingway's only long piece of pure mischief.
holdsworth-history-english-law-vol9-1926:
The ninth volume of Holdsworth's History of English Law came out in 1926, carrying the story toward its author's own time. Holdsworth had begun the history as a young Oxford scholar; by now it was the standard work in its field. Few single-author histories in any subject match its scale.

Volume 9 deals with the later nineteenth century, above all the Judicature Acts that fused the old separate courts into one Supreme Court. Holdsworth explains how law and equity, split for centuries, were at last administered together. The modern court system of England takes its shape in these pages. Nine volumes in, the history approaches its close with the law made new. The set as a whole remains the last word on English legal history for most readers.
holmes-science-of-mind-1926:
Ernest Holmes built a movement on The Science of Mind, whose first edition appeared in 1926. The thick textbook lays out a full course of lessons in what Holmes called Science of Mind and Spirit. Mind, in his teaching, responds to thought as law, and prayer becomes a treatment: a clear statement that heals.

Holmes drew on New Thought, scripture, and philosophy to frame Religious Science as both church and method. Lessons move from first principles to daily practice for health, supply, and peace. The 1926 text launched the Religious Science movement, and its churches still study this founding course.
hughes-weary-blues-1926:
Langston Hughes published The Weary Blues in 1926, his first book of poems. Hughes was a young Black writer linked to the Harlem Renaissance. The poems draw on blues and jazz, with their rhythms, refrains, and plain speech. Harlem streets, clubs, and workers fill the pages.

Some poems sing of joy and music late into the night. Others speak of weariness, low pay, and dreams put off. Hughes writes in voices close to the people he describes. The title poem shows a piano player swaying as he sings of having nobody in the world. The book announced a major new voice in American poetry.
hurston-eatonville-anthology-1926:
Zora Neale Hurston grew up in Eatonville, Florida, one of the first all-Black towns in the United States. The Eatonville Anthology, published in the Messenger in 1926, gathers fourteen short sketches of her neighbors there. Hurston wrote them with the eye of both a storyteller and a trained student of folklore.

Each sketch gives a quick, vivid portrait of a local character. Their talk, tricks, jokes, and troubles fill the pages with town life. Hurston treats the townsfolk with warmth and respect, never as mere curiosities. The anthology was early proof of the gift she later showed in her novels and in her folklore collecting across the South.
hurston-sweat-1926:
Sweat, a short story by Zora Neale Hurston, appeared in the magazine Fire in 1926. Its heroine is Delia Jones, a washerwoman in a Florida town. Delia has worked for years to buy her own house, while her lazy husband Sykes torments her and flaunts his mistress.

Sykes, knowing Delia fears snakes, brings home a rattlesnake to drive her out. The cruelty builds until the snake turns on its keeper. Hurston writes the tale largely in Black Southern speech, handled with care and music. Sweat became one of the best-known stories of the Harlem Renaissance and a lasting study of labor, pride, and revenge.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-26:
Volume 26 of the Jesuit Relations came out in 1898 as part of Reuben Gold Thwaites's vast edition of reports from New France. Jesuit priests in Canada sent these yearly accounts back to France in the 1600s. They wrote about their missions among Native nations in the St. Lawrence valley and the lands beyond, in what the edition calls Lower Canada.

Inside are letters and journals on travel, hunger, sickness, language study, and the slow work of winning converts. The priests also recorded Native customs, councils, and wars with a close eye, even when their judgments were harsh. Historians still mine these pages as a first-hand record of early Canada and its first peoples.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mesquita-moses-:
Moses Gomez de Mesquita, born in 1688, was haham, or chief rabbi, of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews of England. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote his short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He took the office in 1744, succeeding Isaac Nieto, and held it until his death on May 8, 1751.

The article records two marriages that mark his years in office. In 1747 he solemnized the second marriage of his predecessor, Isaac Nieto. Two years later he married his own daughter to Moses Cohen Dazevedo Ferme, who himself became haham in 1760. A brief bibliography points to Gaster's history of the Bevis Marks congregation and the catalogue of the Anglo-Jewish Historical Exhibition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mikwa-ot-baths-:
Miḳwa'ot is the Mishnah treatise on ritual baths, the pools used for purification after leprosy and other conditions named in Leviticus. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The bath had to hold at least forty seahs of water, about 268 liters, enough to cover the whole body at once.

The water could come from a spring, a river, or rainfall, but never from a vessel, and the treatise exists to pin down such rules exactly. It runs ten chapters and seventy-one paragraphs, opening with six grades of water ranked by cleansing power. The article also notes the treatise's wandering place in the order Tohorot across different editions of the Mishnah and Talmud.
journal-of-discourses-vol-26:
Volume Twenty-Six, from 1886, closes the Journal of Discourses for good. Twenty-six volumes span thirty-two years of Tabernacle and frontier preaching. Hundreds of sermons end here, in the set's final gathered book.

The founding generation's voice falls silent as this volume shuts. Apostles who crossed the plains now preach to grandchildren in Zion. Their record covers doctrine, war, law, farming, and the soul's fate. No new faith of the age left so full a firsthand record. Scholars still mine the Journal as Mormonism's great primary source today. Its last pages close an era that print alone could preserve.
kafka-das-schloss-1926:
Franz Kafka left The Castle unfinished at his death in 1924, and it was published in German in 1926. The text here is that first German edition, from Kurt Wolff. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Its hero, known only as K., arrives in a snowbound village claiming the Castle has hired him as a land surveyor.

The Castle's officials never confirm his post, and every effort to reach them snares him deeper. Clerks, letters, and village rules form a maze with no center in sight. K. fights on with stubborn, comic energy against pure fog. The novel became the classic image of life under faceless power. Its cold absurdity still defines the word Kafkaesque.
lawrence-plumed-serpent-1926:
The Plumed Serpent, published in 1926, is Lawrence's Mexican novel and the most argued-over of all his books. Kate Leslie, an Irish widow of forty traveling in Mexico, is drawn into a movement reviving the cult of Quetzalcoatl, the plumed serpent god.

Its leaders, Don Ramon and Don Cipriano, preach a new-old religion of blood and ritual against church and revolution alike. Kate resists and yields by turns, and the novel never settles whether the cult saves or devours her. Lawrence wrote it out of his own Mexican journeys and longings. The result is powerful, disturbing, and impossible to ignore.
levy-bruhl-how-natives-think-1926:
Lucien Levy-Bruhl, a French philosopher, argued in this famous work that native peoples think in a fundamentally different way from modern Europeans. The authorized English translation by Lilian A. Clare appeared in 1926 and spread his thesis widely.

Levy-Bruhl claimed that collective representations, the beliefs a group shares, bend individual thought toward what he called participation mystique. In that mode, a person can feel one with an ancestor, an animal, or a sacred object. Critics attacked the idea as unfair to native reason, and Levy-Bruhl softened it late in life. The debate it started shaped anthropology for decades.
livy-history-rome-books-9-26:
Livy wrote his monumental History of Rome under Augustus, narrating the republic's rise. D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds translated this stretch, covering Books 9 through 26. The Second Punic War dominates the later books here.

Early books here cover Rome's wars with the Samnites and Pyrrhus. Then Hannibal crosses the Alps, wins at Cannae, and nearly breaks Rome. Livy tells the story as patriotic epic, full of speeches and omens. Rome's recovery after Cannae becomes his great theme of resilience. This volume completes the library's main Livy set. Ancient history rarely reads at this scale or with this sweep.
llull-blanquerna-peers-1926:
Blanquerna is the great romance of Ramon Llull, the Catalan thinker of the thirteenth century. E. Allison Peers translated it into English in 1926. Its hero, Blanquerna, climbs step by step through the estates of the world: marriage, the religious life, the bishopric, the papacy, and at last the hermit's cell.

Along the road Llull sets out his whole vision of a reformed Christian world, taught by reason and his famous Art of finding truth. The famous Book of the Lover and the Beloved blooms inside the tale. Blanquerna is part novel, part plan for the church and the schools. It shows medieval Catalonia dreaming of a wiser age.
malinowski-crime-custom-1926:
In 1926 Malinowski returned to the Trobriand Islands in print with a short book on law and custom. Crime and Custom in Savage Society asks how order holds in a land with no courts, police, or written laws. It grew from the same field work as his Argonauts.

Malinowski argues that law lives in daily duty, not in force from above. He shows that custom binds because people depend on each other and fear shame before their neighbors. Gifts, feasts, and duties form a web that no one can lightly break. The book founded the study of law in anthropology and still starts debates about rules without rulers.
malinowski-myth-in-primitive-psychology-:
Malinowski based this short 1926 book on his fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands, where he had lived in a village and learned the language. It states his functionalist view of myth in its clearest form.

A myth, Malinowski argues, is not a bad attempt at science or history. It is a charter: a sacred story that justifies present customs, ranks, and land claims by grounding them in the age of origins. He shows Trobrianders using tales of ancestors to settle real disputes. The book helped move anthropology from the armchair to the field, and its argument still frames debates about myth.
mathnawi-nicholson-vol-2-1926:
Jalal al-Din Rumi, the Persian poet of the 1200s, wrote the Mathnawi, a long poem of Sufi teaching told through stories. R. A. Nicholson spent years turning it into English. His second volume, printed in 1926, gives the English text of the poem's first two books.

Rumi teaches through tales of kings, lovers, merchants, fools, and saints, and each story turns toward a lesson on God and the soul. The tales pile up, short and long, comic and grave, and each one points past itself to truths about prayer, love, and the self. Nicholson's version became the standard English Mathnawi for students of Persian verse.
mcbride-symmes-theory-concentric-spheres:
James McBride, a friend and backer of Symmes in Ohio, gave the hollow earth scheme its first full book in 1826. Symmes had put his claim in short forms, and it drew much scorn. McBride set out to give it a learned, full dress case.

He lays out the spheres within spheres, the polar holes, and the seas and lands inside. He draws on maths, star lore, and the tales of north sea men for his proof. The book is the chief shield of the scheme in its first, bold years.
mirrlees-lud-in-the-mist-1926:
Hope Mirrlees set a prim town by the edge of faerie in Lud-in-the-Mist, her novel of 1926. The town bans all talk of fairy fruit and the wild hills. Yet the fruit slips in. Sons and girls stray, and old rites stir in the calm streets.

The tale blends law, lore, and quiet dread. Mirrlees writes with grace and sly wit. She asks what a town loses when it shuts out awe. The book was long hard to find. Now chief tale-smiths rank it at the top. Mayor Chanticleer, stiff and prim at first, must face his own past. His slow change gives the wild lore a warm, sad human core.
morgan-theory-gene-1926:
Thomas Hunt Morgan led the famous 'fly room' at Columbia, where tiny fruit flies remade biology. His Theory of the Gene, published in 1926, sums up what those flies had taught. Morgan had once doubted Mendel; the flies changed his mind.

Morgan shows that genes sit in a line on chromosomes, like beads on a string. Crossed flies reveal how traits link, swap, and map to fixed places. That mapping let scientists chart heredity with real precision. Morgan won a Nobel Prize, and his book stands as the classic statement of gene theory. Diagrams of fly crosses make the argument easy to follow.
openalex-w1487331926: Aging is the top risk factor for brain diseases — and the brain's immune cells are central. A 2015 review by von Bernhardi and colleagues examines microglial dysregulation in brain aging and neurodegeneration. The review linked glial activation and brain inflammation to the disease process.
openalex-w2030126026: Crop genes meet weather — models must handle both. Jarquín and colleagues' 2013 paper built a reaction norm model for genomic selection using vast genomic and environmental data. The method boosted wheat yield predictions across environments.
openalex-w2066642526: Carbon nanotubes may supercharge crops. Tiwari and colleagues' 2013 study mixed carbon nanotubes with plants, boosting growth and nutrient uptake in maize (Zea mays). The work tested the field's promise — and its consistency problems head-on, honestly.
openalex-w2099600826: The Higgs shone in two photons. The ATLAS collaboration's 2014 paper measured Higgs boson production in the diphoton decay channel at 7 and 8 TeV. The two-photon signal pinned down how the Higgs is made.
openalex-w2101094926: HIV makes TB more infectious — guinea pigs proved it. A 2008 study measured how infectious TB patients with HIV are. The Lima guinea-pig model, with DNA tracking, measured airborne spread from wards — a classic revisited.
openalex-w2113626726: Chocolate's tree needed a family map. A 2008 study traced gene and map differences among Amazonian cacao populations. The work fixed seed-bank labeling errors hampering cacao improvement for breeders — chocolate's future, secured at last for growers and chocolate makers.
openalex-w2130143426: Supersymmetry's partners stayed hidden — ATLAS looked anyway. The ATLAS team's 2014 paper hunted superpartners directly. The record is thin, but the paper covers the superpartner hunt — limits set for all, finally published and out today.
openalex-w2150408626: Higher blood pressure didn't help the tiny vessels. A 2009 study found raising pressure with the drug does not improve tiny vessels. Twenty septic shock patients in two ICUs showed the disconnect — for all — pressure's limit, found at last.
openalex-w2153034426: Asthma's global burden got counted. A 2012 study counted global asthma prevalence in adults. The survey informed strategies for a major cause of disability and poor quality of life — breathing's burden, measured at last for all to see and act on.
openalex-w2260781726: Radiation therapy saves lives in breast cancer, but some patients are more vulnerable to its DNA-damaging side effects. This 2015 paper studies how ionizing radiation injures DNA in breast cancer patients and how that damage can be detected. Understanding who is most susceptible could help doctors tune treatment — killing tumors while sparing healthy tissue.
openalex-w2482115826: Can computers predict how molecules will pack into crystals? Every few years the field holds a blind test — and this 2016 paper reports the sixth. Five target systems, from a small rigid molecule to a bulky flexible one, challenged prediction methods worldwide. The results show how far crystal structure prediction has come, and where it still stumbles.
openalex-w2792366526: Neutrophils — the immune system's first responders — were long treated as a uniform swarm. This 2018 Frontiers in Physiology paper asks whether they're actually several cell types in disguise, reviewing their many roles: phagocytosis, granule release, and more. The emerging picture is of a far more versatile cell than textbooks allowed.
openalex-w2811473826: Non-specific low back pain sends millions to primary care — and guidelines disagree on what to do. This 2018 European Spine Journal paper overviews current clinical practice guidelines, comparing their recommendations on diagnosis and treatment. The synthesis reveals where the world's advice converges — and where it conflicts.
openalex-w2929552226: Gallstones lodged in the common bile duct need extracting — symptomatic or not, if the patient can tolerate it. This 2019 Endoscopy paper delivers the European Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy's guideline on endoscopic management. The recommendations standardize workup — liver tests, ultrasound — and the intervention itself.
openalex-w2985579226: Industrial pollutants are poisoning ecosystems — and enzymes called laccases can help clean up. This 2019 Microbial Cell Factories paper reviews laccase structure, function, and potential in water bioremediation. The enzymes offer a biological strategy against the contaminant molecules of urbanization and industry.
openalex-w3010629926: Genome-scale metabolic models guide biotechnology — but how do you know a model is any good? This 2020 Nature Biotechnology paper, by Lieven, Beber, Olivier and colleagues, introduces MEMOTE: a standardized test suite for genome-scale metabolic models. The tool brings quality control to the models that design tomorrow's microbes.
openalex-w3027520426: Eight years of Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope data, distilled into one catalog. This 2020 Astrophysical Journal Supplement paper presents the fourth Fermi Large Area Telescope source catalog (4FGL) — gamma-ray sources from 50 MeV to 1 TeV, the deepest yet. The catalog is the definitive map of the high-energy sky.
openalex-w4411251826: Germs talk in chemical whispers, and this paper maps who listens in. The authors surveyed how widely butenolide signal molecules show up across Streptomyces strains, beyond the one famous maker. They charted the spread of these chatter chemicals. A germ study of tiny talk with big effects on drug-making.
openalex-w7125123226: Obese adults with sleep apnea may carry hidden heart risks. This study surveyed 500 obese clinic patients to link obstructive sleep apnea with early, silent ischemic heart disease signs. The authors measured the association. A cardiology study of the heart paying for bad sleep.
openalex-w7125428726: The molecules that build proteins moonlight in drug synthesis. This review covers aminoacyl-tRNA-dependent enzymes in natural-product biosynthesis: how these protein-making helpers also craft bioactive compounds. The authors mapped structure-function insights. A biochemistry review of multitasking molecules.
openalex-w7204124426: When antidepressants fail twice, depression is called treatment-resistant, and options narrow. This literature review studies electroconvulsive therapy for such cases: how well it works when drugs do not. The authors weigh the evidence for the much-misunderstood treatment. A psychiatric review that takes ECT seriously as a lifeline.
openalex-w7204549026: Cycling does more than build legs; it rewires nerves, hormones, and immune defenses. This narrative review pulls together studies on how regular riding affects the nervous, hormonal, and immune systems. The authors searched major medical databases to map the adaptations. A sports-medicine overview that gives riders scientific reasons to keep pedaling, beyond fitness alone.
openalex-w7204657526: Rural settlers in western Parana practice politics outside formal channels, and this article studies what that means for democracy. The authors investigate how life in land-reform settlements shapes political engagement and conditional loyalty to republican ideals. Based on field research, it shows citizenship lived informally. A rich sociological portrait of politics beyond the ballot box.
openalex-w7206167326: Brazilian students struggle with applying math and logical reasoning, according to international assessments. This paper tests whether Scratch, the free block-based programming tool, can help high schoolers build computational thinking and math logic. The authors report on using Scratch as a teaching tool and what changed for students. It is a concrete experiment in making abstract reasoning hands-on, aimed at teachers looking for new approaches.
openalex-w7206190426: Anxiety often starts young and can shadow a person for years, so stopping it before it starts matters. This paper sums up systematic reviews, with combined data, on programs meant to prevent first-time anxiety and keep it from coming back. The authors judge which approaches the evidence supports. A careful overview for clinicians and policymakers deciding where prevention money does the most good.
openalex-w7211884526: More autistic students are joining regular classrooms in Brazil, and schools are scrambling to keep up. This study follows one public school in Rio Grande do Norte, documenting the challenges teachers face and the practices that work when including students on the autism spectrum. It is grounded in a real school rather than theory alone. The paper offers concrete lessons for making inclusion more than a slogan.
pero-tafur-travels-letts-1926:
Pero Tafur was a Castilian knight who roamed the late medieval world. His Travels and Adventures cover the years 1435 to 1439 abroad. Malcolm Letts put the old Spanish account into English in 1926.

Tafur visits Constantinople, the Holy Land, Egypt, and the courts of Italy. He notes ships, relics, markets, and the manners of each great city. His eye is curious, shrewd, and often frankly amused by strangers. Few books show the 1400s through one traveler's eyes so well. Readers rank it among the most fun travel works of its century by far. Tafur's voice stays fresh, bold, and plainly human throughout.

Natalay Kouprina, Adam Pavlicek, Ganeshwaran H. Mochida, and their team tracked a brain-size gene in PLOS Biology in 2004. ASPM helps control brain size, and broken copies cause a very small brain at birth. The authors compared ASPM across primates to date its fast evolution.

Their timeline shows the gene's rapid change began before the human brain grew to its modern size. That order matters. It means ASPM was already under strong pressure in earlier primates, not only in our own line. The finding tempers simple stories that tie one gene to one human leap. Brain growth, it hints, was a longer, shared ape story.
plos-pone-0000026:
Ryo Matoba, Hitoshi Niwa, Shinji Masui, and their team profiled embryonic stem cells in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein Oct3/4 is a master switch that keeps stem cells able to become any cell type. The team measured gene activity as Oct3/4 levels changed, to map the networks it runs.

Lowering the switch lets cells start down paths toward specific tissues. The profiles show which gene groups move first and which hold the stem state. Such maps are the working charts of stem cell biology. They help labs grow pure cell types for study and, in time, for therapy. They also flag genes that might make adult cells revert to a stem-like state.
plos-pone-0000126:
Heidi de Wit, L. Niels Cornelisse, Ruud F. G. Toonen, and colleagues published this neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE in 2006. It studies secretory vesicles, the tiny bubbles inside nerve cells that hold chemical messengers. Before release, a vesicle must dock at the cell surface, and the authors test the role of the protein syntaxin in that step.

Their conclusion is in the title: docking depends on syntaxin. Pinning down which protein does which job matters because every nerve signal rides on this release machinery. The paper adds a precise piece to the chain of events that lets one neuron talk to the next.
plos-pone-0000226:
Stephane Esnault, Ruedi K. Braun, Zhong-Jian Shen, and colleagues published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Pin1 is an enzyme that tweaks the shape of other proteins after they are made. The authors study how Pin1 modulates the type 1 immune response, the branch of immunity that fights viruses and other invaders inside cells.

A single shape-changing enzyme can tilt the strength of a whole immune program. The paper maps Pin1's influence on that response. Because type 1 responses also drive some inflammatory diseases, the findings matter both for fighting infection and for calming immunity when it overshoots.
plos-pone-0000326:
Rauf Bhat and Carsten Watzl published this immunology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Natural killer cells attack tumor cells without prior training. The authors study serial killing, one killer cell destroying several tumor cells in a row. They report that therapeutic antibodies enhance this serial killing by human natural killer cells.

Antibodies already used in cancer therapy may work partly by coaching killer cells. Showing they boost repeated killing strengthens that account. The finding matters for designing antibody treatments that squeeze the most out of the patient's own immune cells.
plos-pone-0000426:
Jenifer L. Marks and colleagues sequenced growth-signal genes in lung adenocarcinomas, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. They analyzed EGFR and related signaling pathway genes, which drive cell growth and are frequent sources of cancer-causing mutations. Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common form of lung cancer, and its growth genes shape treatment choices.

Alongside known changes, the team identified a novel somatic mutation in the kinase domain of FGFR4, another growth receptor. Somatic means the change arose in the tumor, not in the patient's inherited DNA. Each new mutation of this kind adds a possible drug target and refines how lung tumors are classified at the molecular level.
plos-pone-0000526:
Kegong Tian and colleagues investigated a devastating pig virus outbreak in China, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. PRRS, porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome, took an atypical, fatal turn. The team described the emergence of fatal PRRSV variants and performed molecular dissection of the unique hallmark that set the outbreak strain apart.

A molecular hallmark, a signature change in the virus's genome, lets laboratories identify the dangerous variant quickly. China's 2006–2007 outbreaks killed huge numbers of pigs and shook pork supply. Pinning the variant's distinguishing marks is the first step toward matched vaccines and surveillance.
plos-pone-0000626:
Istvan Molnar-Szakacs, Allan D. Wu, Francisco J. Robles and co-authors asked how brains react to hand gestures from another culture. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study concerns emblems, gestures with fixed meanings that speak without words. People everywhere use their hands to communicate, but each culture sets its own gesture meanings.

The team studied corticospinal excitability, how ready the brain's movement pathways are, while people watched culture-specific gestures. Watching a gesture your own culture taught you may prime your motor system differently from a foreign one. The work speaks to the neural bases of cross-cultural social communication, where a familiar sign can land instantly and an unfamiliar one cannot.
plos-pone-0000726:
Wei Zhao, Bapi Pahar, Juan T. Borda and colleagues tracked immune signals during early infection with a hybrid immunodeficiency virus. The chemokines CCL3, CCL4 and CCL5 can block CCR5-using HIV from entering host cells and suppress viral replication in the lab. What the body's own chemokines do during real infection was incompletely understood.

Their title reports a decline in CCL3-5 gene expression during primary simian-human immunodeficiency virus infection. If natural blockers fall just as the virus establishes itself, that timing could help the virus win. The finding sharpens interest in treatments that sustain or mimic these chemokines during the earliest phase of infection.
plos-pone-0000826:
Abraham Miranda, Meade Morgan, Leda Jamal and colleagues measured whether HIV treatment also slowed tuberculosis in Brazil. HIV fuels TB epidemics around the world. In controlled clinical trials, antiretroviral therapy reduces TB incidence in HIV-infected patients. The open question was whether, under real programmatic conditions, Brazil's policy of universal ART access achieved the same effect between 1995 and 2001.
