Trials and national programmes often differ: adherence, supply, and late diagnosis all bite in practice. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study tests the policy at national scale. Evidence that treatment-as-delivered prevents TB strengthens the case for funding universal access, beyond the benefit to each treated patient.
plos-pone-0000926:
Jean-Michel Hougardy, Kinda Schepers, Sammy Place and colleagues tested a blood marker for hidden tuberculosis, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Finding latent TB, infection without illness, is central to controlling the disease. The old skin test misses cases, and newer blood tests rely on the release of a signal protein called interferon gamma.

The team used a TB protein named HBHA to trigger that release. A response to HBHA may mark latent infection more sharply than standard antigens. Better latent tests help doctors treat people before they fall ill or spread the germ. The study adds one more candidate to a busy search.
plos-pone-0001026:
Camila Romano, Fernando de Melo, Marco Corsini and colleagues compared ancient retrovirus families in three primate genomes, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Endogenous retroviruses are old infections written into DNA and passed down. The K family is one of the youngest and most studied of these viral fossils.

The team found nineteen complete ERV-K elements in rhesus monkeys and twelve in chimpanzees, then compared them with fifty-five human copies. Those counts sketch each species' demographic history with the virus family. Viral fossils record infections our ancestors survived. Comparing them across primates shows which copies are shared inheritance and which arrived after the species split.
plos-pone-0001126:
Treating drug-resistant tuberculosis takes many months and often fails. Helen Cox and colleagues reported on a treatment program in Karakalpakstan, Uzbekistan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The region had very high rates of multidrug-resistant TB, found in 13 percent of new cases and 40 percent of previously treated ones.

A pilot program to treat the disease began there in 2003. The authors describe how treatment worked in practice, what outcomes patients had, and how often extensively drug-resistant TB appeared among those who failed treatment. Their account shows the complexity of curing resistant TB in a high-burden setting.
plos-pone-0001226:
Some lung cancers carry activating mutations in the EGFR gene, and these tumors behave differently from other lung cancers. Kuicheon Choi and colleagues profiled gene activity in such cancer cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The subgroup is non-small cell lung cancer with somatic EGFR mutations, changes acquired by the tumor rather than inherited.

The transcriptional mediators of EGFR's effects in this subgroup had not been fully worked out. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, the authors mapped which genes switch on downstream of the mutant receptor. That map matters because EGFR-blocking drugs work dramatically in this subgroup, and resistance eventually follows.
plos-pone-0001326:
Grapes and wine form a large worldwide market, and the cultivated grape, Vitis vinifera, could become a model for fruit tree genetics. Riccardo Velasco and colleagues produced a draft genome sequence for a heterozygous grapevine variety, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Grapes are highly heterozygous, meaning their two genome copies differ at many positions, which complicates whole-genome shotgun sequencing.

The authors present a high quality draft consensus sequence despite that challenge. A consensus merges the two differing copies into one reference. Their sequence opened grape genomics to gene discovery for disease resistance, fruit quality, and breeding.
plos-pone-0001426:
Peter Kroth and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on sugar handling in a tiny sea alga. Diatoms are single celled algae that fix about a fifth of the world's carbon. Their cells arose through a merged past, so their chemistry is more complex than that of green algae. The team used the full genome to build a model.

Their model maps how this diatom makes, stores, and burns sugars. By comparing it with other algae, they flagged routes that seem unique to diatoms. Those routes may help explain why diatoms thrive in the sea. The model gives labs a base for tests on carbon flow in the oceans.
plos-pone-0001526:
Sophie Desset and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how fruit flies silence jumping DNA in the germ line. Small RNAs guard the genome by hushing these mobile parts. The team studied a locus that directs the hush of two such parts in body cells, not just germ cells. They asked which paths run that hush.

They show the locus works through both a Piwi based path and a second, free path. Two paths to one hush give the cell a backup. Germ line guards keep the next brood's genome sound. This body cell case broadens where such guards are known to act.
plos-pone-0001626:
Koleka Mlisana, Sara C. Auld, Anneke Grobler, and their co-authors measured anaemia in people with very early HIV infection for a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Anaemia, a low level of red blood cells or haemoglobin, is common in AIDS and is linked to worse illness and higher death rates. Far less was known about blood changes in the first weeks of infection with HIV-1 subtype C.

The study followed women who did not yet have HIV alongside women in acute and early infection, tracking how haemoglobin levels changed. The full text gives the blood values, the share of women who became anaemic, and how those patterns shifted over time. Knowing when anaemia starts in early infection can help clinics plan testing and care for people who have just caught the virus.
plos-pone-0001826:
Ke Zen and co-authors identified a molecule that helps breast cancer cells cross vessel walls in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Endothelial E-selectin plays a pivotal role in interactions between breast cancer cells and endothelial monolayers during metastasis. The counterreceptor on the cancer cell, and its role in transendothelial migration, were unknown.

The team reports that CD44v4 is a major E-selectin ligand that mediates breast cancer cell transendothelial migration. The full text gives the binding and migration assays. Metastasis requires cancer cells to exit the bloodstream; blocking the molecular handle they use could slow that step.
plos-pone-0001926:
Hongbo Zhu and co-authors built a new way to compare how proteins touch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Where two proteins meet, atoms form weak bonds that are not covalent. The pattern of those bonds sets how snug and specific the fit is. Labs had many ways to compare protein shapes and binding sites, but none for these contact patterns.

Their method lines up the weak-bond patterns at two interfaces so like patterns can be scored as alike or not. Aligned in this way, interfaces from unlike proteins can be matched. That helps predict how a new protein will bind, a core task in drug design and in basic cell science.
plos-pone-0002026:
Rongqian Wu and co-authors tested a hunger hormone as a shield against gut injury, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When blood flow to the gut is cut and then restored, a pattern called ischemia-reperfusion, the harm can spread from the gut to distant organs. Immune cells along the gut's vast vessel surface drive a local, then body-wide, inflammatory response.

The hormone is ghrelin, best known for sparking appetite. As the title states, ghrelin attenuated injury both in the gut and in remote organs after this insult. A gut hormone that also calms storm-like injury could aid care in intensive units.
plos-pone-0002126:
David Hendrickson, Daniel Hogan, Daniel Herschlag, and co-authors mapped how tiny RNAs steer gene activity, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that do not code for proteins. Instead, they guide a silencing complex to matching messenger RNAs, which can then be cut down or blocked from making protein.

The team set out to find, in a systematic way, which messenger RNAs one protein pulls in. That protein is Argonaute 2, and the search ran when a given microRNA was at work. They also tracked how the amounts of those messages change. Their approach helps replace guesswork about microRNA targets with direct lists drawn from cells.
plos-pone-0002226:
Nikolaus Steinbeis and Stefan Koelsch compared how the brain handles meaning in music and in language, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Music can plainly carry meaning, yet how it does so is unsettled. The team asked whether the meaning of a musical passage is represented in the brain much as the meaning of a sentence is.

They combined EEG, which times brain activity finely, with fMRI, which locates it. The two methods together gave evidence for neural representations that are partly shared and partly distinct. The study helps map where music and language meet in the mind, and where each keeps its own machinery.
plos-pone-0002326:
Christian Dobel, Christian Putsche, Pienie Zwitserlood, and co-authors recorded brain signals from people born unable to recognize faces, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Congenital prosopagnosia is a severe face perception problem present from birth, not caused by injury. People with it cannot recognize even familiar persons by face.

Using MEG, which tracks magnetic fields from the brain with fine timing, the team looked for early faults in face processing. They found dysfunction in the left hemisphere at early stages. A fault that early suggests the problem starts in the first steps of face analysis. It does not start in memory for people. That reshapes how the condition is classed.
plos-pone-0002426:
Work from Llop-Guevara and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Alba Llop-Guevara, Marc Colangelo, Derek K. Chu, and others. Its subject is in Vivo -to- In Silico Iterations to Investigate Aeroallergen-Host Interactions. Allergic asthma is a complex process arising out of the interaction between the immune system and aeroallergens.

Yet, the relationship between aeroallergen exposure, allergic sensitization and disease remains unclear. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002526:
In 2008, Wei and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Bin Wei, Zheng Chen, Xu Zhang, and others. Its subject is nitric Oxide Mediates Stretch-Induced Ca2+ Release via Activation of Phosphatidylinositol 3-Kinase-Akt Pathway in Smooth Muscle. Hollow smooth muscle organs such as the bladder undergo significant changes in wall tension linked to filling and distension.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002626:
Michael Klompas led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was automated identification of acute hepatitis b using electronic medical record data to facilitate public health surveillance. The catalog record names Michael Klompas first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Automatic identification of notifiable diseases from electronic medical records can potentially improve the timeliness and completeness of public health surveillance. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002726:
Rajkumar Sasidharan led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with transmembrane protein oxygen content and compartmentalization of cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Rajkumar Sasidharan and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Recently. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state. The description here rests only on the title, the author record, and the abstract text held for the entry, with no claims added beyond those sources.
plos-pone-0002826:
Jenee N. Smith led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SdiA, an n -Acylhomoserine lactone receptor, becomes active during the transit of salmonella enterica through the gastrointestinal tract of turtles. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Jenee N. Smith, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. LuxR-type transcription factors are typically used by bacteria to determine the population density of their own species by detecting N-acylhomoserine lactones (AHLs). Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002926:
Maria Camats, Sonia Guil, Mariette Kokolo and co-authors studied how the helicase p68 shapes H-Ras splicing in 2008. H-Ras RNA can be spliced two ways, making either the p21 or the p19 protein, depending on whether a piece called IDX is kept. The p68 protein was known to reduce IDX inclusion.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study shows p68 also alters the activity of other splicing factors that act on the same RNA. Splicing is how one gene yields several proteins. The results add detail on how a single helicase can steer that choice in a cancer-linked gene.
plos-pone-0003026: Stephen Beres, Ricardo Sesso, Sergio Pinto and colleagues reported the genome sequence of a Lancefield group C Streptococcus zooepidemicus strain in PLOS ONE in 2008. The strain caused epidemic nephritis, a kidney disease outbreak, and the subtitle calls the work new information about an old disease. The catalog record gives title, authors, and year, with no further abstract detail. The article presents the full genome of that outbreak strain as a base for studying how this animal-associated streptococcus infects people.
plos-pone-0003126:
Yara C. Blanco, Alessandro S. Farias, Uta Goelnitz and co-authors test a support treatment for cerebral malaria in this 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cerebral malaria brings nerve signs, seizures and coma, and it shares some traits with stroke. Even so, few studies had looked at new supportive care for the disease. Hyperbaric oxygen, given under pressure, had shown success in other settings.

The title states the central finding: hyperbaric oxygen prevented early death in mice with experimental cerebral malaria. Readers find a test of a non-drug support idea for a severe form of malaria. The work points to care that might buy time alongside standard treatment.
plos-pone-0003226:
Kwok M. Ho, Matthew Knuiman, Judith Finn and colleagues build a survival model for critically ill patients in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Long-term survival outcome of critically ill patients is important for assessing new treatments and for making treatment decisions. The team developed a prognostic model for estimation of long-term survival, called PREDICT. It was a retrospective linked data cohort study.

Readers get a tool aimed beyond hospital discharge, at long-term outlook. Families and clinicians often need that longer view when weighing intensive care. A validated model can support those hard conversations with data instead of guesswork alone.
plos-pone-0003326:
Scot E. Dowd, Randall D. Wolcott, Yan Sun and colleagues sequence bacteria from diabetic foot ulcers in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ulcers on the feet and legs of people with diabetes are linked with chronic infections. Such ulcer infections are too often followed by amputation. There is little knowledge of the ecology of such infections, or of how to control or clear this type of chronic infection.

Using bacterial tag encoded FLX amplicon pyrosequencing, the team show the polymicrobial nature of chronic diabetic foot ulcer biofilm infections. Readers learn these wounds host mixed groups, not single germs. That mix explains why antibiotics aimed at one species often fail in such ulcers.
plos-pone-0003426:
Israel Hershkovitz and colleagues found ancient tuberculosis traces in this 2008 paper. They studied bones from a Neolithic settlement in the eastern Mediterranean. The settlement dated to about nine thousand years ago. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the TB germ, was thought to have evolved beside humans for ages.

The team pulled out and characterized DNA of that germ from the remains. Finding it in such old bones backs the long shared history. TB leaves no home outside its human host, unlike many germs. This molecular proof pushes confirmed TB deep into prehistory. Few finds tie a named germ to a dated human settlement so directly.
plos-pone-0003526:
Lucina Q. Uddin and co-authors scanned self-face recognition in autism for this 2008 study. Autism involves less interest in social exchange and stronger self-focus. Earlier theories stressed social impairments in the disorder. The team asked how the brain handles self versus other faces.

Using brain imaging, they watched participants recognize their own faces. Neural patterns for self and other could then be compared. Where those patterns diverge may mark autism's social gap. The study gives a brain-level view of self representation. Face reading is core to social life, which is why its gaps matter.
plos-pone-0003626:
Elena R. Álvarez-Buylla, Álvaro Chaos, Maximino Aldana, and colleagues published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. It asks how a flower takes shape as its genes switch on and off. The team built a model of the gene network that guides flower formation.

In their model, random noise could push the network toward stable flower forms, not just blur them. That runs against the older view of growth as a fixed, preset program. The study presents flower form as the product of a network that can use chance and still stay stable.
plos-pone-0003726:
Galit Tzur, Asaf Levy, Eti Meiri, and colleagues published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Human embryonic stem cells can renew themselves and can also turn into any body tissue. Small RNAs called microRNAs help steer that choice by tuning gene activity after genes are read.

The team tracked microRNA patterns as the cells differentiated toward endoderm, the layer that forms the gut and related organs. They also probed what those microRNAs do in the process. The patterns show small RNAs at work in one of the embryo's first big decisions.
plos-pone-0003826:
Daniel Mietchen, Bertram Manz, Frank Volke, and colleagues published this animal study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Below freezing, ice crystals threaten the structure and function of cells. Insects in seasonally cold places have evolved many strategies to reorganize their tissues against the cold.

The team assessed cold adaptation in insect larvae inside the living animal. They used magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy to watch tissues handle the cold without cutting them open. The in vivo view shows the tricks larvae use to survive deep cold through a hard winter. The study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003926:
Jianfeng Zhou, Wenhong Li, Hiroyasu Kamei, and co-authors compared a growth-control gene in fish in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns IGFBP-2, a protein that binds growth factors. It helps govern growth, development, reproduction, and aging. High levels of it also appear in many advancing cancers.

Teleost fish carry two copies of the gene, unlike most other vertebrates. The team compared the proteins those copies make and how each is used. Form and basic function stayed much the same after duplication. Gene use, though, had drifted apart between the two copies over time. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004026:
Francisco J. Quintana, Avishai Mimran, Pnina Carmi, and co-authors described a new immune control route in 2008. HSP60 is a heat shock protein that shapes T cell responses. It can signal through a receptor or serve as an antigen. The protein rises in stressed and inflamed tissues.

Their PLOS ONE article reports regulatory T cells target HSP60 itself. These anti-ergotypic cells react to the presented stress protein. That reaction forms another loop for calming immune responses. Understanding the loop may help treat autoimmune disease. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004126:
Kristin Field and colleagues published this feeding study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It examines casein hydrolysates, broken-down milk proteins used in foods for their nutrition and useful properties. Their bitter taste often limits how much makers can add to products meant for people.

Earlier evidence hinted that other animals also avoid eating them, but few species had been tested. The team offered animals a choice between foods with and without the hydrolysates. They found that plant-eating species avoided them, while omnivores did not. The result matters for food design and for understanding how taste guides diet across species.
plos-pone-0004226:
Yong Zhao and colleagues published this diabetes study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the pancreas's insulin-making beta cells. Controlling that autoimmunity is essential to any real treatment. Regulatory T cells, the immune system's peacekeepers, play a pivotal role in holding self-attack in check.

The team used human cord blood stem cells to modulate these regulatory T cells. They report that the treated cells reverse the autoimmune diabetes in nonobese diabetic mice, the standard model of the disease. The approach aims at the cause of type 1 diabetes, not just its blood sugar.
plos-pone-0004326:
Martin Schweizer, Markus Henniger, and Inge Sillaber published this stress study in PLOS ONE in 2009. In many depressed patients, stressful life events help trigger the illness. In rats, chronic mild stress can produce depression-like states, and the procedure is a standard animal model. Whether it works the same way in mice was less certain.

The team examined chronic mild stress in mice, looking at anhedonia, the loss of pleasure that is a core symptom, and at activity. They report an anomalous anxiolysis, a paradoxical calming, alongside the expected effects. Mixed results like these warn against assuming one species' model fits another.
plos-pone-0004426:
Health is more than one number, and Alessandra Andreotti, Nadia Minicuci, Paul Kowal, and co-authors set out to draw fuller health profiles in PLOS ONE in 2009. They drew on the World Health Survey, run by the World Health Organization in seventy countries between 2002 and 2004. The survey gathered data meant to be compared fairly across peoples.

The team applied a method called the Grade of Membership model to that survey. Instead of forcing each person into one class, the model lets each person partly belong to several health profiles at once. That gives a richer, multi-sided view of how health, risk factors, and outcomes cluster in real populations. Such profiles can guide health policy across very different countries.
plos-pone-0004526:
Two diseases that look alike can be told apart quickly with a combined DNA test, report Maria Isabel Queipo-Ortuno, Juan Colmenero, Pilar Bermudez, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The diseases are tuberculosis outside the lungs and focal complications of brucellosis, another bacterial infection. They are hard to differ by symptoms alone, and both cause much illness and death in many countries.

The team developed a multiplex real-time PCR assay, a test that detects several targets at once. It picks up Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the brucellosis bacterium in a single run on a patient's sample. A fast, sure answer matters because the two diseases need different drugs. The test shortens the guesswork that delays the right treatment.
plos-pone-0004626:
Doctors and health workers do not always see the same sickness in the same child, a study by John Wagai, John Senga, Greg Fegan, and co-authors shows in PLOS ONE in 2009. Case management guidelines use a limited set of clinical features to guide assessment and treatment of common childhood diseases in poor countries. The whole system rests on workers recognizing those features correctly.

Using video records of clinical signs, the team assessed agreement among experts. They also assessed whether Kenyan health workers could identify the signs shown. Disagreement at this basic level means children with the same illness can receive different care. The findings point to where training and guidelines need strengthening, in the first minutes of a sick child's assessment.
plos-pone-0004726:
Chandrajit Chatterjee and Ram Sarkar proposed a step wise math method to model and forecast malaria cases, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Malaria stays one of the worst health problems in the world today. Case counts shift with age, sex, social life, weather, and how the disease spreads in a place.

A good forecast must weigh those drivers and the spread pattern at once. The team built a staged curve fitting method for that task. Better forecasts help clinics stock drugs and staff in time. They also help target spray and net campaigns where cases will rise. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004826:
José Igual and colleagues asked whether compensatory mitigation for marine bycatch suffices for long lived seabirds, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Following the polluter pays principle, it was proposed that the local long line fishing industry fund eradication of terrestrial predators at seabird breeding colonies. That would compensate for bycatch caused by fishing activity under a mitigation scheme debated by managers and conservation groups.

Models test if predator removal offsets birds lost at sea. For slow breeding species, gains may arrive too late. Buying years to extinction is not recovery. Direct bycatch reduction remains essential. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004926:
The Wnt signal tells cells when to grow and when to specialize. Its key messenger is a protein called beta-catenin. When beta-catenin builds up unchecked, it helps drive many cancers. Geng Wu and co-authors studied one control on it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined the Wnt co-receptor LRP6. They asked how it blocks the enzyme GSK3.

Once Wnt switches LRP6 on, the receptor gains phosphate tags. Those tags sit on repeating motifs in its tail. The study shows the tagged motifs directly inhibit GSK3. So beta-catenin escapes destruction, and the growth signal stays on. The work details a control switch at the heart of development and cancer.
plos-pone-0005026:
Tinnitus is ringing in the ears with no outside source. Its causes remain incompletely understood. Some people blame electromagnetic fields for their symptoms. Michael Landgrebe and colleagues examined a possible link in PLOS ONE in 2009. They asked whether tinnitus and electromagnetic hypersensitivity are associated. They also asked whether the two share a mechanism.

The data hint at overlapping pathways. People reporting electromagnetic sensitivity showed particular tinnitus patterns. That is not proof of a shared cause. It is a first step toward testing one. The work treats both conditions seriously without overstating the evidence. Such care is rare in a field full of strong claims.
plos-pone-0005126:
Aptamers are DNA strands that grip targets like antibodies. Some fold into four-stranded knots called G-quadruplexes. Tao Li, Erkang Wang and Shaojun Dong improved them in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their strategy was grafting. Proven pieces were combined into new designs. Some G-quadruplex aptamers bind hemin and act as DNA enzymes.

The grafting produced aptamers with better binding. It also produced DNAzymes with higher activity. Mix-and-match design beats random search here. The recipe is general, not tied to one target. Biotech gains better molecular tools. Sensors, diagnostics and research reagents all use aptamers. A design shortcut shortens their development. The work shows rational design catching up with selection.
plos-pone-0005226:
Even when a person rests quietly, the brain produces slow, organized waves of activity. Those waves, seen in functional brain scans, are thought to reflect the brain's built-in networks. He and colleagues uncovered the modular layout of that resting activity in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The analysis sorted spontaneous activity into modules, groups of regions that work together. Mapping that layout is one of the hard problems in neuroscience, since it must be drawn from noise-like signals. A trusted map of resting networks helps researchers spot what changes in brain disease.
plos-pone-0005326:
Genes that appear and disappear together across many genomes usually work together. A phyletic vector records, for one gene, the pattern of presence and absence across species. Li and colleagues matched those patterns to detect biochemical pathways in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Their probabilistic matching weighs how closely two genes' patterns align. Closely similar vectors flag genes that likely share a pathway. The method turns genome catalogs from many species into pathway maps, without any wet-lab work for each new organism. Each new genome sequenced makes these maps sharper, since more species means more rows in the table and a clearer view of which genes keep the same friends across time.
plos-pone-0005426:
Akihiko Ozawa, Richard Speaker, and Iris Lindberg described a human enzyme in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Cells often attach fatty tags to proteins after the proteins are made, and those tags change what the proteins do. Yet the enzymes that attach one kind of tag were still poorly known.

The authors found and described an enzyme that adds a short fat chain to a protein building block. They tested what speeds it up, what slows it down, and what it needs to work. The careful profile fills a gap in basic knowledge about how cells mark and control their proteins.
plos-pone-0005526:
Daniela Nitsch and co-authors built a method to find disease genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Gene hunts often narrow a disease to a stretch of chromosome that still holds dozens of genes. Only a few of them can be tested in the lab.

Their method uses networks of known gene links to rank the genes in such a stretch. Genes tied to similar diseases or pathways rise to the top of the list. Ranking well saves years of lab work and helps families learn the cause of a disease sooner.
plos-pone-0005626:
Peter Daley and co-authors ran a pilot study on preparing sputum for tuberculosis tests in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Looking at sputum under a microscope is a main way to diagnose tuberculosis, but it misses many cases. Treating the sputum first can make the germs easier to see.

The team compared two quick preparation methods, each taking under an hour. They measured how much each method added to the accuracy of the smear test. Cheap gains in accuracy matter most in the poor settings where tuberculosis is commonest. Microscopy is still the front-line test in most poor countries, so gains there reach the most patients.
plos-pone-0005726:
Rhona McDonald and colleagues profiled a remarkable protein from horse sweat in 2009. Horses are odd among mammals for sweating a protein-rich fluid to cool down. The main protein, latherin, acts like a soap, helping sweat spread through the oily coat.

The team read latherin's full amino acid chain from its gene. The chain is much the same in horses from four far-apart regions, a sign its job is finely tuned. Latherin also shows up in horse saliva. Knowing its makeup helps explain how horses cope with heat and hard work, a matter of real care in racing and sport.
plos-pone-0005826:
Gail Rattinger and Lisa Bero examined in 2009 whether drug company funding tilts head-to-head trials of diabetes drugs. When a sponsor pits its drug against a rival's, results tend to favor the sponsor. The drugs studied, thiazolidinediones, are among the costliest oral options for type 2 diabetes.

The team looked for factors tied to favorable results and conclusions in such trials. Design choices, like doses chosen for the rival drug, can stack the deck quietly. Documenting those factors helps doctors read industry trials with care. It also supports rules for fairer comparative testing.
plos-pone-0005926:
Eosinophils are white blood cells best known for fighting parasites and driving allergy. In 2009, Fanny Legrand, Virginie Driss, Gaëtane Woerly and colleagues found something unexpected on these cells in humans. Their PLOS ONE paper reports a working receptor complex, built from CD3 and a gamma-delta T cell receptor, on the eosinophil surface.

That kind of receptor was thought to belong to T cells alone. Finding a distinct, working version on eosinophils widens what these cells can do in the body's first line of defense. The result invites a fresh look at allergy and infection, where eosinophils may sense threats in ways no one had credited to them.
plos-pone-0006026:
The microbes in the gut help digest food, but they also talk to the immune system. Joshua Uronis, Marcus Mühlbauer, Hans Herfarth and colleagues asked in 2009 whether changing that microbial mix changes cancer risk. Their PLOS ONE paper studies colitis-linked colorectal cancer, a cancer that grows out of long gut inflammation, as in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis.

Shifting the gut community shifted how prone the animals were to that cancer, the title reports. A result of this kind makes the microbiome a possible lever for prevention, not just a bystander. It also sharpens the question for patients with gut inflammation: which microbes guard them, and which ones raise their risk over time.
plos-pone-0006126:
Circles of DNA float free of the chromosomes in every eukaryotic cell. Zoya Cohen and Sara Lavi asked in 2009 where those circles come from. Their PLOS ONE paper shows extrachromosomal circular DNA forming in a mammalian cell-free system without any DNA replication, testing a pool of circles built from repeated chromosomal sequences.

Circular DNA has been tied to genomic instability, aging and a backup way of lengthening telomeres. A formation route that skips replication changes how each of those links is read. The cell-free system strips the process to its core parts, letting the team name what circle making truly requires.
plos-pone-0006226:
Bacteria that shrug off methicillin pose a lasting threat in hospitals. Ida Autiero, Susan Costantini, and Giovanni Colonna modelled that resistance as a whole-system problem in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Living systems stay functional under attack, a property called robustness, and resistance is one form of it.

A systems biology model treats the bacterium as a network rather than a single drug target. Networks show where several weak points might be hit together. The approach can suggest drug combinations that a one-target view would miss. It also explains why resistance survives single-drug pressure so well.
plos-pone-0006326:
Averaging millions of cells into one measurement hides how individual cells differ. Alan Diercks, Heather Kostner, and Adrian Ozinsky present a new method in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their real-time PCR approach reads several genes at once in many single-cell samples. Decoding multicellular complexity requires procedures that beat those averaged limits.

Simultaneous multiplexed detection lets each cell report several genes, not just one. Cell populations can then be split into real subgroups rather than blurred. Heterogeneity matters in immunity, cancer, and development. The method gives labs a practical route to single-cell detail.
plos-pone-0006426:
Maria Karanika and co-authors drew on a meningitis registry for a 2009 PLOS ONE study of sick children. Meningitis in childhood still kills many patients in many countries. Doctors need fast ways to tell which germ is causing acute bacterial meningitis. The team analyzed clinical symptoms and lab findings recorded in the registry.

The goal was to find signs that point to the likely pathogen before full test results arrive. Early clues can speed the choice of the right treatment. Registry data let the authors test these clues across many real cases. The work supports quicker, better-targeted care for a dangerous disease of childhood.
plos-pone-0006526:
Roberta Pastorino and co-authors studied immune genes and multiple sclerosis in Sardinia for PLOS ONE in 2009. The human leukocyte antigen complex on chromosome 6 has been unambiguously associated with multiple sclerosis. The region's features are especially complex, making fine mapping hard. Sardinia's population has a distinct genetic history that can help.

The team studied association between protective and deleterious HLA alleles and MS in central east Sardinia. Some alleles raise risk while others lower it. An island population with high MS rates is a powerful place to separate those effects. The results refine which immune genes matter in this disease.
plos-pone-0006626:
Anna Barnes, Edward Bullmore, and John Suckling measured slow brain recovery after mental effort in PLOS ONE in 2009. In functional magnetic resonance imaging, the brain's response to experimental manipulation is almost always assumed to be independent of endogenous oscillations. The team tested that assumption. They examined endogenous human brain dynamics following cognitive effort.

Their title reports those dynamics recover slowly following effort. In other words, the brain's background state takes time to settle. Experiments that ignore this carryover may misread task effects. The finding matters for the design of nearly all brain imaging studies.
plos-pone-0006726:
Henrik Walter and colleagues asked how long emotion regulation effects last in the brain in PLOS ONE in 2009. People can voluntarily calm their reactions to unpleasant scenes. Brain imaging shows the amygdala quiets during such regulation. The amygdala is a hub for threat and emotion. Little was known about whether the quieting survives after regulation stops.

The study tracked the temporal dynamics of voluntary emotion regulation. Participants regulated, then stopped, while brain activity was recorded. The key question was sustainability of the neural effect. Lasting effects would mean a short effort buys longer calm. Brief effects would argue for different training designs. The findings inform therapies built on emotion regulation skills.
plos-pone-0006826:
Iraad F. Bronner and his team read gene use across a set of brain diseases in PLOS ONE in 2009. The diseases are the tauopathies, marked by bad tau protein in the brain. The set holds Alzheimer's disease and Pick's disease. It also holds two more: progressive supranuclear palsy and frontotemporal dementia. The four look much alike in the clinic and in the lab. That likeness has long slowed work on all of them.

Full scans of gene use told the four apart. The scans also found paths of cell work that all four share. Marks that split look-alike diseases can sharpen diagnosis. Shared paths hint that one drug might help more than one disease. The scan gives the field a map it had lacked.
plos-pone-0006926:
Zheng Kou, Yongdong Li, Zuohua Yin, and colleagues reported a bird flu survey in PLOS ONE in 2009. They sampled wild birds across fourteen provinces of China. The target was the highly pathogenic H5N1 influenza virus. Sampling ran from April 2004 to August 2007.

H5N1 had emerged in Asia in 1996 and later spread to Europe and Africa. The authors note that monitoring and data analysis in mainland China were not yet sufficient. Their survey gathered field evidence on where the virus appeared in wild birds. Such surveys help health officials track a virus that threatens poultry, wildlife, and people.
plos-pone-0007026:
Shuming Zou, Hiroyasu Kamei, Zubin Modi, and colleagues charted growth factor genes in zebrafish in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulin-like growth factors steer development, growth, and lifespan. Most vertebrates, humans included, carry one IGF-1 gene and one IGF-2 gene. Zebrafish turned out to be different.

The team found and characterized four distinct IGF genes in this fish. They traced how the genes were duplicated and how they diverged. They also found new roles in building the body's midline and the notochord. Extra gene copies let one fish split old jobs in new ways.
plos-pone-0007126:
Alice Mado Proverbio, Serena Mariani, Alberto Zani, and colleagues probed how the brain stores names in PLOS ONE in 2009. A long debate asks whether distinct meaning domains sit in distinct brain systems. Patients with naming problems sometimes lose one class of words only. Brain imaging had not settled the map. The team used paired words as their test.

They compared a proper name, Barack Obama, with a matching common noun phrase, President Elect. Brain responses, recorded as ERPs, differed between the pair. Different storage for names and descriptions supports the domain view. It also shows how identity and role are coded apart.
plos-pone-0007226:
Anna-Karin Roos, Fredrik Eriksson, James A. Timmons, and colleagues studied DNA delivery through skin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Electric pulses can push molecules into living cells, a method called electroporation. It had become popular for delivering DNA in living tissue for gene therapy and vaccines.

The authors test skin electroporation in detail. They measure effects on transgene expression, how long delivered DNA persists, and the local tissue environment. Their results matter for designers of DNA vaccines and gene treatments who need both strong expression and acceptable local tissue damage levels.
plos-pone-0007326:
Angela M. C. Rose, Sibylle Gerstl, Ali E.-H. Mahamane, and colleagues evaluated rapid meningitis tests during an outbreak in Niger in 2009. The Pastorex test is a main rapid diagnostic for meningococcal disease in Africa's meningitis belt. Earlier evaluations used heated, centrifuged spinal fluid under good lab conditions, which field clinics often lack.

The authors test two rapid diagnostics for Neisseria meningitidis serogroup A in the field. The 2006 outbreak setting shows real-world performance. Their PLOS ONE results matter because quick, accurate diagnosis guides vaccination campaigns during fast-moving meningitis outbreaks.
plos-pone-0007426:
Sébastien Ballesteros, Elisabeta Vergu, and Bernard Cazelles published a modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how influenza A changes over time. Flu epidemics return again and again, and the usual explanation was steady, gradual drift in the virus. Newer evidence hinted that change in its main surface protein might instead come in bursts. The authors used simple mathematical models to sort this out.

Their models show how gradual genetic change can still produce a punctuated pattern at the level that matters for immunity. Long quiet stretches are broken by sudden jumps in the surface protein. That pattern helps explain why flu can slip past immune defenses built against earlier strains. The work links small steady changes to the big epidemic cycles people actually experience.
plos-pone-0007526:
Alfredo Mendoza-Vargas and colleagues published a genome-wide mapping study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on E. coli, the most studied bacterium in science. Despite decades of work, a major share of its transcription start sites remained unknown. Those sites mark where reading of a gene begins. Without them, the circuits controlling gene expression stay partly hidden. The team set out to map them across the whole genome.

Their survey identified start sites, promoters, and the binding sites of transcription factors at genome scale. The results enrich RegulonDB, the reference database for E. coli regulation. A fuller map means researchers can model the bacterium's control systems with fewer gaps. Even a model organism, it turns out, still holds basic secrets. This study fills in many of them at once.
plos-pone-0007626:
John Horner and Mark Goodwin published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the dome-headed dinosaur Pachycephalosaurus. Some dinosaurs changed shape dramatically as they grew, through extended youth and late growth spurts. With few individuals preserved, the stages of that transformation are hard to find. The team studied skulls across the growth series of this Upper Cretaceous plant-eater. The domes told an extreme story.

The skull's shape changed so much with age that young and old look like separate species. Late-stage growth did most of the reshaping. That warns paleontologists: some named species may be juveniles of known ones. Counting dinosaur diversity demands care about growth, not just form. The study is a landmark in reading dinosaur lives from their bones. It turns a strange dome into a biography.
plos-pone-0007726:
Haishan Li and C. David Pauza published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests two immune-regulating compounds on a special class of human T cells. The compounds are a natural prostaglandin, called 15d-PGJ2, and a diabetes drug, rosiglitazone. Both are predicted to calm autoimmune disease.

The target cells, Vdelta2 T cells, play a role in autoimmunity in animals and people. Before this study, how the compounds affect them was unknown. The authors measured the cells' responses in the lab. The results help judge whether these drugs could treat autoimmune disease safely.
plos-pone-0007826:
Hua Zhang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links patterns of tiny RNAs to outcomes in children with leukemia. MicroRNAs are short molecules that tune gene activity. They play critical roles in cancers, including adult leukemia.

Their role in pediatric acute leukemia was less clear. The authors measured microRNAs that were abnormally expressed in young patients. Certain patterns tracked with clinical prognosis. Others predicted relapse in the central nervous system, a feared event. If the patterns hold up, a small blood test could flag children who need stronger treatment early.
plos-pone-0007926:
Rodrigo Calado and colleagues reported a family study of severe liver disease in PLOS ONE in 2009. They looked at faults in the genes that build telomerase, an enzyme that keeps the ends of chromosomes at a safe length. Such faults were already known to harm bone marrow.

In the families studied, the same kind of fault tracked with a wide range of grave liver problems. When telomeres grow too short, cells that divide often suffer first, and the liver proved no exception. The work widens the list of ills tied to worn chromosome ends and gives doctors a genetic clue when liver failure runs in a family.
plos-pone-0008026:
Angelique Gougelet and colleagues tested an antibody against stubborn blood cancers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lymphoma and myeloma cells often resist both drugs and radiation. High levels of the signal IL-6 track with that resistance, so blocking IL-6 looked like a way to soften the cells.

Cancer cell lines treated with the antibody stayed just as hard to kill. Neither drug response nor radiation response improved. A clear no is still useful: it steers teams away from a costly dead end and toward other ways of breaking resistance in these cancers.
plos-pone-0008126:
Tao Huang and colleagues forecast drug effects from gene activity watched over time in PLOS ONE in 2009. Side effects often surface late, after years of costly drug work, or even after a drug reaches patients. An early warning drawn from the first hours of gene response could save both money and health.

Profiles of gene activity across time carried enough signal to predict how bodies would answer a drug, including foreign compounds. The forecasts were built on patterns, not single genes. Drug teams could use such a screen to drop risky candidates while dropping them is still cheap.
plos-pone-0008226:
Declan P. McKernan and colleagues studied gut immunity in animal models in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Irritable bowel syndrome is often viewed as a stress-related disorder. It involves faulty communication among the brain, gut, and immune system. Stress is known to alter innate immune responses. Yet little work had linked that fact to bowel symptoms.

The team measured toll-like receptor messages in the colonic lining of two animal models. These receptors sense microbes and trigger immune defenses. Expression rose selectively in models relevant to the syndrome. The result supports a role for innate immunity in irritable bowel complaints.
plos-pone-0008326:
Huabin Zhao, Binghua Ru, and Emma C. Teeling traced a vision gene in mammals in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mammals spread into many light environments, from bright savanna to dark caves. That spread is linked to adaptive changes in their visual systems. Rhodopsin is the light-sensitive protein used for dim-light vision. Its properties help set what an animal can see at night.

The authors studied rhodopsin molecular evolution across mammals in low light habitats. Comparing gene sequences reveals how selection tuned the protein. Such changes show evolution acting at the molecular level. The work links ecology to the chemistry of sight.
plos-pone-0008426:
Nahuel Fittipaldi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010 on Streptococcus suis, a germ that harms pigs. They looked at pili, the thin hair-like parts on the cell surface. Those parts help the germ stick to host cells and spread in the body.

The team changed a gene for one pilus part, called the ancillary pilin. With that part gone, the pili still formed, but they were made of the main part alone. The result shows how the pilus is built, step by step. It also points to parts that drugs might block to weaken the germ.
plos-pone-0008526:
Yizhe Tang and co-authors build a new adenovirus for cancer gene therapy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Safe and effective cancer medicines are still needed. Many patients have diseases that current treatments cannot cure. Adenoviruses can carry therapeutic genes into tumor cells. But a single virus type may infect too narrow a range of cancers. The team derive a triple mosaic adenovirus instead.

A mosaic virus mixes capsid parts from different adenovirus types. Mixing parts can broaden which cancer cells it enters. It may also evade immune defenses that block one type alone. The paper describes how the triple mosaic was made and tested.
plos-pone-0008626:
Reiko Sanokawa-Akakura and co-authors study amyloid toxicity in fruit flies in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Amyloid beta is the protein fragment that builds up in Alzheimer disease. FKBP52 is a large immunophilin, a protein that helps fold other proteins. Copper balance in cells also affects amyloid harm. The team use Drosophila, the fruit fly, to test these factors together. Flies offer fast genetics for brain disease models.

They find FKBP52 controls amyloid beta toxicity in the flies. Copper homeostasis, keeping copper at steady levels, also shapes that toxicity. Both factors may be targets for limiting amyloid damage. Fly work can reveal modifiers hard to find in mammals.
plos-pone-0008726:
Claudio Rolli, Thomas Seufferlein, Ralf Kemkemer, and colleagues watched tumor cells squeeze through tight spaces. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used tiny channels built in the lab. A cancer cell's inner skeleton, the cytoskeleton, gives it shape and stiffness. To invade tissue, a cell must soften and deform. How skeleton layout governs that squeezing was unclear.

Cells crawled through channels narrower than themselves while the team filmed them. Stiffer, well-organized cells struggled where softer ones slipped through. Speeds and shapes revealed which layouts favor invasion. The setup offers a clean way to test drugs meant to slow cancer spread.
plos-pone-0008826:
Qian Han, Haizhen Ding, Howard Robinson, and colleagues solved the structure of a fruit fly enzyme that makes brain signals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, DDC, finishes the making of dopamine and serotonin. It clips a piece off their precursor building blocks. Both finished chemicals steer mood, movement, and sleep. Knowing the enzyme's shape helps explain how it picks its targets.

The crystal structure shows the active site in fine detail. Tests then measured which related compounds the enzyme accepts. Shape and pickiness together reveal its working rules. The fly enzyme models the human version used in brain chemistry.
plos-pone-0008926:
Sinead Leahy and colleagues published the full genome of Methanobrevibacter ruminantium in PLOS ONE in 2010. The microbe lives in the rumen, the first stomach of cattle and sheep, where it makes methane gas. Methane warms the planet far more strongly than carbon dioxide does. Farm animals release large amounts of it through burping.

The team read the microbe's DNA letter by letter and mapped its genes. They looked for weak points that might let farmers or drug makers slow methane output. The genome points to surface proteins and enzymes that are found only in this kind of methane maker. Those targets could guide vaccines or feed additives that cut emissions from livestock.
plos-pone-0009026:
Min Ki Jee and co-authors pushed human fat stem cells back toward a younger state, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stromal cells from fat tissue can become several cell types, but they are not full stem cells. The team combined low oxygen with a new antioxidant compound, called a DHP derivative. Both tricks mimic conditions that keep cells primitive.

Treated cells turned back the clock, a change called de-differentiation. They switched on markers of more primitive stem cells. Reprogrammed fat cells could one day supply repair tissue from a patient's own body. The recipe avoids viruses, which makes it attractive for future medical use.
plos-pone-0009126:
Pierre Becquart and co-authors surveyed rural Gabon for signs of past Ebola infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Zaire ebolavirus is the deadliest member of the Ebola virus family. How widely it circulates between the famous outbreaks was unclear. Gabon contains both regions with past epidemics and quiet forest areas.

The large survey ran for three years and covered 4,349 people in all. Blood tests found antibody proof of past infection in many of them. Immune cells that remember the virus were common as well. High silent immunity suggests the virus reaches these people more often than outbreaks show.
plos-pone-0009226:
Huaiping Zhu, Hong Qian, and Guangpu Li published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It concerns endocytosis, the process by which cells pull material inside. A protein called Rab5 acts as a switch for the early steps. Rabex-5 switches Rab5 on, and Rabaptin-5 helps in the same process.

Rabex-5 can activate Rab5 through two distinct pathways. One route also creates positive feedback, where active Rab5 boosts its own activation. The team found that this feedback switches on only after a delay. That timing detail shapes how cells start forming the vesicles that carry cargo inward.
plos-pone-0009326:
Youri Timsit and Péter Várnai published this DNA study in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA inside cells is twisted into supercoils, and that twisting shapes many cell functions. The overall form of a supercoiled molecule depends on local contacts where DNA segments lie side by side. Those contacts affect both the physics and the biology of the molecule.

The authors examine helical chirality, the handedness built into DNA's twist. They argue it links local interactions between segments to the molecule's global shape. A clear link between the small scale and the large would help predict how DNA folds. That folding decides which genes are reachable and when.
plos-pone-0009426:
Dalia Denapaite and co-authors published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Streptococcus mitis lives quietly in the human mouth and throat. It is the closest relative of Streptococcus pneumoniae, a major killer. Comparing the harmless cousin with the pathogen asks what makes one a commensal and the other a threat.

The team sequenced strain B6, a form unusually resistant to many antibiotics. Its genome runs about 2.15 million letters and encodes some 2,100 genes. A resistant commensal is a reservoir of resistance genes living beside us. The genome gives researchers the full text for asking what separates neighbor from pathogen.
plos-pone-0009526:
Louise Harrington and co-authors tested a drug in rats with lung hypertension in PLOS ONE in 2010. In that disease, pressure in the lung's vessels climbs. The right side of the heart must push harder and can swell and fail. Rats kept in low oxygen develop a like condition. The team gave them a drug called GW0742, which activates a receptor named PPAR beta delta.

The drug relaxed the lung vessels in treated rats. It also limited the swelling of the right heart. Few good treatments exist for this disease in people. A drug that both eases pressure and guards the heart is a lead worth pursuing.
plos-pone-0009626:
Eric McCollum and co-authors evaluated HIV testing of children in Malawi hospitals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many sick children in high prevalence areas are never tested for HIV. Staff shortages are a main barrier. The program shifted routine testing tasks to less costly, trained health workers. Two versions of that model were piloted in an urban hospital. The team reviewed how each performed.

Task shifting improved the program's outcomes, with more children tested and enrolled in care. That gain came without adding scarce doctors. The study backs a staffing strategy that many poor health systems can copy. It shows that who does a task can matter as much as the test itself.
plos-pone-0009726:
After spinal cord injury, nerve fibers usually fail to regrow. Yuxuan Wang and colleagues tested designer DNA strands that might lift that block. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The block comes partly from myelin, the coating around nerve fibers.

Myelin carries inhibitor proteins that stop axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, from growing. The strands, called aptamers, were built to block those inhibitors. With the inhibitors opposed, axons grew better in the tests. The approach points toward new ways to repair injured cords. Regrowing axons is a first step toward restoring lost movement.
plos-pone-0009826:
When cells face stress, they send chemical signals that can end in cell death or growth. Raphael Devillard and colleagues traced one such signal pathway in mouse cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The pathway runs through sphingolipids, fatty molecules that double as signals. A key enzyme, type-2 neutral sphingomyelinase, helped drive the response. The team linked it to both apoptosis, orderly cell death, and proliferation, cell multiplication. Stress signals can push a cell either way. Balancing those two outcomes matters in cancer and tissue repair. Mouse cells stand in for human cells in early tests.
plos-pone-0009926:
When the brain misreads a scene, two leading theories explain the error differently. Guido Hesselmann and colleagues weighed those theories against brain data. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. False inference means drawing a confident conclusion the evidence does not support.

Predictive coding says the brain constantly guesses the world and updates on errors. Evidence accumulation says it gathers proof until a threshold is crossed. Neuronal fluctuations, the noise in brain activity, helped tell the models apart. The debate shapes how scientists picture perception itself. Both theories still shape research on perception.
plos-pone-0010026:
The authors were William Hobbs, Richard Telford, H. John Birks, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study read lake mud in North America and Greenland. Tiny algae called diatoms leave shells in lake sediment. Their mix records the water and climate of past years.

By counting diatom groups in recent layers, the team measured how remote lakes changed in the twentieth century. They compared arctic lakes with alpine and forest lakes over the same years. The record helps separate climate effects from other forces acting on wild, far-off waters. Each layer adds a dated page to that history.
plos-pone-0010226:
The authors were Jing Xu, Jun-Ying Zhou, Wei-Zen Wei, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked why some cancer cells resist a death signal. The signal, called TRAIL, can trigger cancer cells to die by apoptosis. Many tumors resist it, and the mechanism behind that resistance was not fully understood when the team began.

The authors showed that a survival route inside cells, the Akt pathway, plays an important role. When Akt signaling is active, human cancer cells withstand TRAIL better. Blocking that survival route could make TRAIL-based treatment work on tumors that now shrug it off.
plos-pone-0010326:
Catarina Lira-Medeiros, Christian Parisod, Ricardo Fernandes and others examined mangrove plants for PLOS ONE in 2010. Their focus was epigenetic change, meaning chemical marks that alter gene activity without altering the DNA code itself. One such mark adds a methyl group to a DNA base. Plants can pass these marks to their offspring. Stress from salt, heat, or living things may set them off.

The team studied a mangrove species that grows in sharply different natural settings. They compared marks across plants from those contrasting homes. If marks differ where conditions differ, marks may help plants cope locally. That idea matters as coasts change fast under climate pressure. Mangroves protect shorelines, so how they adapt is worth knowing.
plos-pone-0010426:
Jaakko Pohjoismäki and co-workers examined how heart muscle DNA is organized across life and disease for PLOS ONE in 2010. Heart cells carry many copies of a small mitochondrial genome. Adult heart copies form tangled structures, including doubled and branched forms. Why the heart keeps its DNA this way was unclear. The team compared organization, copying, and counts across development and pathology.

Changes over a lifetime could explain why some heart diseases emerge late. A maintenance style fit for youth may fail with age or illness. Mitochondrial DNA faults are tied to several heart conditions. Mapping the normal pattern is needed before faults can be spotted. This study supplies that map for the human heart.
plos-pone-0010526:
Junsong Sun and colleagues coaxed a complex hydrogen-making enzyme to mature in a foreign host for PLOS ONE in 2010. Hydrogen gas is a major candidate biofuel. Microbes make it with hydrogenase enzymes, intricate machines built around nickel and iron. These enzymes are complex and easily wrecked by air. Building them in easy lab hosts had been a bottleneck for biofuel work.

The team got the enzyme expressed and matured outside its native microbe. That step matters because engineering better enzymes needs a workable host. A nickel-iron enzyme that can be produced and tweaked opens design space. Clean hydrogen from biology remains a long-term prize. This study removes one specific obstacle on that road.
plos-pone-0010626:
Jasper van den Boorn and colleagues combined three treatments against melanoma in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma that has spread is hard to treat with standard drugs. Yet the cancer is visible to the immune system, which gives immunotherapy a chance.

One drug, monobenzone, removes skin pigment and exposes pigment cells to attack. Two helper compounds, imiquimod and CpG, then rally immune cells. Together the trio shrank tumors and extended survival in the mice. Turning the pigment system into a target may offer a new route for patients who run out of options.
plos-pone-0010726:
Tanja Musch and colleagues showed how certain drugs force cancer cells to grow up, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some tumor cells keep stem-like traits that help them resist treatment. Nucleoside drugs, which mimic DNA building blocks, can push such cells to mature instead of killing them outright.

After drug treatment, key stem cell factors inside the cells were destroyed. The destruction ran through caspase enzymes, usually known for dismantling dying cells. As the factors fell, the cells lost their stem-like behavior. Forcing maturity is a gentler attack plan than poisoning, and it may work where standard drugs fail.
plos-pone-0010826:
Laura Kananen and fellow Finnish researchers published this study in PLOS ONE in 2010. They asked whether hard experiences in childhood leave a lasting mark on telomeres, the caps that protect the ends of chromosomes and shorten with age and stress. Their data came from a large national health survey carried out in Finland at the start of the century.

The team measured telomere length in blood cells from adults with anxiety disorders and matched adults without them. Telomeres did not differ across the whole group, yet older patients with anxiety showed clearly shorter telomeres. Childhood hardship was also tied to shorter telomeres in adulthood, in patients and controls alike. Kananen and colleagues suggest early stress can echo in the body for decades, which matters for how doctors think about anxiety and aging.
plos-pone-0010926:
E Besray Unal, Attila Gursoy and Burak Erman published this drug design study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Peptide drugs, short chains of amino acids, can block disease proteins with fewer side effects than many small chemicals. But no set way existed to design such a blocker from scratch for a chosen target. Their method, VitAL, needs no examples of known peptides to learn from.

The algorithm builds a peptide step by step, docking residue pairs along a chosen path across the target protein's surface, using a simplified model to find the binding site first. Unal and colleagues present a fully computational route from a protein structure to a candidate inhibitor. If it generalizes, de novo peptide design could shorten the search for treatments against proteins that resist conventional drugs.
plos-pone-0011026:
Berna Atik, S Claiborne Johnston and Deborah Dean published this stroke risk study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Narrowed neck arteries are seeded with plaques that can trigger stroke, and plaques often harbor Chlamydia pneumoniae, a respiratory bacterium. The team had earlier linked the bacterial burden in plaques to inflammatory signals, and now examined an inflammation-mediating enzyme called Lp-PLA2.

They studied tissue from patients having plaque-removal surgery, staining it for the enzyme, immune cells, the bacterium, and inflammatory markers, alongside blood measurements of enzyme level and activity. Atik and colleagues test whether infected plaques are also the plaques richest in this enzyme. The question matters because Lp-PLA2 is both a drug target and a blood test used to judge cardiovascular risk.
plos-pone-0011126:
Touchon and Rocha studied bacterial immune systems in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria carry CRISPR, a stored record of past virus attacks used for defense. In common gut bacteria, the authors found these systems were unusually small, slow to change and narrow in scope.

The team also mapped counter systems that viruses use against CRISPR. Together the results show a stripped down form of immunity, tuned to a stable gut setting. That economy is of interest for gene editing, which borrows CRISPR tools. It also helps explain how gut bacteria and their viruses coexist over long periods.
plos-pone-0011226:
Horney, Moore, Davis and colleagues surveyed North Carolina during the 2009 flu pandemic for PLOS ONE in 2010. A new H1N1 vaccine had just become available. The team asked who planned to take it, who followed advice to keep distance when ill, and where people got their information.

Answers revealed what drove pandemic behavior in that population. Trust and information sources shaped vaccine intent and daily choices. Health agencies can use such findings to craft clearer messages in the next outbreak. Building public trust before a crisis, the study implies, is as vital as the vaccine itself.
plos-pone-0011326:
Mizuno, Hosogi, Park and colleagues studied wheat crosses in PLOS ONE in 2010. Breeding tetraploid wheat with a wild relative can produce hybrids that sicken and die, a barrier called hybrid necrosis. The team linked that death to a reaction like the hypersensitive response plants use against germs.

In effect, the hybrid's own defense alarm fires without any germ present. That explains why some crosses fail despite healthy parents. Breeders can use this knowledge to avoid fatal combinations in advance. It clears a path for bringing useful wild traits into wheat without wasting seasons on doomed crosses.
plos-pone-0011426:
Alexander Seewald and co-authors measured in 2010 how much genetically identical worms still differ from one another. A cage of isogenic roundworms shares the same DNA, yet individuals vary in stress response and lifespan. The team used a glowing reporter that marks a stress protein known to predict longevity and stress resistance in these worms.

They clustered the two-dimensional glow patterns to turn worm-to-worm variation into firm numbers instead of impressions. Quantifying variation among genetic twins isolates the share of difference that DNA cannot explain. That share is where environment, chance, and cell noise leave their marks. The method gives biologists a sharper tool for a deep question: how much of an animal's fate is written in its genes, and how much is decided by everything else?
plos-pone-0011526:
Taku Kashiyama and co-authors compared in 2010 the two calcium channels that frogs use to trigger muscle contraction. Muscles contract when calcium floods out of internal storage through ryanodine receptor channels. Frogs carry two forms, alpha and beta, side by side in the same fibers. The team tested them in a muscle cell line, asking whether the pair is mere backup or a division of labor.

The two receptors produced distinct intracellular calcium signals, differing in shape and timing. One cell can thus tune its calcium messages with fine control by choosing which channel speaks. Calcium is a universal signal, so its dialect matters in heart, brain, and gland cells too. The frog's two-channel system is a clean model of how a cell gets many messages out of one ion.
plos-pone-0011626:
Ta-Chien Chan and co-authors built a daily flu warning system in PLOS ONE in 2010. Public health teams need to spot unusual rises in flu-like illness early, before an epidemic takes hold. Any alert carries uncertainty, so a useful system must weigh how likely a true outbreak is, not just count cases.

Their model combines place and time in a Bayesian framework, which handles uncertainty openly. It watches daily illness reports across areas and flags abnormal patterns with a stated level of confidence. Health officials using such a system can act sooner while knowing how much trust to place in each alert.
plos-pone-0011726:
Todd Brusko and co-authors engineered human regulatory T cells with chosen targets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Regulatory T cells calm immune responses, and boosting them could treat autoimmune disease and transplant rejection. Broadly boosting them, however, risks suppressing the whole immune system, including useful defences against infection.

By transferring T cell receptor genes into these cells, the team created regulators aimed at a specific antigen. Targeted peacekeepers could settle the immune attack where it occurs without a blanket shutdown. The approach points toward tailored cell therapy for autoimmunity and transplantation.
plos-pone-0011826:
Jessica Bogs and co-authors probed what makes H5N1 bird flu so deadly, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Highly harmful bird flu viruses grow out of mild forerunners. They stand apart from all other flu viruses by a polybasic cut site in their surface protein, found in subtypes H5 and H7. That site was long treated as the whole key to their deadliness.

The team tested the power of a low-harm virus to cause grave disease, and found harm factors that sit beyond that famed cut site. The added culprits round out the picture of this flu's deadliness, and they inform risk checks on new strains.
plos-pone-0011926:
Yaolong Chen and colleagues audited in 2010 how well trial results are reported in the abstracts of five leading Chinese medical journals. Abstracts of randomized controlled trials matter because many readers judge, and sometimes act on, a trial from its abstract alone. Little was known about reporting quality in these journals.

The audit checked whether the abstracts carry the details readers need, such as how patients were assigned and what the main results were. Gaps in an abstract can mislead even when the full trial was done well. The findings give editors a concrete checklist of what to demand before a trial abstract reaches doctors' screens.
plos-pone-0012026:
Matthias Negri, Maurizio Recanatini, and Rolf Hartmann studied in 2010 an estrogen-making enzyme by watching it move. The enzyme, 17β-HSD1, catalyzes the final step in making estradiol, the strongest estrogen, making it an attractive target for breast cancer treatment. In solution, such enzymes exist as a shifting ensemble of shapes, not one fixed pose.

By investigating the enzyme's dynamic motion, the team gained insight into its kinetics and how ligands bind. A moving target binds drugs differently than a frozen diagram suggests. Motion-aware design could yield blockers that fit the enzyme as it actually behaves in the body.
plos-pone-0012126:
Xiao Chang, Shuai Liu, Yong-Tao Yu, and co-authors mapped gene activity over time in an antibiotic-making bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bacterium's full genome had been read a few years earlier, and a custom chip let the team watch nearly all its genes at once. They wanted to see how genes group into working modules as the cell grows and produces.

They identified sets of transcript units that rise and fall together, and charted how those sets are organized across the genome. A module map turns a flood of gene data into a readable wiring diagram. Since this bacterium makes a useful antibiotic, understanding its switches may help raise yields in industrial production.
plos-pone-0012226:
Gábor Firneisz, Tímea Varga, Gabriella Lengyel, and co-authors measured an enzyme in the blood of patients with fatty liver disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fatty liver tied to insulin resistance is now extremely common and quietly progresses toward serious liver damage, yet finding it early usually takes scans or biopsy. The enzyme they measured, DPP-4, is already famous in diabetes care, where blockers of it are standard drugs.

Comparing patients with diabetes, patients with fatty liver, and healthy controls, they tested whether the enzyme's blood activity tracks insulin resistance and liver disease. A blood marker would let doctors screen for fatty liver during routine diabetes visits. That matters because the disease is silent for years while still reversible.
plos-pone-0012326:
Martina Wengenroth, Maria Blatow, Martin Bendszus, and co-authors scanned the hearing cortex of people with Williams syndrome, in PLOS ONE in 2010. This rare genetic condition is famous for an unusual love of music and sound, alongside intellectual disability and a friendly social style. The team sought the brain basis of that musicality in the auditory cortex, the strip that first processes sound.

They found the auditory cortex leans leftward in these individuals, matching an all-at-once, holistic way of hearing rather than a detail-by-detail one. Linking a gene condition to both a brain asymmetry and a way of perceiving gives music cognition a rare concrete anchor. It may also inform teaching methods that work through sound for these learners.
plos-pone-0012426:
Aurore Liénard, Isabelle Merckaert, Yves Libert and colleagues followed young doctors after a communication course, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Talking well with patients is a core medical skill, and training courses can teach it. The open question was whether skills practiced in training survive the move to real wards, where time pressure and habit push back.

The team observed residents during real clinical rounds after the program. Many trained skills did transfer to the workplace, though unevenly. Knowing that transfer happens, and where it fades, helps schools design follow-up coaching rather than one-off courses. Better doctor-patient talk improves trust, safety, and how well patients follow treatment.
plos-pone-0012526:
Tomoharu Osada, Hideki Ogino, Toshiaki Hino and colleagues found a chemical tagging step required for nuclei to fuse after fertilization in mice, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. After sperm meets egg, the two parental nuclei must break their envelopes and mingle their genomes. That mingling needs fast rearrangement of chromatin and proteins, driven by chemical tags.

The team showed that polyADP-ribosylation, a fast tag added to proteins, is required for the pronuclei to fuse properly. Without it, development stalls at the first step. The discovery adds a concrete mechanism to the biology of conception and may inform fertility research.
plos-pone-0012626:
Ashworth, Teng, Kaufeld and co-authors traced a kidney problem to a protein called cofilin-1. The kidney's filter cells, podocytes, grip the filter with tiny feet full of actin fibres. Those fibres must shift as pressure changes, and cofilin helps remodel them.

Their 2010 work, spanning zebrafish, mice and human samples, showed that switching cofilin-1 off leads to protein leaking into urine. Protein in urine is an early sign of kidney failure, so the mechanism matters for patients. The study ties a small cell protein to a common disease sign.  Further patient samples would test how general the effect is.
plos-pone-0012726:
Cai, Huang, Feng and co-authors built a thirty-five gene signature for a common lymphoma. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma splits into subtypes that behave differently, and survival varies just as much. Sorting subtype and predicting survival both shape each patient's treatment plan directly.

Their 2010 work found one gene set that does both jobs at once, instead of needing two separate tests. A single readout that classifies and forecasts is simpler for clinics to run. It also hints the two tasks share deeper biology than their separate histories suggest.
plos-pone-0012826:
Sun, Pager, Luo and co-authors blocked hepatitis C copying with pieces of the virus's own core protein. The virus needs a host enzyme, DDX3X, to run its life cycle, and its core protein binds that enzyme. Their 2010 study cut the core into peptides and tested which pieces interfere.

Some core-derived peptides stopped the genome of the common 1b type from copying, by acting on DDX3X. Using the virus's own parts as blockers is a neat route to new antivirals. The host enzyme angle may also resist viral escape mutations better.
plos-pone-0329426: Galvez-Hernandez and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on AI in primary health care. The planned review covers tools that serve whole organizations and systems, not single patients. Examples include scheduling, records, and population health tasks. As a scoping review protocol, it sets the search and sorting rules in advance. Clinics need such a map before buying system-level AI.
plos-pone-0331726:
Sayeeda Tarannum and colleagues studied why staff in a specialist tuberculosis hospital in Bangladesh did or did not wear N95 respirator masks, which guard against catching the disease from patients.
