The team trained twenty-eight doctors, nurses, and support workers in fitting, wearing, and storing the masks, supplied each person with two months of masks. They watched and interviewed staff before and after the training.

At the start, nearly all nurses wore masks while no doctors or support workers did, a gap the study set out to explain. Interviews dug into how staff judged their own risk and what helped or blocked daily mask use, from comfort and supply to habit and workplace norms. The authors aim to guide protection programmes that fit how hospital staff actually behave.
plos-pone-0333726:
Richa Giri led a survey of citrus groves across Nepal. The target was the germ behind citrus greening. The disease is the worst threat to citrus crops in the world. The team took more than a thousand leaf samples from thirteen districts. A gene test flagged infected trees. Five samples were read in full to trace the strain's kin.

One in four samples tested positive. The disease is thus spread wide in Nepal. The strain matched the Asian form of the germ. Its closest kin came from India. The team urges clean young trees for new groves. They also back strict control of the insect that carries the germ.
plos-pone-0342726: Kolen and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on poor nutrition in people who lost a leg. These patients lost a major lower limb due to blood vessel disease. The title states the finding in strong terms: undernutrition is alarmingly common in this group. The team followed patients forward in time. Hungry patients heal slower, so this warning argues for routine nutrition checks after amputation.
plos-pone-0342926:
Mohajon and colleagues assessed a floating solar plant design for a wetland in Bangladesh in a 2026 study. Floating panels save scarce land, but owners need to know how fast output fades and whether the plant pays over its life. The design uses a ring-shaped float that lets some light pass through to water life below.

Checks supported the float's balance and buoyancy, and a light model tested whether water plants could still grow beneath. A learning model forecast how output and energy yield would decline over twenty-five years under local weather. Cost over the plant's life was worked out as well. Together, the checks frame floating solar as workable where land is tight.
plos-pone-0344826:
Ihor Kendiukhov reports an unusual experiment in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. An automated loop of AI programs proposed hypotheses. It then tested one hundred and forty-one of them. The subject was what AI models of cells actually learn. These models read single-cell gene activity. They are widely used in biology. The question was simple. Does the geometry inside them reflect real biology? Or is it just a training artefact?

Several patterns held up well. Gene neighbourhoods had genuine mathematical shape. Curved distance measures found regulatory gene pairs better. Two independently trained models agreed on the overall shape of gene space. Yet the strictest checks told a narrower story. Solid signal concentrated in immune tissue. The paper, negatives included, calibrates how much trust these models have earned.
plos-pone-0345426:
Pierre Lovinfosse leads a multi-center check of a scan meant to spot hidden rejection in transplanted kidneys without a biopsy. Silent rejection can damage a new kidney while blood tests still look calm, so clinics rely on scheduled biopsies. The scan tracks sugar use in the kidney, compared against a back muscle, and earlier small studies had raised hopes for it.

Across several centers and close to two hundred stable recipients, scan values overlapped heavily between normal kidneys and those with borderline or silent rejection. The scan measure did not track tissue damage scores, while older donor age did predict abnormal tissue. Lovinfosse and colleagues conclude the scan should not be used to rule out silent rejection, a clear negative result that can save clinics wasted effort.
plos-pone-0346626:
Iñigo Palacios-Martínez and colleagues censused two hundred thirty-two winter roosts of western jackdaws across the Iberian Peninsula to see who shares the night. Most roosts were shared with other species, mainly other crows, starlings, and cattle egrets, averaging nearly three species per site. Shared roosts held significantly more jackdaws than jackdaw-only ones.

Proximity to towns and landfills encouraged sharing, while high elevation, wide temperature swings, and forest cover discouraged it. Some companions, such as wood pigeons, came with higher jackdaw numbers, while glossy ibises and dense starling crowds came with fewer. Jackdaws dominated numerically in over half the shared roosts, but that dominance depended on who else showed up, painting roosts as negotiated communities.
plos-pone-0347426:
Nilima Thombre and co-workers build a tablet that swells hugely in the stomach so its drug can leak out slowly where it absorbs best. The test drug treats stomach ulcers but passes through the body poorly. Their 2026 study mixes the drug into a super-porous sponge-like gel made by foaming, then tunes the recipe with a structured set of trials.

The best version released nearly all its drug and swelled to about three times its size in tests. X-ray checks in living subjects showed it floating and staying in the stomach for up to twelve hours. Checks also confirmed the drug stayed stable inside the mix. Longer stomach time could mean fewer doses and steadier relief for ulcer patients.
plos-pone-0348126:
Graham Pluck and colleagues created a quick test of vocabulary knowledge for Thai speakers. Judging stored, learned knowledge matters in brain science, but most tests are built for English. Their forty-two item task simply asks people to tell real Thai words from invented ones. Responses from six hundred sixty-two Thai speakers, collected online, were used to polish the test in the 2026 study.

Scores lined up well with verbal fluency and other Thai language measures, rose with age and education as expected, and barely budged when people retook the test, showing stability without practice effects. The authors offer it as a fast way to estimate earlier cognitive ability in Thai patients.
plos-pone-0348426:
Nayiar Shahid and co-authors checked whether a family of cancer drugs can block the cell doorways that other cancer drugs need in order to work. The blockers, called tyrosine kinase inhibitors, are often combined with older drugs built from nucleosides, the letters of DNA. Those partner drugs enter cells through dedicated transporters, and earlier hints suggested the newer drugs jam the doors.

In engineered human cells carrying one transporter each, every drug tested jammed both main transporters, and one also jammed a third. Yet the jamming happens at strengths above those reached in patients, and losing the transporters did not change how one drug affected cell survival. The authors conclude that, at normal doses, this clash is unlikely to undermine combination cancer treatment.
plos-pone-0348726:
Sri Idaiani and colleagues drew on a large household survey of more than nineteen thousand adults across Java, Indonesia, to study how hard life events relate to poor mental health. Events such as loss, illness, or losing work were scored by how much stress they usually cause, and answers were compared with standard checks for depression and anxiety symptoms.

People who had lived through moderately stressful events had about three times the odds of depression, and the link grew much stronger for the most stressful events. Similar patterns held for anxiety. Education, household wealth, and living in a town or city softened the risk somewhat. The authors say support after major life events should account for these social differences.
plos-pone-0349026:
Zekun Zhou and Shuo Yang built a giant map of medical knowledge to rank possible drugs for type two diabetes, and, crucially, to explain each suggestion in plain steps. Their graph merges five databases spanning Western and traditional Chinese medicine, holding a quarter million entities linked by millions of relationships, with genes as bridges. Four learning models read the map to predict missing links.

One model consistently handled the trickiest many-to-many links best and drove the final predictions. On top of the predictions sits an explanation engine that searches for the strongest chain of reasoning, scoring paths by length, importance, and experimental backing. The authors argue that doctors and researchers will only trust machine-suggested drugs when the machine can show its work, and they built the system to show it.
plos-pone-0349226:
Silvers and colleagues evaluated a nurse training program in northern Laos in a 2026 paper. The program runs at a children's hospital in Luang Prabang, a city in a country where many young children still die from treatable illness. The team reviewed course plans, surveyed past visiting nurse mentors, and spoke with former program leaders about the first five years.

Mentors reported that local nurses had grown stronger in hands-on care since training began. They also stressed that teaching had to fit Lao culture and daily hospital life. A train-the-trainer approach, varied teaching methods, and materials built for local needs stood out as reasons the program worked.
plos-pone-0349526:
Brennan Keiser, Stacy Shaw Welch, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for a trial bringing nurse-led pain care to rural adults with chronic pain. Rural communities carry heavy pain burdens yet often get by on medication alone, including risky opioids. The planned trial will recruit four hundred fifty adults from rural health systems and randomly assign them to usual care or to six months of virtual nurse care management.

The nurse program bundles talk therapy for pain, care coordination, and instructor-led online group exercise. The main measure is a combined score of pain intensity and how much pain interferes with life and activity, with mood, sleep, function, and opioid use also tracked. As a hybrid design, the trial will judge implementation, reach, fidelity, and staying power alongside effectiveness.
plos-pone-0349826:
Deena Fremont and co-authors pooled studies in 2026 on blood salt disturbances in people with eating disorders. Low potassium and sodium are among the medical dangers of these illnesses, and how common they are, and what harm follows, needed a single accounting.

Twenty studies covering more than twenty-five thousand people, mostly young women, were combined. Anorexia nervosa dominated the evidence. People with eating disorders had higher odds of salt abnormalities than healthy controls, and rates varied by diagnosis. Most studies looked backward at records, which limits firmness. Still, the pooled figures justify routine blood checks in eating disorder care.
plos-pone-0350026:
Wei Xiong and co-authors built a forecasting and decision system to help power companies predict what their distribution networks will cost and where money is best spent. Shifting loads and supply uncertainties strain older planning methods. Their 2026 model, named TransGrid-CostOpt, fuses deep learning with load forecasting, multi-goal optimization, and a learning-based decision module fed by several data sources.

On two public load datasets, the system beat traditional and recent rival methods, with overall performance gains the authors put between fifteen and thirty percent. Removing single modules hurt results, and the forecasting and decision parts proved most important. The authors present the framework as adaptable to fast-changing electricity markets, where cost control and reliable forecasts must advance together.
plos-pone-0350326:
Ritva Torppa and colleagues measured how well seventy-nine Finnish toddlers and preschoolers can name words from a category on demand, a skill called verbal fluency. Children had one minute to list animals or clothes while researchers counted correct words, groupings, and switches between groups. Parents also reported how much music the children made at home and in lessons.

Every part of the skill grew with age across the two-to-five span, though different parts matured at different speeds. Children with more informal music making at home, singing and playing outside formal lessons, performed better. Lessons themselves showed no such link in this small sample. The results sketch a normal path for early word retrieval and hint that everyday home music, not just training, rides along with stronger language growth.
plos-pone-0350426:
Medical residents in Syria train inside a health system strained by years of conflict. Mohammad Al-Jawad and colleagues surveyed residents across six Syrian regions in spring 2025 about burnout, using a modern assessment tool, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The questionnaire covered exhaustion, distance from patients, shrinking sense of achievement, plus job satisfaction, coping habits, and workplace problems. Burnout in doctors worldwide often passes half of those surveyed, and the authors expected Syrian rates to run high under wartime pressure. Their goal was a careful count with a sharper instrument than older studies used, so training hospitals can target the worst drivers.
plos-pone-0350626:
Su Youn Nam and Junwoo Jo followed nearly three million Korean adults to see how weight change over four years relates to later stomach cancer risk. Weight and stomach cancer have a tangled relationship that may differ by sex, age, and smoking. Their 2026 study used national health exam data from 2009 and 2013, sorting people into twenty-five weight-change paths and tracking cancer cases through 2017.

Staying in the first obesity band was tied to higher cancer risk across most groups. In contrast, men, smokers, and younger adults who gained modestly from normal weight to overweight showed slightly lower risk. Dropping from obesity to overweight lowered risk in women before menopause, while patterns after menopause differed. The authors conclude that the meaning of a weight change depends heavily on who is changing.
plos-pone-0350726:
What China's foreign ministry spokespeople say at daily briefings builds an image of China and its rivals. Feng Pan, Weixiao Li, and Tao Li analyzed a large text collection of briefing answers given during a public health crisis, in this 2026 PLOS One language study.

Spokespeople used cooperative talk to stress China's stance and joint efforts, and sharper talk to push back at criticism led by the United States. The pattern mostly fits a known framework of praising one's own side and blaming others, but it bent with circumstances. The authors trace the shifts to diplomatic beliefs, geopolitics, and traditional Chinese culture, and suggest the old framework needs a flexible update.
plos-pone-0350826:
Maha Bashri and Sameera Ahmed examine, in a 2026 study, whose voices dominate news coverage of climate change and whose get left out. They focus on reporting in American and British newspapers around COP26, the United Nations climate summit held in Glasgow, Scotland.

Their content analysis finds that politicians, scientists, and activists from wealthy northern countries receive most of the attention. Indigenous people and minority communities, who often face the worst climate harm, appear far less often. The authors connect this imbalance to power and access, and call for news coverage that includes a wider range of speakers.
plos-pone-0350926:
Sven Schwabe and Franziska Herbst mapped who provides suicide assistance in Germany, and who takes part. A court ruling in twenty twenty left the practice legal but unregulated. No official count of it exists. The team interviewed sixteen experts in twenty twenty-five. They spoke with scientists, officials, journalists, and members of right-to-die groups.

Five kinds of actors emerged from the interviews. Right-to-die organizations lead the list. Medical and lay assistants follow. Treating doctors play a part, and so do funeral directors. Relatives and friends complete the chain. The result is a whole informal system with no registry watching it. Any future law would have to govern this cast, and this study names it.
plos-pone-0351126:
Paula Barrué-García and colleagues describe a plan to build one combined nursing assessment for patients cared for at home instead of in a hospital ward. Hospital-at-home programs are growing, nurses visit only at intervals, and records there are patchy because nurses juggle many separate forms covering function, skin risk, falls, frailty, food, and sleep. Their planned instrument merges those checks into a single tool.

The study protocol lays out how the tool, named VALENF-HAD, will be assembled from existing validated measures and then tested for whether it is clear, consistent, and truly measures what it claims. No results are reported here. A single well-tested form could cut duplicated paperwork and missed risks, giving home nurses more of their visit time for the patient rather than the clipboard.
plos-pone-0351226:
China's Double World-Class program pours money into chosen university departments, and Jianqin Hang and Xing Ma asked what happens to the departments left out. Their 2026 PLOS One study used discipline-level data from Chinese universities between 2014 and 2023.

Two forces could act: reflected prestige helping neighbors, or drained resources hurting them. For Chinese-language core journals, unchosen fields published slightly less and slightly weaker work after the policy. For English-language journals, the same fields published notably more and better work. The split suggests prestige spilled over internationally while domestic resources tightened, a mixed verdict for a policy meant to lift whole universities.
plos-pone-0351626:
Shobha Islam and three colleagues build a mathematical model, published in 2026, that treats maths anxiety like a spreading infection among students. Their framework sorts students into those currently anxious and those not, then tracks how anxiety passes between them and fades over time.

The analysis finds a threshold value that decides the outcome. Below it, anxiety dies out. Above it, anxiety settles in for the long term. The system stays stable on either side of that line. Two factors push the threshold up most: how many students enter university and how fast anxiety spreads socially. The model suggests schools should focus on slowing that social spread and helping anxious students recover, rather than only drilling skills.
plos-pone-0351726:
Zhi-qiang Zhang and colleagues traced allergic rhinitis back to the bone marrow, where the white cells that drive the allergy are born. Eosinophils, the effector cells, answer to a receptor called CCR3. The team combined gene-data mining with mice engineered to lack CCR3 only in bone marrow cells, then gave the mice an allergen-driven rhinitis and tracked progenitor cells through marrow, blood, and nose.

The receptor's absence blunted the disease: fewer nasal symptoms, less tissue damage and inflammatory infiltration, and a smaller supply line of eosinophil progenitors leaving the marrow. A gene hub tied to the receptor's deletion also emerged from the data screens. Hay fever is usually treated in the nose; this study argues part of the disease is decided earlier, at the cell factory, and names a lever there.
plos-pone-0351926:
Mateus Ribeiro and co-authors describe in 2026 two new species in a small genus of stalked fungi found in northeastern Brazil. The genus is set apart by a cap like cover and a layered stalk, and naming inside it had rested mostly on looks. Specimens from a highland region were studied by shape and by three gene markers together.

Family trees placed the genus firmly apart from its close relative and grouped the two new species as sisters to a known pink species. Each new species differs from all known ones by a mix of shape and gene traits. The count of accepted species in the genus rises with the find.
plos-pone-0353126:
Pedro Fortes and colleagues explore in 2026 how people in Brazil interpret unusual experiences that stand out from everyday life, such as hearing a voice with nobody near. How such moments are judged can lead toward growth or toward distress and exclusion. One study checked and extended a question set on interpretations, and a second asked a large general sample about one experience each.

Most answers followed a smooth, single peaked pattern, suggesting shared ways of making sense across very different experiences. A fifth felt an immediate bad effect, yet about half judged the long term effect on life as positive. The authors highlight human resilience in framing the extraordinary.
plos-pone-0353726:
Mst Sumaiya Khatun and five co-authors catalogue a gene family that helps plants build lignin, in this 2026 PLOS ONE comparison of two model legumes. The CAD genes also support water-conducting tissue and defences against fungi and pests. Until now nobody had mapped the whole family across both Medicago truncatula and Lotus japonicus side by side.

The search found fifty-one such genes in the first species and thirty-five in the second, spread across several chromosomes. Their proteins share the same core building blocks, though the Lotus set looks more uniform in ancestry. Stress-response data show which family members switch on under drought and similar hardships, pointing breeders toward hardier legumes.
plos-pone-0354026:
Xiaojuan Chen and co-authors propose a lean computer method for scoring risk in the communication networks that carry power grid data. Grid operators need monthly warnings, but they often have little past data and cannot run heavy models. The new method trims weak measures, weighs the rest with a light attention step that favors measures tied to risk, and fits the score with a regression that resists overfitting.

On a year of small-sample data, the method cut average error by roughly a fifth against a standard fixed-weight approach and by a smaller margin against a heavier attention model. It also spotted key risk measures faster. Chen and colleagues present it as a practical early-warning tool that runs on modest hardware.
plos-pone-0354126:
Aekyoung Kim and co-authors argue that peak fertility raises women's interest in flashy luxury goods, and they explain the claim as a mating signal. Earlier work suggested women use luxury to set high standards and narrow the field of suitors. Kim's team proposes the opposite first step: visible luxury draws wide attention, which grows the pool of possible partners before any choosing begins.

Their account splits courtship into an attraction phase, where being noticed helps, and a selection phase, where standards filter the pool. Under this view, a fertility-linked pull toward showy goods fits both the new claim and the older findings. Kim and colleagues present the argument to sharpen debate among consumer researchers about why desire for luxury rises and falls.
plos-pone-0354526:
Yonas Abebe Tarefa and Abdul-Fatawu Abdulai map what research exists on technology-facilitated abuse of women and girls in sub-Saharan Africa, in this 2026 scoping review. Phones and social platforms have created new channels for harassment and control, yet the regional evidence had never been gathered in one place. From several hundred candidate articles across major databases, seventeen studies met their criteria.

The review identifies how technology enables abuse: anonymity for perpetrators, constant access to victims, surveillance used as coercive control, and harmful content that spreads fast and shames publicly. Victims reported psychological harm, damaged reputations, worse school performance, and obstacles to getting help, with depression among the longer-term effects. The authors say the evidence, though thin, already shows a serious problem, and they highlight how much research is still missing.
plos-pone-0354726:
Negin Kassiri and five colleagues published this 2026 study of nearly a thousand middle-aged industrial workers in Tehran, Iran. Factory noise damages hearing, and the team asked whether hearing loss also tracks with heart and blood vessel risk over the coming decade. Workers received hearing tests and standard cardiovascular risk scoring during routine occupational checkups.

Hearing loss patterns were described alongside predicted risk, and the authors kept the combined risk score out of models built from its own ingredients. Kassiri recommends weaving noise control, hearing checks, quitting support, and heart risk review into one surveillance habit.
plos-pone-0354826:
Elisabeth Bandak and colleagues outline in 2026 a ten week test of a kindergarten programme meant to bring more movement and joy in moving into daily life in Denmark. The programme was designed together with staff, leaders, and movement experts. Its parts mix formal setup, activity woven into existing routines, staff training, and inspiring materials.

Because this is a feasibility study, the focus falls on whether kindergartens can adopt the plan and whether the planned measures work. Mixed methods will check both. Findings will shape a refined version and guide a later, larger study of whether the programme truly changes children's activity.
plos-pone-0355226:
Ribal Karim and colleagues study in 2026 how stepping faster or slower than one's natural rhythm affects body and mood during walking in men and women. Healthy adults walked on a treadmill at their preferred pace and at paces a tenth faster and slower. Oxygen use, heart rate, effort ratings, and feelings were recorded across the sessions.

The fresh preferred pace used least oxygen, felt easiest, and gave the most positive mood compared with forced paces. Even a pace set from an earlier session cost more than the pace chosen that day. Women's hearts recovered faster after walking, but no other sex differences appeared in the main measures.
plos-pone-0355726:
Sho Matsushita and colleagues follow more than sixteen hundred independent older adults in Japan. They test whether a strong sense of coherence guards against losing independence or dying. Coherence means feeling that life is understandable and manageable. The trait is central to healthy aging theory, but hard outcome evidence was missing. Participants answered a short coherence scale at the start and were followed for roughly six years through care insurance and death records.

About one in thirteen participants lost independence or died during follow-up. Each step down the coherence scale raised that combined risk by about a quarter, and the death-only link looked similar in size. Matsushita and colleagues argue that supporting older adults' sense of meaning and control could be a real lever for longer independent life.
plos-pone-0355826:
Takao Arai and Hiroyasu Inoue published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on predicting which patents will be licensed. They use survival analysis, the statistics of time until an event, rather than a simple classifier. They compared old and new methods on over six hundred thousand American patents: classical regression, a plain neural network, a neural survival model, and fancier cure-rate versions assuming some patents never license.

All the deep learning approaches performed strongly, far ahead of classical regression at spotting the patents that did license. The standard neural survival model gave the best balance of simplicity and accuracy. The cure-rate extensions added almost nothing in practice, despite one statistically detectable edge, and survival framing itself beat static classification only modestly. The real gains, they conclude, come from deep learning's grip on complex patent features, not from modeling time or hidden subgroups, so users can keep the simpler model.
plos-pone-0356426:
Di Wang and seven colleagues test a simple index built from routine blood fats and sugar, in this 2026 study from a hospital in Harbin, China. They ask whether it tracks how badly the heart's arteries are narrowed. Just over eight hundred sixty patients with coronary heart disease who underwent angiography were sorted into mild, moderate, and severe narrowing using a standard scoring system. The index, which combines triglycerides and glucose, is thought to reflect insulin resistance.

Index values differed significantly between severity groups, and as a continuous measure the index was clearly associated with the extent of narrowing. After adjustment for age, sex, diabetes, and blood pressure, however, the step-by-step rise across index quartiles weakened and lost statistical significance. The authors conclude the index is positively tied to stenosis severity and may flag atherosclerosis burden, a reading best used alongside fuller clinical assessment.
plos-pone-0356726:
Phatchanat Klaihmon and colleagues examined NECTIN2, a cell-surface protein that helps cells stick together, in triple-negative breast cancer, the subtype with the fewest treatment options. Their 2026 laboratory study first checked public tumor data, then silenced the protein's gene in two aggressive breast cancer cell lines and watched how the cells behaved.

Tumors carried more NECTIN2 than healthy tissue, and patients with more of it relapsed sooner. Silencing it in the highest-expressing cell line sharply cut the cells' ability to migrate and invade, an effect partly reversed by restoring a partner protein that reshapes the cell skeleton. In the second cell line, silencing changed little. The contrast marks NECTIN2 as a candidate drug target worth testing, with effects that may depend on the tumor's makeup.
plos-pone-0357026:
Mi Ok Song and So Young Yun built a virtual reality program that trains nursing students to prevent and manage patient falls. They tested it on eighteen final-year students. Their 2026 usability study followed a standard software development cycle. It measured whether students finished the scenarios. It also measured how usable the system felt, how sick the headsets made them, and how present they felt inside the simulation.

Every student completed the program. Usability scored in the acceptable range. Motion sickness stayed mild, and the sense of being there scored high. Falls are a leading hospital harm that students rarely get to practice handling live. So a convincing simulator offers rehearsal without risk. The authors propose extending the tool to new graduate nurses.
plos-pone-0357126:
Javaria Baig led a team of eight authors asking adults how they feel about their own smiles, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How people see their teeth shapes confidence more than any clinical chart. The team ran a cross-sectional study of how adults judge the look of their own teeth, how satisfied they are with their smile, and the factors linked to both.

Baig's findings tell dentists what patients actually care about, which often differs from the clinical ideal of perfect alignment. A dentist chasing textbook symmetry may miss the one flaw that bothers the patient daily. Cosmetic dentistry is a large market, and evidence on patient priorities can steer it toward need rather than sales. The study also flags social factors that shape smile satisfaction, useful for public dental health planning.
plos-pone-0357726:
Nila Ravindran and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review in PLOS ONE on the toll caring takes in medicine: compassion fatigue, secondhand traumatic stress, and vicarious trauma among doctors. Caring for seriously ill patients can exhaust doctors emotionally, but newer work suggests the damage runs deeper, into beliefs and work identity. The team searched five databases plus an AI-assisted source for a quarter-century of literature, then analyzed qualifying studies through a theory of personhood.

From nearly nineteen thousand initial records, just over a hundred studies survived full screening. Across them, the three conditions overlapped heavily, sharing moral, cognitive, relational, and identity features that reshape what doctors believe about themselves and their work. The review maps what worsens and what softens these strains, and what help exists. Hospitals, they argue, should treat the cost of caring as an identity problem, not merely tiredness, when designing support.
plos-pone-0357826:
Azhar Al-Busaidi and three colleagues published a materials study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They worked on a way to keep sea life from fouling surfaces such as ship hulls and sensors. Their coating used tiny rods of zinc oxide laid over polymers molded with fine surface patterns.

Al-Busaidi's team tested how well the coated surfaces resisted fouling growth. The mix of nano-scale texture and the oxide's own effects kept surfaces cleaner than plain material. Coatings like this could cut the fuel ships waste dragging growth through the water, and reduce the harsh chemicals now used to scrub hulls. Marine sensors that stay clean also keep sending good data for longer.
plos-pone-0358126: van Aert and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on whether research findings hold up when repeated. They took a statistical view of what counts as a successful repeat study. Their extended analysis drew on the SCORE data set, a large record of replication attempts. Clearer yardsticks for success help science tell solid findings from lucky ones.
plos-pone-0358226:
Lucia Martina Scalise leads a team of eight testing whether CT scans can stand in for digging into cremation urns, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Ten urns from the Bronze Age cemetery of Vicofertile near Parma, Italy, were scanned whole, then carefully excavated in the laboratory so the two pictures could be compared bone by bone. Cremated remains are fragile, and scanning promises answers without destruction, but image quality is often poor and materials blur together.

Where the scan data could be read, they held up well. Age classes of the dead, the burial's disturbance history, and heat damage such as fractures matched what physical analysis later found. The authors also trialed a simple segmentation routine for mapping where remains sit inside a vessel. Their verdict is measured: virtual examination is a genuine exploratory tool for urns that cannot be opened, provided its blind spots are respected.
plos-pone-0358326:
Anna Ohlson leads a team of eight grading sewage as a COVID-19 early warning system in Sweden, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nineteen treatment plants, covering about forty-three percent of the population, reported virus levels in wastewater from mid 2023 through 2024. The team lined those curves up against officially reported cases, plant by plant, for Stockholm, and nationally, asking whether the sewage signal arrived earlier or tracked faithfully.

The tracking was faithful. Wastewater levels correlated strongly with reported cases, most tightly in Stockholm and the national aggregate. Tests of prediction showed solid accuracy, especially for ruling out rises. But the hoped for head start never appeared. Under weekly sampling and reporting, the sewage signal moved at the same time as case counts, not before them. The authors conclude wastewater earns its place as an independent mirror of circulation, valuable when clinic testing fades, rather than as a crystal ball.
plos-pone-0358426:
María Lloret Avellá and three colleagues count what it costs Spain's health system just to give leukemia drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Older patients with acute myeloid leukemia who cannot face intensive chemotherapy receive a class of drugs by vein or under the skin, meaning repeated hospital trips. An oral version exists and works equivalently. The team priced everything except the drugs themselves, from preparation to transport, catheters, and infections, using a survey of thirty professionals at sixteen hospitals.

The non drug cost per patient came to roughly ten thousand euros for the intravenous route and over twelve thousand for the under skin route. The oral route cost barely thirteen hundred, a saving of nearly ninety percent. Fewer visits drive nearly all of the gap. The authors frame the switch as an organizational relief for crowded hospitals as much as a budget saving.
plos-pone-0359326:
Stefanie Wilhelm and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a prospective multicenter study, planned in advance and run at several hospitals. The topic is rebuilding the floor of the eye socket after injury, using a material called ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene.

The outcomes tracked are patient-related, meaning results that patients themselves report, such as comfort, appearance, and daily function. Surgeons choosing implant materials need evidence about how people feel and function after surgery, not only how scans look. Eye and facial surgeons weighing this implant material are the main readers of the study.
plos-pone-0359426: Lu and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study proposing a new angle on motion sickness. They suggest a heart hormone, atrial natriuretic peptide, may ease the sickness. The proposed route runs through aldosterone, another hormone, which can raise fluid volume in the inner ear. Motion sickness blights travel and training for many people, so a hormone-based route could open new treatments.
plos-pone-0359626:
Faisal Adi Irawan, Ferry Efendi, and Praba Diyan Rachmawati published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its title gives a young person's own words of protest at being labeled a glue kid. The study shares what street-connected adolescents in Indonesia's Merauke Regency say about their use of glue.

Glue sniffing is a cheap high among homeless and street-working youth, and the label glue kid adds stigma to harm. Hearing users' own experiences shows why the habit starts and what help would be accepted. Social workers and health outreach teams in Indonesia are the readers who meet these adolescents daily.
pmc-10635526:
Tang, Chen, Huang, and co-authors introduce SRplot, a free online platform for making charts and graphs from research data. Clear pictures help readers grasp complex results in papers. Many chart tools, though, demand coding skill, charge fees, or run on only one kind of computer.

SRplot answers those limits with a free site that is meant to be easy for anyone to use. Users can build publication-ready figures without writing code. For students and labs with small budgets, that lowers a real barrier between raw data and a chart that others can read at a glance.
pmc-13397326: The team engineers shape-shifting molecules that work well together. They tune inner and outer folds. The 2026 Europe PMC paper shows the boost. It may aid drug design. Shapes drive function. Teams beat solos. Design guides drugs. The findings add useful detail for readers today.

Senescent cells are old cells that have stopped dividing. Marks of such cells show up in diseased lung tissue. In old mice, clearing these cells made lungs work better. Benjamin Callahan, Paul McMurdie, and Susan Holmes argued for a change in marker-gene analysis in 2017. Studies of microbes often group DNA reads into clusters that differ by less than a set cutoff. Those clusters, called operational taxonomic units, blur real differences between strains.

New methods can instead recover the exact DNA sequences present in a sample. Exact variants give finer detail, can be compared across studies, and carry stable labels. The authors show the older clustering step is no longer needed. Their case helped shift the field toward exact sequence methods, which are now standard in microbiome work.

For each condition, the study estimates how many people live with it, how many die from it, and how much healthy life it costs. Finland is a population isolate, shaped by a founding bottleneck long ago. Harmful variants that are rare elsewhere often survive there concentrated in a smaller number of low frequency variants, which makes them easier to find and study.

FinnGen links genetic data from hundreds of thousands of Finns with detailed health records. The article explains the resource and the discoveries that structure makes possible, including variants that point to disease mechanisms and drug targets. queste-holy-grail-comfort-1926:
The Quest of the Holy Grail is W. W. Comfort's 1926 English version of the Queste del Saint Graal. That French text formed part of the vast Vulgate cycle of Arthurian romance. Its mood is stern and monastic, quite unlike the lighter tales of Arthur's court.

Only the pure may achieve the Grail in this telling. Galahad, Perceval, and Bors ride out and, by grace, they succeed. Lancelot, the greatest knight of the world, is shut out by his sin with the queen. The quest becomes a lesson in repentance, and it changed how all later writers told the Grail story.
radin-crashing-thunder-1926:
Crashing Thunder was a Winnebago (Ho-Chunk) man who told his life story to Paul Radin, who published it in 1926. Few books of the era let a Native American speak at such length in the first person about his own life.

He tells of his upbringing, his visions, his years of drinking and violence, and his turn to the peyote religion. His story moves through the Thunderbird clan's world of spirits, feasts, and obligations. Radin kept the telling close to the man's own voice and order. The result reads like a novel but is a real life, and it opened a new kind of native autobiography.
rasa-jala-nidhi-or-ocean-of-indian-chemi: Rasa-Jala-Nidhi, or Ocean of Indian Chemistry and Alchemy, vol. 1, 1926. The Indian ocean. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
schleiermacher-soliloquies-1926:
Schleiermacher's Soliloquies, his Monologen of 1800, are a New Year gift the young thinker wrote for himself and his friends. Horace Leland Friess translated them for the Open Court edition of 1926. Friedrich Schleiermacher had just published his famous Speeches on Religion, and the Soliloquies turn the same searching mind inward.

The romantic self holds dialogue with itself on freedom, youth, aging, and the shape of a worthy life. Schleiermacher vows to stay true to his inner law against the world's pressure to conform. The prose glows with the ideals of his circle: friendship, love, and self-culture. Readers meet here the private voice of liberal theology's founder, thinking aloud.
scott-hermetica-vol-3-1926:
Walter Scott closed his Hermetica project with a third volume of notes in 1926. Commentary here covers the Latin Asclepius and the Hermetic excerpts in Stobaeus. The volume completes one of the fullest commentaries on ancient mystical writing.

The Asclepius is the famed dialogue on God, man, and Egypt's coming ruin. Stobaeus, a later collector, preserved Hermetic scraps found nowhere else. Scott walks through every hard line and links pieces to the wider tradition. His notes connect philosophy, religion, and magic in late antiquity. Together the three volumes gave English readers a complete Hermetic library with guidance.
smuts-holism-evolution-1926:
Holism and Evolution, published in 1926, is Jan Christiaan Smuts's philosophy of wholes. Smuts, the South African soldier-statesman, coined the word holism here for his claim that nature builds ever richer wholes, and that this building is evolution's deepest fact.

From matter to life to mind to personality, each level is a whole more than the sum of its parts, and mechanism cannot exhaust it. Smuts writes as a field naturalist and a statesman, not a laboratory man. The book influenced ecology and systems thought far beyond philosophy. Its vision of wholes remains its author's most original legacy.
spengler-decline-west-vol-1-1926:
Oswald Spengler's The Decline of the West, Volume 1, appears in Charles Francis Atkinson's translation of 1926. Subtitled Form and Actuality, the volume states Spengler's bold scheme. Cultures, he argues, are organisms that pass through birth, growth, maturity, and decay. Each has its own soul and its own mathematics, art, and science.

The West, in his reading, has entered its late, hard phase of civilization. Spengler compares cultures side by side in vast tables of parallel ages. Critics call the method prophetic rather than scientific. The book was the most debated philosophy of history of its century. Atkinson's version carried the debate into English.
summers-history-witchcraft-1926:
Montague Summers was a Catholic priest and a firm foe of witchcraft. His History of Witchcraft and Demonology came out in 1926. Summers held, as few of his day did, that the witch cult was real. His book tells the tale with vast stores of fact.

Pacts with the Devil, sabbats, and spells fill the early parts. The great trials of Europe and the New World take up the rest. Summers cites trial rolls, old tracts, and church law in bulk. The book is a mine of tales, read best with a keen eye on its slant.
swift-gullivers-travels-1726:
Jonathan Swift published Gulliver's Travels in 1726, in the first edition text used here. The full title sends Gulliver into several remote nations of the world. Readers took it first as a true travel tale, then as fierce satire.

Gulliver visits Lilliput, where men are six inches tall and wars turn on eggs. In Brobdingnag he is tiny, and a huge king scorns England's pride and guns. Later trips reach a flying island and the wise horse Houyhnhnms and brutish Yahoos. Man looks worse at each stop, and pride takes the hardest knocks of all. Swift's prose stays cool while the charges grow more and more savage.
tawney-religion-capitalism-1926:
R. H. Tawney published Religion and the Rise of Capitalism in 1926, a classic of economic history. Tawney, an English historian and socialist, studies how Christian teaching met the new market world. Medieval bans on usury gave way as commerce grew. Puritan teaching, he argues, could both discipline greed and bless success.

The book is often called the English answer to Weber's Protestant ethic. Tawney writes with moral force and fine irony. He mourns a lost age when faith set limits on acquisition. His closing plea joins economics to ethics. The work remains a humane, learned critique of acquisitive society. It shaped British social thought for decades.
tilden-toxemia-explained-1926:
John Henry Tilden blamed nearly all illness on one cause, and Toxemia Explained of 1926 states his case in full. Tilden, a Denver doctor who had turned against drug prescribing, taught that waste the body fails to clear poisons the blood. That state, toxemia, then shows itself as many different diseases.

Rest, fasting, and right living form his cure, since drugs only mask the warning signs. Tilden walks readers through digestion, habits, and the slow build-up of enervation, his word for drained nerve energy. The book became a classic of natural hygiene, and its plain, stern advice still finds readers.

He loves a good ghost story too much to be dull, and knows stagecraft too well to be fooled. Edwin Arnold published The Light of Asia in 1879, an epic poem telling the Buddha's life in Miltonic blank verse. Spinoza had been excommunicated from Amsterdam's Jewish community and published nothing under his name during his life; the Ethics appeared after his death. Waite prints rites of evocation and pact in detail, then judges them with a scholar-magician's dry scorn. His critical sorting shaped how the next century read the whole grimoire shelf. Verified from the 1919 edition, the book remains a sharp, skeptical guide through magic's darkest library.
toland-celtic-religion-druids-1726:
John Toland was an Irish free thinker. He wrote this study of Celtic faith and learning late in life, and it came out in 1726, after his death. The text here is from the 1815 printing. Toland was known for bold views on faith and church power.

He treated the druids as men of their time, not as priests of dark rites. With a cool eye he sifted old Greek and Roman reports from Welsh and Irish lore. His book was the first clear, sharp account of the druids in the age of reason.
tombazi-photographic-expedition-kangchen:
Nicholas Tombazi took a camera to the glaciers of Kangchenjunga and came back with a tale for the ages. His Account of a Photographic Expedition to the Southern Glaciers appeared in 1926. In it he tells what he saw on the Sikkim side in 1925.

At 15,500 feet he watched a wild man, as he took it, moving on the slope below him. He tells of the form, the gait, and the measured footprints left in the snow. His is the most detailed early yeti report from a trained observer. The book anchors the whole shelf of yeti lore.
twelfth-night-pg1526: Shipwrecked Viola serves her master Orsino disguised as a boy while secretly loving him, in this edition of Shakespeare's most perfect comedy. un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 26, from the first session in 1946, is a brief founding order. Bosnia's peace deal had just been initialed when the Council met in November 1995. On 30 November 1995 it extended UNPROFOR until 31 January 1996. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed on the peace process. His reports would carry facts and advice on carrying out the deal. The short extension bridged an awkward gap. A NATO-led force was about to take over the military task. UNPROFOR's troubled three years were nearly over.
un-sc-res-126:

The Council asked both governments to make no statements and take no steps that could worsen the situation. Each was to urge calm on its own people so that talks could go forward. The United Nations Representative for India and Pakistan was asked to propose further action to the parties. He was authorized to visit the subcontinent for that purpose. He had to report on his efforts as soon as possible. Demilitarization remained a key step toward any settlement.
un-sc-res-1526:
Terrorism financing is the battleground of Resolution 1526, adopted in January 2004. It tightened the sanctions system aimed at Al-Qaida and the Taliban, which listed people and groups whose money had to be frozen. A new team of experts was created to watch how states complied.

The text sharpens the list's rules, presses states to act against listed names at home, and gives the monitoring team a wider reach. Sanctions texts like this one run quietly in the background of counterterrorism for years. This one shows the machinery being rebuilt after early lists proved patchy and uneven.
un-sc-res-1626:

The Council extended UNMIL's mandate for six months. Liberian parties were called to show full commitment to a democratic process free of violence. With troop contributors' consent, UNMIL could help guard the Special Court for Sierra Leone's premises once UNAMSIL left. A temporary rise in the mission's personnel ceiling was authorized to cover the elections. Extra staff would secure the vote and the weeks around it. un-sc-res-1726:

Elections had been delayed again that autumn.

The brief term covered the year-end while a new plan was weighed. An African Union backed roadmap had set fresh deadlines weeks earlier. The mission's troops held the zone between government and rebel areas. The Council stayed actively seized of the matter. A longer renewal with a revised mandate followed in January.
un-sc-res-1826:
Côte d'Ivoire returns in United Nations Security Council Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou peace deal was slowly taking hold. A first round of presidential elections was set for 30 November 2008. Rights abuses, including sexual violence, still scarred daily life.

un-sc-res-326: The official series of Council decisions runs through Resolution 326, catalogued here for 1970. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-426:
One day after the Council created UNIFIL on paper, it gave the new force its legal shape. Resolution 425 had ordered Israel's withdrawal from southern Lebanon and called for a United Nations force there. The Secretary-General reported on 19 March 1978 on how to carry that order out. Resolution 426 was adopted the same day.

The Council approved the Secretary-General's report in full. It decided that the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon would be established on the terms set out in that report. The force was set up for an initial period of six months. After that, it would continue in operation if required, provided the Council so decided. The short text is the founding decision for UNIFIL. The force it created in March 1978 is still the basis of the United Nations presence in southern Lebanon.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Peace came to Bosnia on paper in November 1995. The Dayton talks had birthed a pact. The sides first signed their names to it on 21 November in Ohio. A formal rite would come later. UNPROFOR, the much-tried force in Bosnia, still held the field. Resolution 1026 passed with no dissent on 30 November 1995.

The force's term stretched to 31 January 1996, and no more by this grant. The pause let the Council plan the handover. The chief had to send word fast on how the pact would shift tasks. His report of 23 November fed the choice. The goal was a clean pass of the baton, as the pact set out. The force won warm praise for its hard years of work.

Kashmir's stalled settlement is the subject of Resolution 126, adopted on 2 December 1957 by ten votes to none with one Soviet abstention. A Swedish envoy, Gunnar Jarring, had traveled to India and Pakistan for the Council that spring and reported on his mission. Both governments still accepted the older UN plan: Kashmir's future decided by a free and impartial vote of its people.

The Council thanked Jarring for his careful work. It noted with concern that his report showed no real progress toward a settlement. Demilitarization of the state featured in the text as one of the steps on the way. The resolution kept the plebiscite framework formally alive even as the two countries' positions hardened into the pattern that still defines the dispute.

Belgrade's fresh start at the UN ran through this line of 2000. On 31 October, the Council adopted Resolution 1326 without a vote. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was now just Serbia and Montenegro. A decade of wars had shrunk it. Its president had fallen that same month. The state applied as a new member, not as heir to the old seat.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit it. The Assembly seated it the next day. The step settled a long legal fight in quiet fashion. The old federation's membership had passed to no heir on its own. Belgrade accepted a clean slate, and the world body moved on.

Switzerland, the great holdout, joined the UN by way of this line. On 24 July 2002, the Council adopted Resolution 1426 without dissent. It met twice in one day to do so. Swiss voters had backed joining in a national vote that March. Decades of strict neutrality had kept the country out until then.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit the Swiss Confederation. The Assembly seated it that September. The arrival closed the largest gap in the UN's claim to speak for all states. Switzerland kept its lasting neutrality all the same. It also kept its role as host of the UN's Geneva hub.

Sanctions on Al-Qaida and the Taliban are strengthened on 30 January 2004. The measures — asset freezes, travel bans, and an arms embargo on listed people and groups — dated from earlier resolutions. States, the Council found, needed clearer duties and better help in applying them.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sharpened how the measures should be carried out and widened the sanctions committee's role in watching over them. A stronger monitoring arrangement is set up to help the committee track compliance and breaches. States are pressed to enforce the freeze and bans fully against everyone on the committee's list, and to report on the steps they have taken.

Resolution 1626, adopted on 19 September 2005, links Liberia's elections to safety for the Special Court for Sierra Leone. Liberia was preparing for October presidential and legislative votes, state authority was spreading, and a new economic management program had been signed. Next door, the UN Mission in Sierra Leone was due to end on 31 December 2005, leaving the court without its guard force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the UN Mission in Liberia, UNMIL, until 31 March 2006. It lets UNMIL send up to 250 soldiers to Sierra Leone from November 2005 to guard the Special Court, with a matching short-term rise in UNMIL's ceiling. It also lets UNMIL rush more troops in to pull those guards and court staff out if a grave safety crisis hits. A drawdown plan for UNMIL is requested for March 2006.

A short extension for a peacekeeping operation in crisis is what Resolution 1726 delivers. Adopted on 15 December 2006, it concerns Côte d'Ivoire, where a civil conflict had split the country and stalled elections. The Council voiced serious worry about worsening conditions and the suffering and displacement of civilians.

Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council extended the mandates of UNOCI, the UN operation there, and of the French forces backing it, but only until 10 January 2007. That brief window, less than a month, shows the Council buying time while a political deal remained out of reach. It also kept the matter under active review.

Côte d'Ivoire's long-delayed presidential election anchors Resolution 1826, adopted on 29 July 2008. The Ouagadougou Political Agreement of March 2007 had set a peace path, and the first round of voting was set for 30 November 2008. Voter identification and registration still lagged, militias had not fully disarmed, and rights abuses, including sexual violence, continued despite general improvement.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI, and the French forces supporting it until 31 January 2009, above all to back free and fair elections. UNOCI must help deliver security for the vote and logistics for the electoral commission. The Council urges faster progress on identification, disarmament, and restoring state authority nationwide. It will review the mandate and troop levels by January 2009, with a report three weeks before that includes benchmarks for a possible phased drawdown.

A judge from the United States chose to step down in 2010. Thomas Buergenthal had sat on the world court for a decade. His term still had time to run. Word of his choice reached the Council that spring. He would leave on 6 September 2010. Resolution 1926 passed on 2 June 2010.

The poll to fill his seat was set for 9 September 2010. Voters in the Council and the Assembly's sixty-fourth session would cast at the same hour. That joint poll is how court judges are always picked. The new judge would serve just the rest of the old term. Buergenthal had fled Nazi camps as a boy. He grew to shape world human rights law. The text marks his exit with the court's plain, set form.

Talks on reuniting Cyprus were moving into a more intensive phase at the end of 2011. Resolution 2026, adopted on 14 December 2011, concerns UNFICYP, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were negotiating a settlement. The aim was a federation with two zones and two communities. Cyprus's government had agreed that the force should stay.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate until 19 July 2012. It urged both leaders to speed up the talks. The core issues had to be settled before a planned meeting in January 2012. The text also pressed for steps that build trust. More crossing points on the Green Line were one example. Renewed mine clearing in the buffer zone was another.

Mercenaries in Congo drew the Council's fire in the fall of 1966. Congo's envoy said Angola was their base. Angola was then ruled by Portugal. Lisbon's man swore no such camps stood there. Both tales were heard at the 1306th meeting. Resolution 226 passed with no dissent on 14 October 1966. The same day, Botswana won its seat vote.

Portugal was urged, on its own sworn word, to bar the use of Angola. No armed bands could train there to meddle in Congo's affairs. All states were told to keep out of Congo's home fights. The chief had to watch how the call was heeded. Congo's tale had a long tail: this text fed the chain of bans that the 1967 mercenary text would build on.

How judges of the International Court of Justice are elected is the only subject of Resolution 26, adopted unanimously on 4 June 1947. The General Assembly had adopted a rule for its election meetings the year before. Under that rule, a meeting continues until candidates win an absolute majority of votes for all the seats to be filled. The Council agreed to the Assembly's rule. It then adopted the same rule for its own election meetings. The resolution was sent to the General Assembly for its information.

Zambia complained in early 1973 about attacks by the illegal regime in Southern Rhodesia. Zambia said the Rhodesian actions included an economic blockade and military threats. South African forces were working with the regime, Zambia charged. The actions were hurting Zambia's security and its economy. Resolution 326 was adopted on 2 February 1973.

The Council condemned every act of provocation and harassment against Zambia. It also condemned repression inside Rhodesia, including recent collective punishments. South Africa's military and armed forces had to withdraw at once and in full. They were to leave Southern Rhodesia and the border with Zambia. Britain, as the ruling power, was told to make sure that happened. Britain also had to bring the illegal regime's actions to an end.

Southern Lebanon gained a UN force in the spring of 1978. On 19 March, the Council adopted Resolution 426. Twelve members voted yes, none voted no, and two held back. China took no part in the vote. Days before, Resolution 425 had demanded that Israel pull out of the south.

The text backs the Secretary-General's report on how the force would work. It sets up the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon for six months at first. The Council could renew it later if need be. The force, known as UNIFIL, had three tasks. It would confirm the Israeli pull-out, restore peace, and help Beirut regain control of the south.
whitehead-religion-making-1926:
Alfred North Whitehead published Religion in the Making in 1926, based on his Lowell Lectures. Whitehead treats religion as a human response to a vision of truth. He traces religion from tribal rites and ritual to more rational, universal forms. Solitude, he argues, stands at the heart of mature faith.

He asks how religion can stay honest in an age of science. Dogmas, he says, are formulas that point beyond themselves and must not harden. The book became a source text for process theology. Whitehead links God to the lure toward value in the world. It is a brief, humane work of religious philosophy.
widger-s-quotations-from-the-project-gut: David Widger gathers choice quotations from a Project Gutenberg text. The best lines are set out here for browsing at leisure. Wit and wisdom come in small, pleasing doses. A reader's companion to a classic work.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol26:
The Journal of Discourses closes with Volume XXVI, printed at Liverpool in 1886 after more than thirty years. Twenty-six volumes hold sermons from 1854 onward, the longest such record of the Latter-day Saint movement ever made. Brigham Young's generation and its heirs speak across the whole run, caught in shorthand and fixed in print.

The final volume keeps the familiar form: doctrine, counsel, and defense from the senior elders of the church. With it, an archive ends that historians of American religion use daily, since nothing else preserves a faith's pulpit so fully. The set stands complete, a church's own voice across three decades.
